Sports.title: Some of the elites criticising Gianni Infantino are sheer hypocrites. How can the money-obsessed leeches behind the Super League expect us to listen to their confected moral outrage as they bleed our beloved game dry, writes IAN HERBERT
Sports.content:
Some of the elites criticising Gianni Infantino are sheer hypocrites. How can the money-obsessed leeches behind the Super League expect us to listen to their confected moral outrage as they bleed our beloved game dry, writes IAN HERBERT

Unlock more of the best of our football coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

The most preposterous man in football is staggering on, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself, so perhaps that’s why the biggest hypocrites of another dark week for football appear to have got away with it.

On Sunday, Real Madrid decided to weigh in on the Gianni Infantino scandal, instructing their media people to put out a sanctimonious statement welcoming the scrapping of the egghead’s plans to sell off a slice of the World Cup, and thanking UEFA for fulfilling their ‘duty’ to ‘protect football’.

You really could not make some of this stuff up. Yes, that moralising really did come from the same Real Madrid whose avarice stank football out when they led the contemptible group of 12 clubs who attempted the European Super League breakaway coup, a few years back.

Infantino’s intellectual and moral decrepitude may have been there for us all to see in his email offering nations a small cash consideration if they back his plans to raise $20billion, but have we forgotten the European club men with whiteboards and coloured marker pens, explaining their own despicable little earner in 2021?

Real’s executives back then were just as atrocious as Infantino is now – worse, in fact, given that the FIFA scheme was not actually a breakaway proposal designed to leave the have-nots behind – while the money men they indirectly inveighed against on Sunday are the one and the same suits from JPMorgan Chase, hired by them to advise on the Super League.

Given that the US finance house were forced to apologise for their part in that episode, you might have fancied they’d learned their lesson about how ferocious the backlash to a sell-out like this would be. No. They just couldn’t resist getting their snouts in the football trough again.

Gianni Infantino is somehow staggering on as FIFA President, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself

But many of his critics do not have a leg to stand on. These are clubs that tried to form the breakaway European Super League - and only buckled after immense fan pressure (pictured)

So, please let’s get this right. The new flank in football's civil war is not between the idealists and the profiteers, but between competing profiteers fighting over who gets to cash in on the game.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin, are currently casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions, protectors of the meritocracy, guardians of the fans against billionaire opportunists. Yet this is the self-same organisation which expanded the Champions League into a sprawling competition with 64 extra fixtures in 2024, to create greater TV income and more sponsorship revenue.

The self-same organisation which has been engaged in a pitched battle for territory with FIFA. That fight has spawned the Nations League and the expanded Club World Cup, with each governing body viewing the other’s new tournament with deep suspicion. UEFA’s objection is not to football becoming more commercial but to someone else collecting the commercial rewards.

Our own Premier League claim a moral high ground for themselves, too, proclaiming to be the world's greatest and most unpredictable domestic competition, while generating more money than any such league in history. Yet it is driven by the same monopolistic greed, behaving as though sharing a fraction of the wealth with the rest of the football pyramid would be an act of unconscionable sacrifice.

Don’t let it be forgotten that its biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020. Or that the Premier League held talks with CVC Capital Partners, one of the world's largest private equity firms, about selling a stake in future broadcasting and commercial revenues, at the same time.

That came to nothing, either, but here was an elite equally willing to explore new ways of extracting financial value from our game. The people’s game.

Whenever the redistribution of Premier League wealth is discussed, we witness the language and narrative suddenly change and those overseeing the competition which has negotiated television contracts worth billions begin to fret about the pennies.

It was clear when a White Paper on football governance was published a few years back that a greater flow of money down from the Premier League would be egregiously hard to extract.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin (right), are casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions. Yet they expanded and distorted the Champions League to generate more revenue

It shouldn't be forgotten that the Premier League's biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020

The gilded elite division continued to maintain the fallacy that they were helping the rest, when 70 per cent of the money they sent down below was Championship parachute money. An insurance policy for the division’s own members laughably dressed up as ‘solidarity payments’.

It has taken Government intervention to force a more equitable share of the Premier League’s wealth throughout the game, in the shape of the Independent Football Regulator, with its ‘backstop’ power to force a settlement if none is agreed.

Faced with such a prospect, the Premier League have finally just voted for an additional £1.5billion from those in the gilded cage, to be shared with the EFL’s clubs, though even that is not allocated yet. The cash, to be funded by a two per cent lift in the transfer levy on all top-flight deals, will clearly need to be crowbarred from clubs swimming in wealth, given the opposition led by Manchester City’s petro-dollar billionaire owners – another of the merry little European Super League band.

We understand other members of the so-called ‘Big Six’ are also unhappy that they may now find themselves coughing up more than less elevated Premier League clubs. It’s been left to the more moderately wealthy members of the division, who faced down the big clubs over the Super League, to challenge them again.

If there was one positive to come out of the Super League scandal, it was the way it cut the grasping, spiritually remote 'Big Six' down to size. 'It's like emerging from a slightly abusive relationship,' the owner of one of the smaller Premier League clubs told me at the time.

This weekend, the FA Cup begins its beautiful seasonal arc once more, carrying the customary thrill and sense of pride among all who will compete in its extra preliminary round. North Ferriby, at home to St Helens, Northwich Victoria, playing away to Beverley Town, and Nelson, entertaining Stockport Georgians, are just three of those taking part who know what a precarious financial reality and existential threat look and feel like.

For all the weekend’s 438 competing clubs, reaching the first round proper – six ties away, in November – would be monumental, with £47,750 prize money for those who win at that stage.

But any who progress that far will also experience the chill of strictures forced down from the top of the game. This will be the second season with no replays from the first round proper onwards – a diminishment the FA said was necessary because of increasing pressure on the calendar, particularly following UEFA's expansion of their club competitions.

The early rounds of the FA Cup still bring with them a sense of thrill and pride - though replays with England's top clubs are now sadly a thing of the past

Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go

Critics, especially in the EFL and non-League, have argued that a vital source of income is being removed from smaller clubs, who can no longer earn lucrative replay gates against bigger opponents.

But those little people are shouting in the dark. The abolition of replays, fourth-round matches spread over five days and the scheduling of the 2027 final before the Premier League campaign finishes, rather than as the climax to the season, belong to the story of the competition’s devaluation and diminishment. The Cup has been crushed into virtual irrelevance by football's high and mighty.

As of last night, Infantino’s brazen conceit and vanity were keeping him in a job which any intelligent and self-respecting industry would by now have forced him from. He is no doubt banking on the relentless news cycle moving on and UEFA’s threat to boycott FIFA’s competition receding into the distance.

Qualification games for the 2030 World Cup are just a year away and Infantino can safely calculate that national associations will not want to take the financial hit that a boycott would carry. It seems significant, and concerning, that a mere 11 national associations, including England and Wales, have voiced opposition to him remaining in post.

Yet for all the sound and fury, there is something deeply unsettling and incomplete about some of this moralising. Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go. He is the most despicable emblem of a game which is slowly devouring itself, but by no means the only one.

Sports.title: Inside Sir Ben Ainslie's mission to finally end Britain's wait for America's Cup glory: How history - and a secret weapon - are inspiring Olympic legend's team in Naples
Sports.content:
Inside Sir Ben Ainslie's mission to finally end Britain's wait for America's Cup glory: How history - and a secret weapon - are inspiring Olympic legend's team in Naples

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

A couple of notable letters crop up on the wall. They are correspondence from Lord Nelson and nestle among the high-value art in the Royal Yacht Squadron ‘Castle’, in Cowes, Isle of Wight.

The handwriting looked fine to me, a nice round hand.

Said James, steward of the place, where he has worked, other than for a brief spell elsewhere, since he was 16, with a degree of understatement: ‘There is a reason it is not quite as legible as it might have been.

‘By this stage, the Admiral was no longer able to write with his stronger arm.’

So, we are at the very citadel of sailing, a place built with eight-feet deeper walls on the land side than on the waterfront. ‘The French would have known better than to have approached us by sea,’ was the thrust of James’s non-negotiable reasoning.

He was wearing a black tie. All staff and some 540 members of the Royal Yacht Squadron wear the same neckwear along with their dark blazers. They are in mourning.

Sir Ben Ainslie is looking to help end Britain's long wait for America's Cup glory

For it is merely 200 years since Admiral Nelson left us, aged 47, aboard Britain’s flagship HMS Victory, shot by a French sniper during the Battle of Trafalgar off the coast of Spain. Dead but victorious.

Which sort of brings us to today, and Sir Ben Ainslie’s attempt, now as team boss rather than helmsman, to win the technology-led, F1-on-water America’s Cup, the oldest international sports competition in the world dating back to 1851, when it is next held in Naples next year. We have famously never won it.

Ainslie was made an honorary member of the Squadron (you can’t apply, chaps or chapesses), under whose banner the British attempt fights, soon after winning his fourth Olympic Gold medal at London 2012, before being elevated to full membership three years ago.

There is a major departure in his latest attempt, however, in the male-dominated Royal Yacht Squadron. Jemima Lines, 29, a kitefoiler and adventurer, is enlisted to become a participating member of the on-board team of five, and thus the first woman to participate in the Cup since aviation pioneer Sir Thomas Sopwith’s wife Phyllis in 1934 and 1937.

Lines was given the role for her exceptional background, one entirely in keeping with the traditions of the event. For one thing, she is the fourth daughter of a special forces soldier, born in Kent and educated at Bristol University as an engineer. Her father was Ralph Crathorne, who died earlier this year, aged 67, in a mountaineering accident in Scotland.

‘I owe so much to him and how I see everything in life,’ she said during Cowes Week, only a few weeks after getting married. ‘Everything I have achieved is down to his influence. He wanted us to explore everything in the world, and I am pleased to be doing this as a result.

‘We’d often be late for school because my father had taken us all to the beach and we’d be kiting, that was from the age of eight, and he always wanted us to do bigger adventures. This is the biggest change I have ever made, to be involved in the America’s Cup.’

Ainslie, as ever, had a busy week in Cowes, being his sport’s most celebrated figure. A day earlier he had welcomed Anne, Princess Royal, as the new Admiral of the Yacht Squadron, in succession to her father, the late Duke of Edinburgh. She is a loyal supporter of the old cause.

Ainslie's wife Georgie (left) is his stalwart supporter in his ambition, now as team boss

Ainslie is now sipping a restorative drink and eating sandwiches on the Royal Yacht Squadron terrace after sailing competitively for the first time since the last America’s Cup in Barcelona a couple of years ago. He is doing his best to pretend it is not the case, but his 49-year-old body has been given a decent examination out on the water.

He is off next to the annual Squadron Ball later, along with wife Georgie (née Thompson), previously of Sky Sports News, his stalwart supporter.

Sitting close to where the America’s Cup began under the gaze of Queen Victoria, Ainslie said: ‘I’m confident we can win the Cup in the end. You know how it is with our maritime history. We have to do it.’

Handwriting, good, bad or indifferent, it is a story that would earn its place on the Castle wall.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino's 'alleged mistress received six-figure pay-off from UEFA following affair while he was in senior position' - as FIFA president faces mounting calls to quit
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino's 'alleged mistress received six-figure pay-off from UEFA following affair while he was in senior position' - as FIFA president faces mounting calls to quit

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The pressure on Gianni Infantino to resign as FIFA president has grown after it emerged UEFA paid off his alleged mistress during his time with the European governing body.

The Telegraph reported the woman received a six-figure sum following an alleged affair with Infantino when he was UEFA general secretary.

It is claimed the junior employee was promoted by Infantino and given a 30 per cent pay rise at the time of their relationship. UEFA's then president, Michel Platini, was reportedly aware and raised concerns with Infantino.

The organisation decided she would depart her role with a substantial sum, paid for by UEFA, which also covered the costs for her to do an MBA course at a business school worth £45,000 per year.

UEFA confirmed the payment and its awareness of the relationship between Infantino and the woman in a statement to The Telegraph.

Infantino has been married to Leena Al Ashqar since 2001 and the couple have four daughters.

UEFA paid off a female employee who had an alleged affair with Gianni Infantino during his time at the organisation

Infantino is under pressure to quit following his failed FIFA Forward Enterprise scheme

'We are aware of the allegations and can confirm a departure payment was made to the individual in question, coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school,' UEFA said. 'The payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time.

'Such regulations have been tightened since 2016 and the current staff regulations – which apply to all UEFA employees at whatever level – reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation.'

The Telegraph also reported there had been complaints about Infantino's behaviour at FIFA, claims strenuously denied by football's worldwide governing body.

Infantino became UEFA secretary general – a position second only to the presidency in terms of power – in 2009. He started in 2000 as a lawyer before working his way up in the organisation.

The now 56-year-old was elected FIFA president in 2016 following the downfall of Sepp Blatter. He was re-elected in 2019 and 2023, and had been expected to secure a fourth term in March.

The revelations cast further doubt on Infantino's position at FIFA with the Swiss-Italian facing widespread calls to quit after he was forced to abandon a widely condemned plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

UEFA are leading the charge to dethrone Infantino as FIFA president in response to the scrapped proposal, pledging to boycott any FIFA tournaments so long as he remains in the role.

But he appears to retain support from Africa, South America and Asia – which is enough to fend off any leadership challenge ahead of the election, scheduled to take place at the FIFA congress in Morocco in March.

Mexico this week broke ranks from CONCACAF's opposition to Infantino, reaffirming their confidence in the FIFA leadership.

UEFA's current refusal to play in FIFA competitions will cause the governing body significant commercial problems, potentially prompting Infantino to reconsider his position at the top of world football.

But the FIFA president has shown no sign of relenting thus far after being supported by the governing body's hierarchy following crisis talks on Wednesday, vowing to fight on despite demands he resign.

Infantino is facing a possible investigation after Norwegian FA president Lise Klaveness said she would report him to FIFA's Ethics Committee.

The complaint will not only challenge the proposed sale of a £3.1billion stake in the World Cup to private investors, but also the decision to award an ad hoc FIFA Peace Prize to President Donald Trump and the suspension of Folarin Balogun's red card at the World Cup following alleged political pressure from Trump.

Sports.title: British tennis bans transgender women from ALL competitive female matches - including internal club competitions - after World No 1 Aryna Sabalenka backed sport's new mandatory sex testing
Sports.content:
British tennis bans transgender women from ALL competitive female matches - including internal club competitions - after World No 1 Aryna Sabalenka backed sport's new mandatory sex testing

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The Lawn Tennis Association has banned transgender women from competing in any female matches, including internal club competitions.

It comes after the Women's Tennis Association introduced new transgender eligibility rules, backed by world No1 Aryna Sabalenka, which implemented genetic testing in a bid to establish players' eligibility to compete as a female.

Rules were already in place that transgender women could not compete in county, regional and inter-club matches, but clubs were able to use their own policies to decide if competition was allowed in internal matches and competitions.

Those rules have now changed, however, following new laws issued by the Equalities and Human Rights Commission this week.

Said laws moved in line with the Supreme Court ruling that 'sex is binary', with the LTA feeling it had no choice but to expand its regulations.

The WTA's previous policy, meanwhile, permitted biological males to compete in the women's category if they maintained testosterone levels below a certain level.

The Lawn Tennis Association has banned transgender women from competing in any female matches - pictured: Wimbledon finalists Linda Noskova (left) and Karolina Muchova (right)

But now a tweak to the rules states that WTA players must undergo a sex screening for the SRY gene, which is found on the Y chromosome and is typically involved in male sex development.

Only once they have passed the test – which is completed through a simple cheek swab, blood test or saliva sample – will players be eligible to compete on the female-only WTA Tour.

A positive test, meanwhile, will spark further medical assessment before a player is cleared to play against their female rivals. Players must also sign documentation acknowledging that refusal to be tested could result in disciplinary action.

Speaking about the move, world No1 Sabalenka was in favour of the changes and said she would have no hesitation in undergoing the testing herself.

'It's very important to maintain fairness in our circuit,' the 28-year-old said.

'It's obvious that, biologically, men are much stronger than women, so it wouldn't seem fair to me for a woman to compete against a biological man.

'I think it took them a while to make this decision and, yes, I support it.

'But I'm concentrating on myself, on my goals, on whatever it takes. If you want to test us all, I will gladly do so, it's pretty fair, and let's keep it that way.'

World No 1 Aryna Sabalenka had backed the Women's Tennis Association's new transgender eligibility rules

There have been next to no controversies involving non-binary athletes in tennis or padel – which is also covered by the Lawn Tennis Association - though last December Sabalenka competed in a 'Battle of the Sexes' match with Nick Kyrgios which she lost 6-3, 6-3 in Dubai. That exhibition drew much criticism, with many brandishing it as a publicity stunt that risked trivialising the women's game.

Other organisations, such as World Boxing and World Athletics, have already implemented similar testing for their athletes seeking to compete in the women's category.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has also confirmed it will sex test athletes ahead of the next Olympic Games, which will be held in Los Angeles in 2028.

In its original guidance from 2024, the LTA stated: 'It is clear that tennis and padel are gender-affected sports – the average man has an advantage when playing against the average woman.

'This includes longer levers with which to reach and hit the ball and increased cardio-vascular capacity means being able to get around the court more easily'.

Sports.title: Named: The seven Premier League youngsters who have shone in pre-season and could stake a claim to feature in the first-team
Sports.content:
Named: The seven Premier League youngsters who have shone in pre-season and could stake a claim to feature in the first-team

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

As the Premier League season curtain-raiser on August 21 draws closer, there is an onus to reflect on pre-season performances with several youngsters staking their claim for first team minutes.

A number of young talents have caught the eye of supporters, showing off their skills with several having been given the chance during tours across the globe.

Daily Mail Sport runs the rule over the youngsters who have staked the greatest claim to earn Premier League minutes and who they would have to leapfrog to claim these opportunities.

Brian Madjo (Aston Villa)

First on this list is Aston Villa’s Brian Madjo, who recently made headlines after being cleared to play in this upcoming season.

Aston Villa were successful in their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, with the 17-year-old having initially been blocked from playing for the club owing to FIFA rules around the international transfer for minors.

Madjo was born in London but the issue of his eligibility had arisen due to him being raised in Luxembourg, whom he made three international appearances for before switching nationality.

The teenager joined the club from Metz in January for £10million, a price that initially raised eyebrows across the league, but he is already pushing for first team opportunities with his displays.

Madjo, towering at 6ft 4in, has scored four goals in pre-season and is already drawing comparisons to Romelu Lukaku.

England international Ollie Watkins has had an extended break following the World Cup and Tammy Abraham is returning from a shoulder issue. This combined with Champions League football and departures of Morgan Rogers and Jadon Sancho gives Madjo, and Villa fans, hope of him becoming a regular contributor.

Nearly three years after Emery handed a 19-year-old Jhon Durán his debut, another teenage forward seems destined for minutes.

Brian Madjo has been cleared to play for Aston Villa after a Court of Arbitration for Sport decision

The 17-year-old, who cost Aston Villa £10m, scored in Aston Villa's pre-season win at Walsall

Dastan Satpaev (Chelsea)

Dastan Satpaev, a Kazakh forward, is doing the rounds on social media after his coolly struck finish capped off a wonderful team goal just seven minutes into Chelsea's game against Western Sydney Wanderers in Australia.

The post has over one million likes and has catapulted the 17-year-old into the spotlight. The post has also led to debate over which is Satpaev’s dominant foot as the winger is so gifted with both.

New Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso praised the youngster after the game, saying: ‘He is really strong, really quick, you will be really impressed with him.’

The biggest obstacle for Satpaev is Chelsea’s squad size, with 40 other players and a wealth of attacking talent proving a tall task to overcome.

However, the winger will be hoping to leverage his experience playing in Kazakhstan and technical ability to force Alonso to make uncomfortable decisions.

Kazakhstan teenager Dastan Satpaev has caught the eye during pre-season with Chelsea

Satpaev, however, does face a challenge in breaking through due to Chelsea's squad size

Jonah Kusi-Asare (Fulham)

Another forward aiming at securing more first-team football is 6ft 5in striker Jonah Kusi-Asare, who plays at west London neighbours Fulham.

The 19-year-old joined the club from German powerhouses Bayern Munich permanently this summer after a successful loan period.

Kusi-Asare featured in ten first team appearances last season, while he also proved highly effective for the U21s, scoring four goals in five appearances.

The Swedish forward continued this fine form and produced an encouraging display against Al-Ahly, winning several free-kicks in the latter stages of the game.

The departures of Raul Jimenez and Harry Wilson have left a gap in terms of attacking output that Kusi-Asare could exploit with his imposing size and Bayern Munich pedigree.

New Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa has signalled that he wants to place a greater emphasis on youth talent, that could provide Kusi-Asare a path to regular football.

Jonah Kusi-Asare, left, could benefit from Raul Jimenez's exit as he seeks more minutes at Fulham

Trey Nyoni (Liverpool)

Trey Nyoni must have seen Rio Ngumoha’s breakout season and decided that he’s next.

The 19-year-old midfielder has been one of the leading stories out of Liverpool’s pre-season because of the confidence and creativity he exudes, summed up by his pass in the build-up to Florian Wirtz’s goal against Leeds. In the same game he also had the most passes into the final third, with eight.

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola praised Nyoni, reflecting on his performance: ‘Even when he [Trey] has one opponent quite close, he asks for that ball and he's confident, he doesn't rush. For me, that is very valuable.’

This bravery and maturity seem to be the traits that make Nyoni poised to take the next step in his career.

Nyoni has certainly made the most of the absence of Alexis Mac Allister and Ryan Gravenberch’s World Cup break and is exploiting Curtis Jones’ inconsistent performances to pave himself a pathway to first team opportunities.

Trey Nyoni has been one of those to impress during Liverpool's pre-season under Andoni Iraola

The 19-year-old will look to follow Rio Ngumoha in establishing himself in the first team squad

Jacob Devaney (Manchester United)

Jacob Devaney, a Republic of Ireland Under-21 International, announced in a pre-season press conference: ‘The main aim for me is to play for Manchester United week in, week out’.

His pre-season performances have not harmed his cause.

Despite Manchester United’s lacklustre performance against Wrexham, Michael Carrick highlighted Devaney’s efforts, saying: ‘JD playing centre-half, it’s not natural to him, he’s played there a little bit, but not a lot and I thought he did ever so well.'

The 19-year-old had a promising long loan spell at St Mirren last season, where he gained valuable experience.

'He had a really successful few months up there [in Scotland] and it was good to see him kind of take that next step,' Carrick said.

'And you could see today the confidence and the assurance in his game, even though he was playing a slightly different position.’

This sense of positional fluidity and Carrick’s emphasis on Man Utd’s youth and academy will certainly help the 19-year-old midfielder as he aims for first team minutes at the club.

Jacob Devaney earned the praise of Manchester United boss Michael Carrick during pre-season

Ryan McAidoo (Manchester City)

Ryan McAidoo, a player signed from Chelsea two years ago, is also making waves in Manchester and hoping for a bigger role next season. The 18-year-old winger was given his debut last season by Pep Guardiola and rewarded his trust with a goal in City’s 10-1 thrashing against Exeter City.

On Saturday, McAidoo impressed against Inter Milan where he proved a constant threat against the Italian backline and nearly nestled a beauty into the back post.

Maresca certainly seemed to be impressed with the winger, commenting after the game: ‘We have been speaking with the club about Ryan and since day one, he is that kind of winger I love… very aggressive one v one, always trying, making the right decision.’

This is encouraging news for McAidoo because this is the same club that handed opportunities to Phil Foden, Nico O'Reilly and Cole Palmer. Maresca himself is also no stranger to youth players.

‘When I was at Leicester, that season there was a record number of debutants. When I was at Chelsea, record debutants from the academy,’ he pointed out.

Although Manchester City do not lack attacking options, these comments must provide hope that McAidoo will be given opportunities to shine in the coming season.

Ryan McAidoo made his Man City debut last season and will be hopeful of more opportunties

Ibrahim Osman (Brighton)

Ibrahim Osman is another player who has taken his opportunities from pre-season and given Fabian Hurzeler food for thought.

Brighton, a club known for plucking talent from thin air and improving them, may have struck gold with the 21-year-old Ghanaian winger.

Osman has scored two goals in pre-season, a spectacular overhead kick against Wycombe and a coolly taken penalty against Strausberg.

The youngster is something of a forgotten man after joining Brighton from FC Nordsjælland in 2024, before loan spells at Feyenoord and Auxerre.

Ibrahim Osman spent last season on loan at Birmingham and now will eye a breakthrough at Brighton

Osman spent the last season at Birmingham where he got his first taste of English football, scoring four goal contirbutions in 17 matches, and the Championship outfit were desperate to keep him.

However, it seems that Hurzeler has other plans. The Brighton manager has been vocal in his praise for Osman and another teenager Amario Cozier-Duberry: ‘So just talking about Osman, about Amario, they had a very impactful pre-season so far.’

With the extra demands of the Conference League, the departure of Danny Welbeck and injuries to Mitoma, could we see Osman become the next wonderkid produced by the East Sussex outfit?

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Semi-final: Italy vs Northern Ireland

Semi-final: Wales vs Bosnia and Herzegovina

Final: Wales/Bosnia and Herzegovina vs Italy/Northern Ireland - Tuesday, 7.45pm kick-off
