He stressed that the alleged misinformation would not distract the PDP leadership from its efforts to build what he described as a formidable coalition of Benue people capable of providing the state with a credible alternative in 2027.

World.title: Naira appreciates to N1,412/$ in parallel market
World.content:
By Elizabeth Adegbesan

The naira appreciated to N1,412 per dollar in the parallel market on Friday, from N1,416 per dollar recorded on Thursday.

Similarly, the local currency strengthened to N1,364 per dollar at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM).

Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) showed that the indicative exchange rate for the naira stood at N1,364 per dollar, compared with N1,365.10 per dollar on Thursday, representing an appreciation of N1.10.

Consequently, the gap between the parallel and official markets narrowed to N48 per dollar from N50.90 per dollar recorded on Thursday.

Meanwhile, interbank turnover at the NFEM increased sharply by 298.2 per cent to $393.5 million on Thursday, from $98.8 million recorded on Wednesday.

World.title: Alaafin: Oyo passport office autonomy’ll boost local economy, ease travel burden
World.content:
By Adeola Badru

IBADAN — The Alaafin of Oyo, Oba Abimbola Owoade, has welcomed the newly granted autonomy to the Oyo Passport Office, describing the development as a significant step towards decentralising government services and stimulating economic activities in the ancient city.

The monarch said the development would bring critical government services closer to residents, particularly those in rural and semi-urban communities who previously had to travel to Ibadan or Ilorin to access passport-related services.

Oba Owoade stated this through a high-powered delegation led by a member of the Oyo Traditional Council (Oyo Mesi), High Chief Asimiyu Atanda, during a visit to the Oyo Passport Office to felicitate with its management on the autonomy recently granted to the facility.

Before the development, the Oyo Passport Office operated as an appendage of the Ibadan Passport Office and was required to refer certain operations to the latter.

With the new status, however, the Oyo Passport Office can operate independently, while international passports processed through the facility will bear the name of the Oyo Passport Office.

The Alaafin said the development was significant because having a local passport office was essential to decentralising government services and improving accessibility.

He noted that the autonomous facility would “eliminate long-distance travel to state capitals” and reduce pressure on major passport processing centres.

According to him, residents would no longer have to bear the additional transportation costs and time associated with travelling outside Oyo for biometric capture, documentation and other passport-related services.

Oba Owoade said the development would “bring biometric capture and documentation services closer to rural or semi-urban residents, saving travel time and transport costs.”

The monarch also linked the development to broader economic benefits for Oyo, arguing that increased movement of applicants and visitors to the city would generate additional patronage for local businesses.

He said the office would “alleviate massive workloads and long queues at Central State or Regional Passport Headquarters” while creating opportunities for businesses operating around the facility.

“It would also increase local commercial activities as travellers from neighbouring towns visit the city for administrative processing, as well as create jobs directly through facility staffing and indirectly via local micro-businesses that support office visitors,” the Alaafin said.

Earlier, the Chief Passport Officer of the Oyo Passport Office, Assistant Controller of Immigration Oladejo Taiwo David, expressed appreciation to the Alaafin and his delegation for the visit.

Oladejo acknowledged the role played by the monarch and other prominent Oyo indigenes in securing the autonomous status for the office.

“This feat wouldn’t have been achieved if not for the efforts of His Imperial Majesty,” he said, while also acknowledging the support of prominent Oyo sons, particularly Alhaji Daud Igi-Ogun.

The Chief Passport Officer appealed to the Alaafin to assist the office in creating awareness among residents about the services now available in Oyo.

He urged residents to take advantage of the development by patronising the Oyo Passport Office instead of travelling to Ibadan or Ilorin for passport-related services.

“We solicit the support of His Imperial Majesty in the creation of awareness for the people to start patronising the Passport Office instead of going to Ibadan and Ilorin,” Oladejo said.

He assured residents that the new autonomous status would lead to more efficient service delivery.

According to him, “Oyo Passport Office would serve the people better as it would be faster to get their passports.”

The Alaafin’s delegation comprised the Director of Administration to the monarch, Prince Adesola Sanda, and renowned Sheikh, Alhaji Daud Igi-Ogun.

World.title: French Language Village Emerges Winner of Inaugural Word-Wise Bilingual Varsity Debate
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The Nigerian French Language Village (NFLV) has emerged winner of the maiden Word-Wise Bilingual Series – University Edition, defeating five other tertiary institutions in a competition aimed at promoting bilingualism, leadership development and stronger African integration.

The four-day competition, organised by the Word-Wise Educational Support and Advancement Foundation in partnership with the Embassy of France in Nigeria through the French Embassy Fund Bilingual And Competitive Project (FEF-BAC), brought together student debaters from six universities and higher institutions across Nigeria’s Southwest region.

Representatives from the University of Ibadan, University of Lagos, Lagos State University, Obafemi Awolowo University, Olabisi Onabanjo University and the Nigerian French Language Village competed in both English and French, engaging in debates on contemporary national and continental issues.

Beyond conventional debating, the competition featured an Africa Solution Room, where finalists were tasked with developing practical solutions to some of the continent’s most pressing challenges, including youth unemployment, education, governance and regional integration.

The organisers said the initiative was conceived to show that language acquisition should extend beyond classroom learning by equipping young people with the confidence, communication abilities and leadership skills required to address real-world challenges.

Speaking on the outcome of the competition, the Cooperation Attaché and Coordinator of the FEF-BAC Project at the Embassy of France in Nigeria, Madam Magaly Losange, praised the participants for the confidence and depth of engagement displayed throughout the event.

“What impressed me most was not simply the quality of the debates, but the confidence and intentionality the students demonstrated, particularly during the Crossfire rounds,” she said.

Losange noted that the students were able to apply the French language skills acquired in the classroom to spontaneous discussions, critical thinking and collaborative problem-solving.

She explained that such practical use of language reflected the broader objective of the FEF initiative, which seeks to position bilingualism not merely as a communication skill but as a tool for building confidence, expanding opportunities and strengthening connections among young people.

She congratulated all participants, saying their performance demonstrated the importance of preparing young Africans for an increasingly interconnected global environment.

The Co-Chief Executive Officer of the Word-Wise Educational Support and Advancement Foundation, Senami Ohiomokhare, said the competition had highlighted the power of bilingualism in developing a new generation of African leaders capable of bridging cultural and linguistic gaps.

“At Word-Wise, we believe that every young person has a story worth telling and a voice worth hearing,” Ohiomokhare said.

She added that the four-day programme enabled students to build confidence, exchange ideas respectfully and communicate across linguistic boundaries, stressing that leadership begins with “listening, understanding and connecting with others.”

Also speaking, the foundation’s Co-Chief Executive Officer, Mr Victor Ibrahim, described effective communication as the foundation of leadership.

“Leadership is impossible without communication,” Ibrahim said, adding that participants had gone beyond memorised speeches to demonstrate authentic conversations, thoughtful debate and meaningful collaboration.

He said the competition proved that language could serve as a unifying force rather than a barrier, while empowering young people to play a greater role in shaping Africa’s future.

The university edition attracted more than 200 students as a live audience, building on previous Word-Wise Bilingual Series programmes targeted at upper primary and junior secondary school pupils.

According to the foundation, the two editions of the initiative have now directly reached nearly 1,000 young people, providing them with communication, leadership and employability skills while promoting stronger ties between Anglophone and Francophone communities.

The organisers said the impact of the programme would continue beyond the competition through a digital storytelling campaign featuring participant profiles, mentorship opportunities, behind-the-scenes experiences, debate highlights and success stories across social media platforms.

They added that preparations were already underway for future editions, with plans to expand participation, strengthen partnerships and create more platforms for young Africans to collaborate across linguistic and national boundaries.

World.title: Transcorp Power CEO Reaffirms Commitment to Powering Delta’s Economic Growth
World.content:
Transcorp Power Plc, a subsidiary of Transnational Corporation Plc (Transcorp Group) and one of Nigeria’s leading power generation companies, has reaffirmed its readiness to partner with the Delta State Government to close the state’s power supply gaps and unlock its full economic potential.

Speaking as a panellist at the Delta State Economic and Investment Summit 2026, themed Energy Ecosystem in Delta State, held in Asaba, the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Transcorp Power Plc, Engr. Peter Ikenga reiterated the earlier submission of Transcorp Plc’s Group Chairman, Mr Tony O. Elumelu, that every developmental aspiration for Delta State needs to be powered.

At the 3-day event hosted by the Governor of Delta State, Rt. Hon Sheriff Oborevwori, and attended by several dignitaries including the Vice President, Senator Kashim Shettima, and other dignitaries across the country and the world, Engr Ikenga stated that Transcorp Power Plc had been operating in Delta State for over a decade.

“We own a nearly 1,000-megawatt-capacity power plant in Ughelli, Delta State, capable of powering two million homes, industries, schools and hospitals. We are heavily vested in powering the state to greater prosperity,” he said.

Engr. Ikenga observed that Delta State is uniquely endowed for power generation, with huge gas reserves and a total grid-installed generation capacity of almost 3,000 megawatts, a significant asset if fully revived and operated at maximum potential. He identified the key gaps as the need for continuous investment in gas feedstock to power the state’s thermal plants, and the extension of transmission and distribution infrastructure across the state. “Transcorp can bring its experience to develop an integrated power strategy for Delta State, all the way from gas production and generation to investments in transmission and distribution, to power the state to progress,” he said.

“We are ready to collaborate with Delta State, to work with the government to close the gaps and deficiencies, and to bring our systems and processes to play to meet the state’s transformation objectives.”

Engr. Ikenga expressed strong confidence in the state’s prospects, describing Delta as capable of becoming a leading economic force on the continent.

“Delta State can be the number one economic engine in Nigeria, and indeed in West Africa, and Transcorp is poised to help make that a reality,” he said.

The Delta State Economic and Investment Summit 2026 convened government officials, global business leaders, investors and development partners to explore strategies for accelerating industrialisation and positioning Delta State as a leading investment destination in Nigeria. Transcorp Power’s participation underscores the Group’s enduring commitment to driving inclusive economic growth across Nigeria through reliable and sustainable power.

World.title: 1xCup 2026 Gains Momentum: Key Highlights from Opening Weeks of Qualifiers
World.content:
The 1xCup 2026 qualifiers are gaining momentum. Over the first six matchdays, 48 teams played 24 matches and scored 78 goals. The opening matches have already highlighted several standout teams and players, although it is still too early to identify the tournament’s clear favorites.

Lopsided wins and battles down to last kick

From the opening matches, the qualifiers have delivered plenty of goals, with teams averaging more than three per game. Dosu Joseph FC set the pace on July 23 by routing Ikosi FC 5–1. OOA FA produced an even more convincing performance, defeating Ikoyi Dolphin FC 6–2.

Ighalo FA also made a strong impression on the fans with a 5–0 win over Panthers FA. The team stood out not only for its scoring but also for its cohesive play: the players were organized, understood one another well, and gave their opponents almost no opportunities.

However, most matches were much more hard-fought. In a format consisting of two 30-minute halves, the cost of every mistake is particularly high, so a single moment can often decide the outcome. Six of the 24 matches went to penalty shootouts, while another five were decided by a single goal. Somolu Bariga FC staged a remarkable comeback. The team was trailing Cityfut Escola 1–0 and was down a player, but managed to equalize before claiming victory in the penalty shootout.

Arich FC and The Pro Select FC produced a real thriller. The more experienced Arich side was considered the underdog before the match, but despite falling behind, the team managed to equalize and force a penalty shootout, which it won 6–5. Veteran striker Paul Aba, who wears the number nine shirt, was especially emotional in his celebrations.

Early Heroes

It is still too early to assess the balance of power based on just one match, but the tournament’s first heroes have already made their mark. Oladapo Albert scored a hat trick and led Vinmo Energy FC to a commanding 5–1 victory over Budu Elites FA. After six matchdays, the striker sits alone at the top of the qualifying stage’s scoring chart.

John David Kelechi of Daja United was the real revelation of the opening games. In his 1xCup debut, the striker scored twice and received the Player of the Match award. He dedicated his success to his family, who support him from his hometown of Aba. Kelechi displayed not only skill but also humility. When asked who else deserved the award, John immediately named his teammate Samuel Choice, highlighting his hard work and love of football.

Four other players also began the qualifiers with two goals each. Alidu Mohammed and Ezeji Ikenna both scored twice for Ighalo FA, Alabi Hammed netted two goals for OOA FA, and Adeleye Emmanuel Odunayo did the same for AMA Smile FC. Marcus Promis, Greenlock FC’s number seven, also deserves a special mention. He is an excellent player who seemed to be everywhere on the field. Scouts should definitely keep an eye on him, especially if his club advances to the group stage.

The heroes of the opening weeks included not only players but also spectators. Dynamic FC’s fans were particularly memorable, with their loud and energetic support playing an important role in the team’s victory.

This is only the beginning

The fourth season of the 1xCup features 100 teams from Ikeja, Lagos Island, Ikorodu, Badagry, and Epe, so the start of the tournament offers only an initial glimpse of the scale of the qualifiers. For now, the competition is taking place within individual zones, where clubs face opponents from neighboring areas. The winners of these local matchups will continue through the qualifying bracket, while the top 24 teams will advance to the group stage.

The 1xCup gives players not only an opportunity to compete for the trophy but also a chance to take the next step in their careers. More than 30 participants from previous seasons went on to sign contracts with professional clubs in Nigeria and other countries. For the current players, the qualifiers also provide an opportunity to showcase their abilities and attract the attention of scouts.

Battle for 24 Spots Continues

The qualifiers are still far from over. After six matchdays, 24 teams have advanced to the second round, while another 52 are still preparing to play their opening games. On August 6, matches in the Lagos Island zone will take place at Inspire Sport Arena in Oshodi, followed by the Ikorodu zone on August 7 and the Badagry zone on August 8. The upcoming matchups are sure to produce new heroes and could significantly reshape the top scorer race.

In the second round, the teams that made a strong start to the qualifiers will have to confirm their ambitions in more difficult matchups. Ighalo FA will face Arich FC, OOA FA will take on Daja United, which opened the tournament with a 3–0 victory, and Vinmo Energy FC will play Ajuwa FA, which needed only one goal to defeat Kosas Phantom FC.

The qualifiers will conclude on September 4, when the 24 participants in the main stage will be determined. The opening fixtures have already produced their share of heroes and revealed several favorites, but everything can still change. After all, every new clash begins at 0–0.

World.title: Breaking: 5 Abducted Gateway Poly Students, 2 Others Rescued, 5 Suspects Arrested, Abiodun Hails Army, DSS, Police, Others
World.content:
Five students of Gateway ICT Polytechnic, Saapade, in Remo North Local Government Area of Ogun State, who were abducted by suspected kidnappers earlier this week, have been rescued.

Also rescued were two non-students, bringing the total number of victims rescued to seven.

The victims were rescued in the early hours of Friday in an intelligence-led operation around Alamala community, off Ayetoro Road Roundabout, in the state capital.

The rescue operation was carried out by security agencies, including the Department of State Services (DSS), the Nigerian Army, the Nigerian Police and the Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC).

Five suspects were also arrested in connection with the abduction.

Governor Dapo Abiodun of Ogun State lauded the DSS, the Nigerian Army, the Nigerian Police, as well as Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), for rescuing the victims.

The governor described the rescue as a major breakthrough in its fight against kidnapping, even as he reaffirmed his administration’s unwavering commitment to ensuring that kidnappers and other criminal elements have no hiding place in the state

He described the operation, which included members of the State Security Network Agency (Amotekun Corps), local vigilantes and hunters, as a demonstration of the success that can be achieved when security agencies work together.

“One of the victims sustained a gunshot injury during the incident and was immediately evacuated for medical attention. The student has since been stabilised.

“This operation is still ongoing, and I wish to assure the good people of Ogun State that our security agencies remain on the trail of every individual connected with this criminal enterprise,” said the governor.

“Our resolve is very clear. Ogun State will remain hostile to criminality and safe for every law-abiding citizen, resident and investor,” the governor declared, stressing that

According to him, recent joint security initiatives, particularly Operation Kò S’Áyé, have demonstrated the effectiveness of intelligence sharing, inter-agency collaboration and sustained operational pressure against criminal elements.

The governor also commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for his administration’s commitment to combating banditry, terrorism and kidnapping across the country, noting that the recent rescue of 308 abducted victims by Nigerian security forces underscores the growing effectiveness of coordinated security operations nationwide.

“At this juncture, I must acknowledge the purposeful leadership of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, whose administration has placed the restoration of peace and security at the centre of Nigeria’s development agenda through sustained investment in the operational capacity of the Armed Forces and other security agencies.

“The strengthening of intelligence coordination, the acquisition of modern security assets and his deliberate reforms have continued to deepen inter-agency collaboration,” he said.

The governor further noted that the Federal Government has continued to strengthen the nation’s security architecture, adding that the recent approval of a substantial salary increase for officers and men of the Armed Forces would further boost personnel welfare and morale.

World.title: DTN@100 Heroes Awards Honour National Devt, Sustainability, Social Impact, National Global Champion Award Recipients
World.content:
The Organising Council of the Daily Times Nigeria Centenary (DTN@100) Heroes Awards has announced the recipients of four of its prestigious special honours, recognising exceptional individuals and institutions whose visionary leadership, innovation and transformational contributions continue to advance Nigeria’s economic growth, environmental sustainability, social development and global competitiveness.

The latest announcement forms part of activities leading to the DTN@100 Conference, Grand Book Unveiling and Times Heroes Awards, a landmark event commemorating the centenary of Daily Times Nigeria and celebrating a century of impactful journalism, national discourse and nation-building.

This year’s special honours recognise outstanding achievements in the categories of National Global Champion Award, National Development Award, Sustainability Award and Social Impact Award, celebrating recipients whose work continues to create measurable impact across Nigeria and beyond.

Announcing the recipients, Chairman of the DTN@100 Organising Council, Bolaji Okusaga, said the awards reflect the Council’s commitment to recognising individuals and institutions whose leadership has delivered lasting value to society and inspired national progress.

“The DTN@100 Heroes Awards were conceived to celebrate exceptional leadership, innovation and service that have contributed meaningfully to Nigeria’s development over the past century while inspiring the country’s future. These honours recognise individuals and institutions whose achievements extend beyond personal success to creating lasting impact on communities, industries and the nation as a whole,” he said.

He added that the Awards have become one of the defining legacies of the Daily Times centenary celebrations, preserving and celebrating the stories of outstanding Nigerians and institutions whose contributions continue to shape the country’s development trajectory.

The Organising Council announced that Dr Mahmoud Ahmadu, OON, President of the Nigeria Arabian Gulf Chamber of Commerce (NAGCC), was honoured with the National Global Champion Award for his exceptional leadership in advancing Nigeria’s global economic engagement and strengthening strategic trade and investment partnerships between Nigeria and the Arabian Gulf region.

Through visionary leadership, enterprise promotion and economic diplomacy, he has expanded opportunities for cross-border investment, enhanced Nigeria’s international competitiveness and contributed significantly to positioning the country as a preferred destination for global commerce and sustainable economic development.

The National Development Award was presented to Dr Olasupo Olusi, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the Bank of Industry (BOI), for his outstanding leadership in driving industrialisation, enterprise development, job creation and inclusive economic growth.

Under his leadership, the Bank of Industry has continued to expand access to finance for businesses, strengthen local manufacturing, empower entrepreneurs and accelerate Nigeria’s industrial transformation, reinforcing its position as one of the country’s foremost development finance institutions.

The Organising Council also recognised Mr Abdulhamid Umar, National Project Coordinator of the Agro-Climatic Resilience in Semi-Arid Landscapes (ACReSAL) Programme, with the DTN@100 Sustainability Award for his outstanding leadership in driving one of Nigeria’s most ambitious climate-resilience and landscape-restoration initiatives. Under his stewardship, the World Bank-supported programme has strengthened environmental sustainability, restored degraded ecosystems, enhanced agricultural resilience, and improved livelihoods across participating states, positioning ACReSAL as a model for sustainable development.

The Council also honoured Professor Oyelaran Oyeyinka with the Social Impact Award, recognising his remarkable contributions to public policy, innovation, knowledge development and inclusive socio-economic transformation across Africa.

For decades, Professor Oyeyinka has distinguished himself through exemplary service in academia, international development and policy advisory, influencing development thinking, strengthening institutions and advancing inclusive growth across the continent.

According to Okusaga, the selection process reflected the high standards that have come to define the DTN@100 Heroes Awards.

“Our Awards Board undertook a rigorous and independent assessment of nominees, focusing on measurable impact, transformational leadership, innovation and enduring contributions to national development. The recipients announced today exemplify excellence, integrity and visionary leadership, and their achievements deserve national recognition,” he added.

The Organising Council also announced that public voting remains open for the Financial Innovation Award, encouraging Nigerians at home and in the diaspora to participate in recognising organisations that are redefining financial innovation and expanding access to financial services.

Okusaga emphasised that public participation remains an important pillar of the awards process. “These awards belong to Nigerians. Public participation reinforces the credibility, inclusiveness and national ownership of this initiative. We therefore encourage citizens to continue supporting individuals and organisations whose work is creating meaningful impact and contributing to Nigeria’s progress.”

The DTN@100 Conference, Grand Book Unveiling and Times Heroes Awards will culminate in a grand public presentation on Thursday, September 3, 2026, at the THISDAY Dome, Central Business District, Abuja, where award recipients will be formally honoured before an audience of national leaders, policymakers, captains of industry, diplomats, development partners and other distinguished stakeholders.

The event will also feature the unveiling of the Nigeria Grand Book, a landmark commemorative publication documenting the remarkable achievements of outstanding personalities, institutions and organisations whose contributions have shaped Nigeria’s political, economic, social and developmental journey over the past century.

World.title: Agbese Opposes Frequent Change of Service Chiefs, Urges Nigeria to Exit ICC
World.content:
A member of the House of Representatives, Hon. Philip Agbese, has cautioned against the frequent replacement of Nigeria’s service chiefs, saying such changes undermine military operations and provide opportunities for terrorists and other criminal elements to regroup.

Agbese, who represents Ado/Okpokwu/Ogbadibo Federal Constituency of Benue State, made the remarks in a television programme on Thursday while discussing the country’s security situation and the ongoing efforts of the Armed Forces.

The lawmaker said the military had recorded appreciable successes in tackling insecurity and deserved sustained public support rather than recurring calls for the removal of service chiefs whenever security challenges occur.

According to him, changing military commanders at critical moments often disrupts operational momentum, as newly appointed officers require time to settle into office and implement their strategies.

“Each time there are security issues, some people begin to call for the removal of the service chiefs. Those things cause setbacks because when you remove them and bring in new ones, they try to introduce different approaches, and it takes time for them to settle down. Within that period, insurgents gain mileage and launch fresh attacks,” he said.

Agbese, a member of the Labour Party, stressed that although opposition parties have a constitutional responsibility to hold governments accountable and advocate better policies, national security should remain a non-partisan issue.

“As members of the opposition, we believe government can always do more in providing leadership and security. But when it comes to the Armed Forces, they belong to all Nigerians and deserve our collective support,” he stated.

He commended Nigerians for increasingly countering misinformation and false narratives about military operations on social media, describing public cooperation as essential to the success of security agencies.

The lawmaker disclosed that based on available records, the Armed Forces had rescued no fewer than 1,000 persons from captivity this year, urging citizens to verify information before circulating reports capable of undermining national security.

Agbese also called for stronger international collaboration in intelligence sharing and counter-terrorism efforts to strengthen Nigeria’s fight against insurgency, banditry and kidnapping.

On international justice, the federal lawmaker advocated Nigeria’s withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC), arguing that continued membership no longer aligns with the country’s security realities.

He argued that while terrorist groups commit atrocities against civilians without regard for international humanitarian law, the ICC has not demonstrated the same level of commitment in ensuring that such actors are prosecuted.

According to him, there have instead been recurring concerns that Nigerian troops could face international prosecution for actions taken while confronting terrorists, despite the country’s established legal and judicial institutions for investigating allegations of human rights abuses.

“Nigeria has a functional legal and judicial system capable of addressing cases involving human rights violations. Considering the scale of security threats confronting the country, government should critically review whether continued membership of the International Criminal Court remains in our national interest,” Agbese said.

Drawing comparisons with countries such as the United States, Russia and China, he maintained that Nigeria should empower its Armed Forces to respond swiftly and decisively to security threats while reviewing international commitments that may impede effective military operations.

The lawmaker reaffirmed his confidence in the Armed Forces, urging Nigerians to continue supporting security agencies in their efforts to restore peace and safeguard the country’s territorial integrity.

World.title: Review: Josplay, Where African Music Lives
World.content:
Vanessa Obioha

For a continent of 54 countries, reducing its music to just a handful of genres hardly does it justice. This is often the experience on many global streaming platforms, where African music is largely represented by sounds from West Africa or South Africa. What, then, of the musical traditions of Lusophone Africa and the many other genres that rarely make global playlists? Africa’s sonic landscape surely goes beyond afrobeats, amapiano and house music.

Enter Josplay, an Afrocentric audio entertainment platform that delivers music, news, stories and audiobooks to listeners around the world. Since its launch in 2019, the platform has been intentional about creating a distinctly African listening experience, from its intuitive interface to AI-powered recommendations that adapt to each user’s preferences.

After signing up, users are introduced to a feature called Frames, which curates music around daily rhythms and moods. First-time users are presented with 10 Frames and asked to choose six, with the flexibility to customise their selections later. The feature tailors recommendations to different moments of the day. Select the Flow Frame, for instance, and the app curates music designed to aid concentration. Choose Unwind, and it shifts to mellow grooves suited to winding down after a busy day.

The app then invites users to select their preferred genres, and this is where Josplay truly distinguishes itself. Its catalogue reflects an impressive breadth of African music that goes beyond the genres that dominate international playlists. That diversity has only expanded through a partnership with Sony Music Entertainment, bringing a significant portion of the company’s catalogue to Josplay listeners worldwide, including recordings distributed through The Orchard and the complete catalogues of Lusafrica and Africa Nostra, comprising more than 4,000 songs.

Here, listeners will discover music they never knew existed, or knew existed but never knew what genre it belonged to. There is Tishoumaren, also known as Assouf or Desert Blues, a style that originated among the Tuareg people of the Sahara. Blending traditional Tuareg music with blues and rock influences, it creates a haunting yet captivating sound.

If Desert Blues is not quite your style, there is Sungura, the energetic Zimbabwean genre that fuses traditional Zimbabwean music with Congolese rumba, pop and rock. Driven by lively guitars, basslines and infectious percussion, it is almost impossible to sit still while listening. A good introduction is Eriki’s ‘Lost and Found.’

Those looking for smoother, romantic rhythms will appreciate Kizomba, the Angolan genre that combines traditional Angolan rhythms with Caribbean zouk and French-Caribbean compas to produce music that is both intimate and danceable.

Perhaps what is most exciting is how it celebrates a country’s musical diversity. For instance, rather than reducing Nigerian music to afrobeats and highlife, the platform also showcases Ogene, Apala, Juju, Fuji and Afrobeat, giving listeners a fuller appreciation of the country’s musical heritage.

Josplay’s homepage invites listeners into a world of culture and entertainment. Through Africa News Brief, users can catch up on news from across the continent, while Stories and Reads brings African history, folklore and personalities to life. Curious about the legendary Nigerian traditionalist Chief Pericoma Okoye? There is ‘Pericoma and the Tax Collectors.’ Prefer folklore? Then ‘How the Tortoise Got His Cracked Shell’ offers a nostalgic return to one of Africa’s storytelling traditions.

The platform also features a growing selection of podcasts, further broadening its appeal.

Josplay appears to be on track to becoming one of Africa’s most compelling music platforms. One question, however, is sustainability. Unlike most streaming services, its free tier currently carries no advertising, relying instead on limits to the number of songs users can stream each day. Whether that model proves financially sustainable remains to be seen. The company in 2021 diversified its revenue through Josplay Enterprise, which curates enterprise-grade playlists tailored to businesses and organisations, while also ensuring that creators are compensated for the use of their work.

Josplay celebrates Africa’s extraordinary musical diversity while reminding listeners that the continent’s sounds deserve far more than a corner of the world’s playlists. Whether its business model can sustain that ambition remains to be seen, but its vision is one worth paying attention to.

World.title: Debate on the Selection of Head of Service of the Federation in Perspective
World.content:
By Tunji Olaopa

In every administrative system across the world, the selection and appointment of critical officers and officials plays a very crucial role in the overall health of these systems. Indeed, the effectiveness and efficiency of any management system depend significantly on the helmsman who possesses the requisite vision, knowledge, drive and the bureaucratic competences to drive institutional reform and administrative progress. And when this discussion is situated within the context of an ongoing institutional reform process of a public administration system like the one Nigeria requires to manage the successes and consolidation of its democratic governance, then the issue of administrative leadership becomes even more cogent as it positions the public service at the very core of the building of a developmental state that Nigeria needs.

No wonder then that an extensive debate over the succession plan for the next head of the civil service of the federation (HCSF) has focused on why the HE the President needs to take a critical out-of-the-box decision on the modalities that will throw up not just the next HCSF but ground a veritable civil service leadership and administration that will serve as the basis for a functional bureaucratic institution and reprofessionalised civil service that will backstop Nigeria effectively into the fourth and fifth industrial revolutions. That this protracted concern is being championed by the leadership of the Council of Retired Federal Permanent Secretaries (CORFEPS) is even more significant. CORFEPS has over time become a veritable platform for interrogating germane issues revolving around the functionality and future of the civil service, as well as the operational mechanics and dynamics that could make for an efficient civil service.

This responsibility could have become even more grounded if the National Association of Public Administration and Management (NAPAM), the public administration professional body, is currently and sufficiently functional as to also be able to join the fray of discussions and deploy policy-engaged research agenda to deepen the conversation. This is for the sole reason that NAPAM’s expansive membership—drawing on the communities of practice and service of the numerous associations of retired heads of service and permanent secretaries across the states of the federations, public administration researchers, scholars and development workers, etc.—would have contributed an even more rounded and focused debate that pushes the issues beyond the federal civil service to the appointment of heads of service in all the states as well as how administrative leadership in the civil service can complement political leadership. My op-ed pieces over the years have provided the critical grounds for interrogating critical elements of civil service administrative leadership as reform imperatives. I have especially explored for example the generalist-professional distinction as one important item in understanding the transformation of the civil service as a world class institution in Nigeria.

For our present purpose, we take deep reflective direction from the African proverb—the fish rots from the head. This has become a metaphor for leadership vision, accountability and direction. When leadership falters, then the organization weakens and ultimately crumbles. Institutional and administrative reform is therefore ultimately about a leadership that invest frontier ideation, design thinking and policy acumen in visioning the present and future of a new civil service system that constitutes the mechanism for making the state work on behalf of her citizens. Within the Nigerian civil service, the focus and locus of this leadership template is the HCSF. And this is the most cogent reason why the administrative succession plan to install a new one is seen by those who should know to carry such a huge weight for the Tinubu administration and the bureaucracy itself.

In my modest opinion, therefore, the best way to initiate the inquiry into the matter, and beyond the generalist-professional distinction, is the urgent need to rethink the most fundamental questions around the status and operational capacity of the HCSF that enable us to probe deeper into the directions that the system needs to take in terms of a functional, ethical and strategic leadership and the reform processes the leadership needs to drive. The fundamental questions are: (a) Who is the HCSF and what does the job entail? (b) How are the two elite cadres—the administrative and professional officers from which the occupants of the office are selected—related to the challenges of leading the civil service? (c) What are the competencies required of administrative and professional officers to lead institutional reform and provide leadership to the service?

To tackle the nature of the leadership challenge and administrative succession therefore, we need to first understand what the office entails in theory and practice. The HCSF is considered the number one civil servant in the country; indeed, the HCSF is the chief policy adviser to the Federal Government of Nigeria on civil service matters. Given that the HCSF is appointed from among the serving permanent secretaries, s/he is therefore a primus inter pares charged with the responsibility of leading, administering and managing the public service through the permanent secretaries in terms of appointment, posting and performance. The managerial capacity of the HCSF is to be directed at rigorously building and professionalizing the federal workforce through the implementation of training and capacitation policies and programs, including managing the oversight of the governance of the government training institutions and manpower development institutes. The significance of the HCSF becomes glaring given the fact that she drives the civil service modernization plans and institutional reform strategies. The HCSF is the chief visionier and design/implementation officer that oversees how government’s democratic governance policies are translated through performance management into productivity.

Once we achieve this understanding of the persona and status of the HCSF, it becomes very clear why the appointment to that office would be this cogent and rigorous. But more fundamentally, it demonstrates why serious reflection has to go into the selection framework in terms of the processes, procedures and administrative philosophy that must undergird the selection into that office. It must stand to administrative reason that in choosing a visionary public administrator and manager who is in charge of the entire civil service institution, we cannot afford to play the politics of selection that install just anybody for the sake of political and administrative patronage. That will only go to damage the system and keep delaying its urgent transition into a structure at the cutting edge of professional service delivery that will backstop democratic governance and therefore the capacitation of the veritable institutional game changer-engine room in the national development change management dynamics.

The selection, by implication, must also not be undermined by administrative overreach. What does this mean? It means that in the appointment of the HCSF, we must be perceptive enough to look beyond the generalist-professional distinction that the permanent secretaries might fall into, or even the principles of seniority or geo-political balance that often play a very key role in administrative career progression. To be fair, being a generalist or a professional in this role comes with their significant advantages, in so far as merit overrides the choice, over and above the unknowing emergence of the run-of-the-mill street-wise misfits that sometimes feature in the tiny privileged bureaucratic space. A generalist is favored for such a position because of the broad and broadminded capacity for policy coordination and insight that is derived from experiences across diverse ministries and multi-sector coordination. On the other hand, the professional public servant, brings a wealth of domain technical acumen and expertise that is a sine qua non for a data-driven governance that the government requires from the civil service. Unlike the generalist, the professional comes with a specialized albeit narrow problem-solving competence rather than the presumably rounded administrative acumen of the well-groomed generalist administrative officer who are now hard to find really. And yet, each of these cadres, simply so called, lack the depth of what is demanded by that office. Indeed, the office of the HCSF is too important to be left to the limitations of these cadres and the vagaries of these two subsisting criteria for electing the head of the civil service.

The nature of the twenty-first century knowledge society, the demands of the fourth industrial revolution, and the dynamics of a developmental state require that the HCSF must possess a leadership quality and a multidisciplinary capability that is a creative mixture of tactical, strategic and operational competences not limited to any cadre. The HCSF that Nigeria and the Nigerian civil service system need must be appointed not only based on individual merit and moral characteristics, but must fundamentally be able to reflect a critical blend of technical expertise that distinguishes a pubic sector specialist, the reform passion of a change agent, and the project, program and change management acumen. These requirements provide a strategic combination of critical attitude and skills that prepares the HCSF for the leadership and administrative tasks ahead.

To possess the technical administrative skills implies that the aspirant is thoroughly grounded in the bureaucratic skills that underpin the working of government and its administrative system backend, and therefore familiar with public service rules and financial regulations, mechanics of working government business and constitutional stipulations. The candidate, in other words, should be some sort of institutional memory; an achievement that comes from possessing a minimum of ten to fifteen years of engaging and navigating the administrative dynamics of the MDAs. This has to be couple with having a track record of policy formulation experience, including the political skill of defending the policy initiatives at the Federal Executive Council, as well as implementing them.

As a change agent with a passion for reform, it is expected that the incoming HCSF must be sufficiently courageous to disrupt the subsisting bureaucratic inertia that has locked the civil service into an inefficient mode. This means that the candidate for that office must be capable of an innovative and creative vision and strategy that can drive the Federal Civil Service Strategy and Implementation Plan (FCSSIP) through the introduction of modern governance and administrative solution frameworks, from performance-based budgeting, contracting and evaluation to open data geared towards evidence-based citizen-centered service delivery. The persona of the candidate must be thoroughly investigated to determine the ability to prioritize national development goals over base ethnic objectives.

Lastly, no HCSF can ever hope to succeed in the office if she is lacking a significant amount of change management acumen, the absence of which makes the most excellent reform idea very useless. The capacity to implement policies and reform ideas is what transforms the institution into an effective one. The fundamental elements of that change management framework the candidate must possess include the experience of driving and supervising digital transformation like the ones involved in the civil service automation, digitalization and process reengineering, the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Information System (IPPIS) HR modules rooted reprofessionalisation, etc.; stakeholder management capacity; strategic capability for retraining a workforce to adopt twenty-first century competences; and should have the capacity to maneuver away from the status quo reinforcing standard annual evaluation report (APER) in favor of a result-based performance management system.

The candidate to be chosen eventually must therefore come across as a transformational permanent secretary with a track record of managing reforms, possess a clean bill of integrity, has the capacity for managing administrative and institutional crises, possess a history of meritocratic credentials team spirit and mentoring of subordinates. And then a last critical point. Making impacts as the HCSF is something that will take time, if the appointment and succession plan are strategically articulated. Given that the civil service is in a debilitated state, such a HCSF needs a minimum of three years in office. Tenure must therefore be founded on a non-renewable performance-based contract that is conditioned by certified annual performance assessment rather than by age or length of service alone. The succession plan cannot therefore start when the incumbent is just some few months away from exiting the office. A grooming framework serves the purpose, for instance, of providing sufficient time to prepare the appointed candidate to familiarize and understudy the incumbent. The pool of groomed candidates’ cohort makes it possible for the President to replace the incumbent if his performance is not encouraging and, to better plan and manage succession.

World.title: WEATHER: Severe cold, rain and snow to hit one province this weekend
World.content:
Very cold, wet and windy weather to hit this province this weekend. Image: File

A cold front and cut-off low will bring bitter cold, heavy rain, strong winds, rough seas and a risk of localised flooding from Sunday.

Very cold, wet and windy weather will spread across the Free State from Sunday evening, with snow expected on Monday and Tuesday.

KWAZULU-NATAL

Morning fog will affect the interior, while most areas will stay fine to partly cloudy and warm.



The south-west will remain cool. Along the coast, moderate to fresh northerly to north-easterly winds will turn south-westerly.

The UVB sunburn index is expected to be extreme.

DURBAN

The weather will remain fine before becoming partly cloudy in the evening.



Moderate northerly to north-easterly winds will turn south-westerly in the evening.

Temperatures will range from 15°C to 27°C.

The UVB sunburn index is going to be extreme.

FREE STATE

Free State is going to be fine and cool, becoming partly cloudy.



BLOEMFONTEIN

Bloemfontein is going to be fine.

Temperatures will range from a minimum of 4°C to a maximum of 24°C.

NORTH WEST

North West is going to be fine and cool to warm, becoming partly cloudy over the southern parts.



MAHIKENG

Weather in Mahikeng is going to be fine.

World.title: How MUCH is Lotto and Lotto Plus jackpot?
World.content:
This is the lay of the land for Lotto and Lotto Plus on Saturday 8 August 2026. Should you enter? Image: File

How much is Lotto and Lotto Plus on Saturday, 8 August 2026 worth? Well, it breaks down like so: Straight Lotto is worth R9 million, Lotto Plus 1 sits at R6 million and for Lotto Plus Max 5 you can tag on another R2 million.

All tallied up that put’s the total worth at R17 million for the next roll. That’s an increase of R3 million across all three games since the last roll on Wednesday.

Nevertheless, success for Lotto and Lotto Plus on Saturday, 8 August 2026 comes from knowing how recently one of the three has just paid out.



However, for a second successive game, we see amounts increasing across all three games. This suggests there’ve been no winners – big or small – recently. Payouts, while more frequent than before, are rarely climbing high anymore.

LOTTO AND LOTTO PLUS

Lotto and Lotto Plus on Saturday 8 August 2026 has always been the National Lottery’s bread-and-butter game. Cheaper than PowerBall and PowerBall XTRA, much easier to win, but less dramatic in jackpot size. Nevertheless, Sizekhaya’s 1 June 2026 takeover reshaped it even further. The core mechanics require players to choose six numbers from a pool of 1 to 52, which is reduced from 1 to 58 previously. As ever, numbers can be chosen manually or auto generated through the popular Quick Pick.

Pricing sits lower than PowerBall’s increase. A standard Lotto board costs R5, with Lotto Plus 1 adding R2.50 and Lotto 5 Max adding a further R2.50 on top. Therefore, playing all three together costs R10 per board. What players are still wrapping their head around is the new MultiPlay (MP1) option. It lets players add a seventh number to their existing six in each of the three games. And it gets proportionally more expensive as you go. The total combination if you add MP1 across all boards is R70 – that’s R35 + R17.50 + R17.50. However, your odds are massively improved if you do go down this rabbit hole.

HOW TO HANDLE MULTIPLAY

Do you prefer to choose numbers manually or use the auto-generated Quick Pick? There’s good reason to opt for the latter … Image: File

If you add MP1 to Lotto and Lotto Plus on Saturday 8 August 2026 across all three games, your total ticket will cost R70.00. Plus, if you’re using your banking app, be sure to lookout for digital banking fee of roughly R2.95 added to the transaction. So, the question remains, is it worth spending the extra money?

Jackpot odds have already improved substantially under the new number matrix. The chances of matching all six numbers now sits at 1 in 20 million. That’s twice as likely as the old 1 in 40 million under ITHUBA. However, dabble with the MP1 and all of a sudden, you’re playing with seven numbers instead of six. This means your odds now become just 1 in 2.9 million, which represents a straight sevenfold improvement. And don’t forget that’s across all three games since they share the board.

DRAW TIMES AND CLAIMING POWERBALL WINNINGS

Remember, if you’re playing Lotto and Lotto Plus on Saturday 8 August 2026, decide on a budget before buying lotto tickets, and don’t chase a bad week by spending more. The National Responsible Gambling Programme runs a toll-free counselling line on 0800 006 008 for anyone who is struggling.



Lotto and Lotto Plus draws twice weekly at 21:00. Sizekhaya brought back live televised draws using physical draw machines. Ticket sales cut off half an hour before the draw typically at 20:30. All lottery prizes must be claimed within 365 days of the draw date. World.title: Final hours: A timeline of one tragic weekend in Sabie for Cameron Waldeck-Cooks and Ethan Coetzee
World.content:
A hiking trip meant to mark a milestone for one Saints pupil ended in tragedy at a Mpumalanga lodge. Here is what we know, step by step, about the days before and after Cameron Waldeck-Cooks and Ethan Coetzee were found dead. Image: ChatGPT

Sensitive content: this article deals with the death of a minor and details of an ongoing murder investigation.

Background: Cameron Waldeck-Cooks, 17, a Grade 11 pupil at St Stithians Girls’ College, was working towards the Gold level of the President’s Award for Youth Empowerment.

The South African version of the Duke of Edinburgh’s International Award requires a multi-day adventurous journey.



When she was invited to join two families on a hiking trip to Sabie, Mpumalanga, she saw it as her chance.

Ethan Coetzee, 19, who matriculated from St Stithians Boys’ College in 2025, was also part of the group.

Monday, 3 August, morning Discovery: Graham Coetzee discovers Cameron’s body at the lodge in Sabie. Both Cameron and Ethan are found dead in a room at the lodge. No specific time of morning is given in any of the reports.

Monday, 3 August Family Action (Cameron’s parents, Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks): Cameron’s family appoints an independent forensic pathologist.

Tuesday, 4 August Social Media Update: St Stithians College posts two separate tribute statements on Facebook, one for Cameron and one for Ethan. Full details in The South African’s report.

Wednesday, 5 August, 21:34 Police Statement: Colonel Mavela Masondo confirms an inquest has been opened. A post-mortem will be conducted to determine cause of death. No indication of foul play, suicide, accident or illness is given at this point. Reported in full by The South African.



Friday, 7 August, 12:39 Police Statement: The inquest is upgraded to a murder case. Masondo states preliminary post-mortem findings show the female may have died by strangulation, while the male is believed to have died by suicide. See The South African’s coverage.

Friday, 7 August (assumed, same statement) Police Statement: Police ask the public to refrain from speculating about the circumstances of the deaths while the investigation continues.

Friday, 7 August, 18:37 Cameron’s Parents’ Statement (Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks): Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks release a full statement , confirming their own independent pathologist’s findings of strangulation and suffocation. Full statement carried by The South African.

Friday, 7 August (same statement) Cameron’s Parents’ Statement (Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks): Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks say they are not in a position to give interviews or comment further at this stage. They ask media and the public to protect the privacy of the family and the children affected by Cameron’s death.

Friday, 7 August (same statement) Cameron’s Parents’ Statement (Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks): Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks thank the Saints community, Cameron’s friends, and the netball and rowing communities for their support during this time.

Friday, 7 August (same statement) Cameron’s Parents’ Statement (Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks): Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks confirm a memorial service for Cameron will be held later in August, with further details to be shared at the appropriate time.

World.title: Disjointed All Blacks survive Stormers scare
World.content:
The All Blacks got their Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry campaign off to a winning start against the Stormers, but not in the way they would have wanted. Image: X @TheStormers

A late flurry of tries helped the All Blacks to a unconvincing 38-21 victory over the Stormers at Cape Town Stadium on Friday night.

They got the result in the bag, but Dave Rennie and co will look back at this performance and think how their charges were so horribly outplayed by the hosts.

Granted this is not the Test team that’ll front the Springboks, but side put out for this match looked disjointed, sloppy and were physically inferior to the Stormers, whose players were superb by all accounts.



The 40-year-old Deon Fourie was the leader of the pack and emerged as arguably the best player on the field. Yaqeen Ahmed didn’t take a backward step and held his own against his more accomplished opponent Beauden Barrett.

Andre-Hugo Venter was another who stood out after an early missed tackle, while outside backs Warrick Gelant and Seabelo Senatla performed equally well against New Zealand’s lethal back three.

One big takeaway from this encounter is that the All Blacks have a lot of work to do ahead of their mid-week game against the Sharks in Durban on Tuesday.

FIRST HALF RECAP

As expected, the All Blacks made a bright start to their seven-week South African excursion, but the Stormers to their credit settled well into the game once they got over initial jitters – or butterflies, depending how you look at it – and actually emerged as the more physically dominant side.

The Cape side suffered an early injury-enforced setback when scrumhalf Imad Khan had to be replaced by Dewaldt Duvenhage after the former freakishly pulled up with an injury without being touch.

New Zealand would be first on the scoreboard through hooker Samisoni Taukei’aho with Beauden Barrett converting. But their stay in front didn’t last long as the Stormers hit back after wrestling back the momentum. They exerted dominance at scrum by winning the first penalty at that set-piece.



Two quick penalties and a yellow card to All Black Anton Lienert-Brown later, veteran Deon Fourie went on a surging run to get them inside the 22. The pressure eventually took its toll on the strained All Blacks defence as Andre-Hugo Venter crashed over from the back of a driving maul. But the five-pointer was chalked off for obstruction by Evan Roos. It made little to no difference, though, as Fourie powered over and Yaqeen Ahmed converted to level the scores.

With the exception of a few individual errors, the Stormers were by and large the better side for the remainder of the first half. But as is customary with All Blacks, they struck right before the break to take – one could say undeserving – lead at the break.

SECOND HALF RECAP

If New Zealand’s sloppy first half display was cause for concern, their dire second half showing should sound alarm bells. Yes they won the game, but it has to be said that their get-out-of-jail-free card was more because the Stormers ran out of steam.

The Stormers bossed possession and territory after the restart, but the All Blacks defence forced to take hit after hit. They couldn’t successfully absorb all that pressure and their line was carved open when Seabelo Senatla sliced through to score a stunning solo effort to draw the Stormers level.

The Stormers continued to take the fight to the All Blacks, but a couple of handling errors were all the visitors needed to open up that pressure valve.

They scored a flurry of tries – four to be exact – in the last 10 minutes or so to ultimately take the game away from the Stormers.

SCORERS

Stormers

Tries: Deon Fourie, Seabelo Senatla

Conversions: Yaqeen Ahmed (2)

All Blacks

Tries: Samisoni Taukei’aho, Simon Parker, Rieko Ioane, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby, Asafo Aumua

Conversions: Beauden Barrett (3), Josh Jacomb

World.title: Ethan Coetzee’s former teacher: ‘Amazing young man’
World.content:
Ethan Coetzee – the St Stithians Boys College alumnus – has been remembered with fondness following his passing. According to police, the 19-year-old is believed to have taken his own life at a Sabi game lodge, allegedly in the same room as Cameron Waldeck-Cooks, a Grade 11 St Sitithians Girls College learner, who was also found deceased.

Authorities have the young woman’s inquest into a murder investigation.

ETHAN COETZEE REMEMBERED WITH FONDNESS

On Facebook, the St Stithians College has been inundated with tributes in memory of Cameron Waldeck-Cooks and Ethan Coetzee.



A friend of Cameron’s, Gabriella de Gama, shared on her own account: “I will forever love and miss you, Cam. You were kind and the most beautiful person I have ever met. Was a blessing to have known you all these years”.

In tribute to an Old Stithian Association, several members within the community remembered Ethan Coetzee, too.

A St Andrews educator posted: “This is just too sad! You were just the kindest little boy in the JP, and you grew into an amazing young man. You will be missed”.

Others, who knew Ethan personally, shared: “What absolutely devastating news💔 Ethan was an incredible young lad, so full of life!”, and “Absolutely heartbreaking. Both my sons remember Ethan with fondness”.

WHAT WE KNOW ABOUT THE ST STITHIAN ALUMNUS

Unlike Cameron Waldeck-Cooks’ parents, Ethan Coetzee’s loved ones have not spoken publicly.

The 19-year-old matriculated from St Stithians Boys College in 2025.



In a tribute to the teen, the “Saints” remembered him for his sporting achievements, the most notable being his drafting into the first team rugby, where he earned his rugby colours.

Ethan was a national champion in the equestrian sport of Eventing and a respected senior student at Penryn House.

The tribute read: “Ethan possessed a natural warmth and charisma that drew people to him, forging strong friendships. He had the ability to instil confidence in others, offering encouragement when it was needed most and making those around him feel seen, valued, and supported”.

World.title: Anti-gang unit members among four shot dead
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Four people are dead after a shooting in Reiger Park, Boksburg, on Friday.

Two of the victims are members of the SAPS anti-gang unit.

Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said preliminary reports indicate that the members were part of a crime prevention team conducting patrols in the area and driving towards the scene of a shooting when they were ambushed.

In a statement, authorities said maximum resources, including specialised investigative units, have been mobilised to hunt down the killers. Lieutenant General Dimpane believes that members of the community hold the key to solving this case.

Acting National Commissioner Puleng Dimpane has urged the community of Reiger Park and surrounding areas to stand with the police and assist investigators in bringing to justice those responsible for the brutal murder of two Anti-Gang Unit members.

"We know that someone saw what happened. Someone knows who pulled the trigger, who planned this attack, or where the suspects are hiding. We are pleading with the community not to protect ruthless criminals who have no regard for human life. Your silence only emboldens those who continue to terrorise your community," said Dimpane.

She said the deceased were fathers, mothers, husbands, wives, sons and daughters who left their homes every day knowing they may not return.

"Today, two families are mourning because these brave officers answered a call for help. Stand with the families of these fallen heroes. Stand for justice. Stand against criminals who continue to rob communities of peace and safety. If you know something, say something. Help us ensure that those responsible are arrested and face the full might of the law," she said.

Mathe said the scene remains active with necessary resources already mobilised.

World.title: Over 500 Toyota vehicles recalled
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - If you drive a Toyota, it may be worth checking if your vehicle is on the recall list.

The National Consumer Commission (NCC) has announced a safety recall of 518 Toyota vehicles.

The recall relates to a combination meter reprogramming issue affecting certain Toyota RAV4 PHEV, Corolla Cross, Corolla Hatchback, Crown and GR Corolla vehicles.

READ | Toyota recalls over 2,200 Urban Cruisers

According to NCC, due to improper programming of the combination meter, unnecessary data may be repeatedly written to a memory device while the meter is operating, causing the memory device to deteriorate earlier than intended.

"Should certain vehicle malfunctions occur while the monitor is not functioning, the driver may fail to notice the relevant warning indicators if they do not see the notification displayed on the centre multimedia screen. Depending on the malfunction, continued driving may increase the risk of an accident," NCC said.

The vehicles were sold through the Toyota dealer network nationwide between 2022 and 2024.

Consumers have been urged to take their vehicles to a Toyota dealership to have the faulty components reprogrammed.

World.title: Bela Act| Expert says regulations don't address issues in teacher support
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Education expert's confidence in the new draft regulations under the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act is low.

Expert Mary Metcalfe said the draft regulations fail to address the day-to-day problems teachers face in classrooms.

"The draft's been there for about eight years. It sets out what the physical infrastructure should be for provinces when they establish a provincial teacher development institute and centres. "Why I'm frustrated is because the budgetary requirements to do what the regulations say are completely challenging for the majority of provinces."

Metcalfe argued that it's not just about having the right physical architectural space, but about having the right people in the right place where teachers can come in and be treated as they should be and as envisaged in the 15-year-old policy on teacher development.

READ | Draft BELA regulations published for public comment

Basic Education Minister Siviwe Gwarube has released new draft regulations under the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act.

Parents, teachers, pupils, and schools can now review the proposals and submit feedback before they are finalised.

The drafts cover school governing body elections and operations, state teacher pay, standards for provincial teacher development institutes, and the National Education Information System.

Public comments close on 5 September.

World.title: Beyond Game Day | When Sport Loses Control: SAFA Elections Scandal Exclusive | 7 August 2026
World.content:
WHEN TRUST BREAKS, SPORT STOPS BEING JUST A GAME

Sport depends on rules, but rules alone are not enough. Every system also depends on trust: trust that selection is fair, that leadership is legitimate, that governance processes are credible and that the people responsible for protecting the game are not bending it around their own interests.

That trust can begin to unravel long before an institution formally fails.

At school level, the consequences are immediate. If parents believe money, sponsorship or influence can improve a child’s chances of selection, then merit becomes harder to defend. Coaches become vulnerable to suspicion. Schools risk being judged not only on how they develop talent, but on whether access to opportunity can be distorted by wealth or relationships.

THE DAMAGE IS BIGGER THAN ONE TEAM SHEET

Young athletes learn what systems reward. If they see influence outrank ability, that becomes part of their understanding of how institutions work. If adults become aggressive around children’s sport, that behaviour teaches something too. If racism appears in spaces supposedly built around teamwork, competition and shared identity, the question is no longer simply what happened on the field. It becomes what children are absorbing from the environments around them.

That is why one of the most uncomfortable ideas in this week’s Beyond Game Day lands so hard. The hosts ask how a teenager born long after apartheid can still know language associated with that history. The implication is obvious: discriminatory ideas do not survive by accident. They survive because they are repeated, normalised and passed down.

THE SIMPLE PRINCIPLE APPLIES HIGHER UP THE SPORTING SYSTEM

Football governance relies on process. Elections, nominations, disciplinary systems and leadership structures work only if participants believe the rules are being applied consistently and confidential information is being protected where required.

Once that confidence weakens, even a legitimate outcome can become harder to defend.

Questions raised around SAFA’s presidential nomination process illustrate why institutional credibility matters so much. If stakeholders begin wondering who knows what, when they knew it and whether information was handled properly, the issue stops being only about which candidate wins. The process itself becomes part of the contest.

THAT IS DANGEROUS FOR ANY ORGANISATION

Governance systems are designed to make leadership transitions predictable. When the process feels opaque, personalities become more important than institutions. That makes renewal harder, factionalism stronger and public trust weaker.

The leadership question is equally uncomfortable.

Sporting administrators often build immense legitimacy through historic achievements. Those achievements matter. They should be recognised.

But legacy cannot become permanent insulation from scrutiny.

LEADERSHIP HAS TO ANSWER THE PRESENT, NOT ONLY THE PAST

That applies in South African football and at FIFA. Gianni Infantino’s leadership has repeatedly placed the global governing body at the centre of political, commercial and ethical debates around the sport. The question is not whether powerful leaders will face criticism. They will. The real test is whether institutions remain strong enough to absorb controversy without allowing trust in the organisation itself to collapse.

THE LESSON REACHES FAR BEYOND SPORT

Schools, companies, governments and federations all face the same risk: once people believe access depends on influence, information is not protected or leadership no longer feels accountable, confidence drains away.

And trust is difficult to rebuild because it cannot be ordered back into existence.

It has to be earned through visible fairness, consistent rules and leadership willing to accept that authority is temporary.

Sport may provide the stage.

But the real story is what institutions reveal about themselves when the pressure rises.

Catch up on all previous Beyond Game Day episodes here: https://www.enca.com/beyond-game-day-podcast

World.title: More extramural activities needed in schools to deal with violence
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - The Western Cape Education Department said schools need more extramural activities to keep pupils engaged.

School violence is under scrutiny after a Grade 10 pupil’s death at Bellville South High School.

The pupil died after an alleged classroom assault by another learner, reportedly linked to a cellphone theft two months earlier.

Western Cape Education spokesperson Bronagh Hammond has noted with concern how violence in society, particularly gangsterism, tends to spill over into the school grounds.

READ | 'How many more children must die?' Mother demands answers after school

She said pupils participate in gangs in their community and sometimes that comes into the school environment.

As such, she said it is very important to create a healthy school environment where there are after-school activities to keep pupils active and off the streets.

World.title: Severe cold, wet and windy conditions expected from Sunday
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - South Africa has been warned to prepare for a severe cold front expected to reach the country from Sunday.

The weather system is forecast to bring heavy rain, damaging winds, rough seas and snowfall to parts of the Western and Northern Cape before spreading to the Eastern Cape and inland.

READ | Cold, windy weekend expected in parts of KZN

Authorities have warned that flooding and hazardous driving conditions are likely, especially in mountain passes.

Farmers have been urged to protect livestock from the severe cold expected.

Government has encouraged the public to monitor official weather updates, avoid flooded roads and plan before travelling.
