World.title: Household income plunges in Greece, Austria despite overall OECD growth
World.content:
Household budgets across the OECD are barely keeping pace with inflation, as fresh data reveals income growth has slowed sharply just as GDP ticks higher, a divergence that is playing out very differently from one country to the next.

 

Real household income per capita in OECD countries increased by 0.2% in the first quarter of 2026, slowing from the 0.6% rise recorded in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Over the same period, real GDP per capita grew by 0.3%, edging up from 0.2% in the final quarter of 2025.

While GDP growth captures changes in overall economic activity, growth in household income reflects changes in the income households receive, that is, the income available for consumption or saving.

Of the 21 countries for which data are available, 13 recorded an increase in real household income per capita, while the remaining 8 saw a decline.

How G7 economies compare

Among G7 economies, real household income per capita rose by 0.2% in the first quarter of 2026, although developments varied from country to country.

In Italy, real household income per capita bounced back after a 0.9% fall in the fourth quarter of 2025 and increased by 0.8% in the first quarter of 2026.

The rebound was driven mainly by higher employee compensation, linked to a slight drop in the unemployment rate (from 5.7% to 5.4% in the first quarter of 2026), which offset a decline in social benefits.

At the same time, growth in real GDP per capita held steady at 0.3%.

In Canada, Germany and the United States, real household income per capita increased by 0.2%, compared with 0.0%, 0.1% and -0.2%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2025.

By contrast, in the United Kingdom real household income per capita fell by 0.8% after a 1.1% increase in the previous quarter. This drop reflects a higher tax burden on income and wealth, partly due to the reduction in the capital gains tax allowance, combined with lower net social benefits and stronger inflationary pressures.

Meanwhile, real GDP per capita in the United Kingdom rose by 0.6%, following two consecutive quarters of zero growth.

A slight decrease was also recorded in France, where real household income per capita edged down by 0.1% after a 0.3% increase in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Among the other OECD countries, the largest increases in real household income per capita were recorded in Hungary and Chile.

In Hungary, a 6.3% rise in employee compensation led to an acceleration in real household income per capita, from 1.7% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 6.0% in the first quarter of 2026, far outpacing the 0.9% increase in real GDP per capita.

In Chile, higher compensation for employees and the self-employed, together with an increase in net property income, resulted in a 4.8% rise in real household income per capita in the first quarter of 2026, after no change in the previous quarter.

Conversely, the sharpest declines in the first quarter of 2026 were recorded in Greece and Austria, where real household income per capita contracted because of falls in net property income and social benefits, dropping by 3.6% and 2.8%, respectively.

What happened in Greece in the first quarter of 2026

Real household disposable income per capita fell by 3.6% compared with the previous quarter, the steepest drop among OECD countries.

According to the OECD, the decline is mainly due to two factors: a reduction in net property income, such as interest, dividends and investment income, and a reduction in net social benefits to households.

World.title: Forget Venice and Amsterdam: Beat the crowds in Europe’s best alternative canal cities
World.content:
Venice introduced an entry fee for daytrippers on peak days in 2024, with current rates €5-€10 but calls to up that to €50.

 

Amsterdam, too, is oversaturated by tourists. It has launched several campaigns over the years to encourage better visitor behaviour, but with numbers still rising, residents resorted to suing the city last year.

If you want to avoid contributing to overtourism and have a better traveller experience, consider visiting some of Europe’s lesser-trod but equally picturesque canal cities.

Admire industrial beauty in Hamburg

Despite boasting more canals than both Amsterdam and Venice, Hamburg perhaps isn’t the first city you’d place on a romantic European canal trail map.

But as Europe’s third-largest port after Rotterdam and Antwerp, this is a city where its waterways have always had much more pragmatic uses.

The industrial beauty of the canals of modern Hamburg. Christian Lue

There’s a hard-edged industrial beauty to the canals of modern Hamburg, especially the historic warehouse district of Speicherstadt, which is now designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Though half of the warehouses were destroyed during the Second World War, their grandeur is enduring and a walk or a boat tour here is a must-do.

Take a stroll along Stockholm’s waterways

Situated on an archipelago of fourteen islands, Sweden’s capital is full of intersecting canals and rivers crisscrossed by a tapestry of more than 50 bridges. In fact, the original name for Stockholm’s historic Old Town was ‘The Town between the Bridges’ – Staden Mellan Broarna.

Situated on an archipelago of fourteen islands, Sweden’s capital is full of intersecting canals. Margo Evardson

Despite being located in the city centre, the Djurgårdsbrunnskanalen Canal is one of the quietest and most picturesque waterways.

Stretching 5km between attraction-heavy Djurgården and the mainland, its meandering tree-lined path is one of Stockholm’s most popular walking routes.

Drink at canal-side bars in Birmingham

Birmingham in the UK also famously has more kilometres of canal than Venice – and they have undergone a significant glow up since their industrial heyday.

Birmingham in the UK also famously has more kilometres of canal than Venice. Gabriel McCallin

With more than 160km of canals still navigable, the buzzing bars and cafes at Gas Street Basin show off the city’s canals at their most vibrant, while the gently curving towpath running down to the University of Birmingham is a bucolic escape from the hum of the city centre.

Take a boat tour in Copenhagen

With the 17th-century waterfront district of Nyhavn at its heart, Copenhagen is one of Europe’s most charming cities to take a canal cruise.

Famed for its brightly coloured townhouses and old wooden ships, Nyhavn’s a superb location to stroll on a summer afternoon or take a boat tour.

Copenhagen is one of Europe’s most charming cities to take a canal cruise. Ava Coploff

But while it may project an air of sophistication today, during its early years (from around 1670) Nyhavn was a notorious area for hedonistic sailors in search of alcohol and prostitutes.

In the 19th century it was home to Hans Christian Anderson and in 1980 it was pedestrianised, leading to its revitalisation as a tourist area.

World.title: Exclusive: Euronews ‘extremist’ label is Lukashenka’s revenge, Tsikhanouskaya said
World.content:
Belarus’ decision to classify Euronews as “extremist” is an act of revenge for its reporting on the country’s disputed 2020 election, political prisoners and Russia’s war against Ukraine, opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said on Friday.

 

In an exclusive interview with Euronews, Tsikhanouskaya said the move showed that Aliaksandr Lukashenka’s government remained afraid of independent information six years after the mass protests that followed the presidential election.

“It is revenge - revenge by the regime for Euronews’ reporting,” she said.

“Euronews covered the 2020 protests, it covered the election, which Lukashenka lost. It covered the stories of political prisoners and the war, which started from Belarus.”

Belarusian information ministry placed Euronews’ website on its "Republican List of Extremist Materials," according to Belarus-based media. The ruling is subject to immediate execution under Belarusian civil procedure rules.

The decision means access to the Euronews website will now be restricted in Belarus, while readers could face administrative penalties for storing or distributing its content.

Euronews’ television broadcast was already banned in Belarus in 2021.

Tsikhanouskaya noted called the decisions “hypocritical” given that Lukashenka himself gave an interview to Euronews before.

“Now even watching them can be considered a crime in Belarus".

She warned that the designation could turn viewing and sharing independent news into a pretext for repression.

“Watching Euronews or reading the Euronews website can land you in jail. Sharing Euronews news can become a crime.”

The ruling gave the regime and its law enforcement agency KGB “another excuse to prosecute people who are simply looking for information”, Tsikhanouskaya said, adding that journalists, contributors and those assisting news organisations could also be at risk.

FILE: FILE - Protesters with old Belarusian national flags march at an opposition rally in Minsk, Belarus, on Sept. 6, 2020. AP Photo

Her comments come ahead of the sixth anniversary of the August 2020 election, which was followed by an unprecedented wave of peaceful demonstrations against Lukashenka’s declared victory.

The opposition, the EU and many western governments rejected the result as fraudulent.

The authorities responded with a sweeping crackdown on protesters, activists, independent media and civil society.

Tsikhanouskaya said repression had become the operating principle of the state because the government feared that a relaxation could trigger another public uprising.

“If it stops, people will rise up again,” she said. “Constant, systemic repression has become the modus operandi of the entire system.”

She added that arrests continued daily and that the true scale of the crackdown remained unclear because many detainees were not publicly identified.

“Under such terror, visible protest is almost impossible. It has gone underground,” she said. “But I know that people haven’t given up. They are waiting and preparing for new momentum.”

FILEL: Police officers detain Nina Bahinskaya, 73, during an opposition rally to protest the official presidential election results in Minsk, Belarus, Sept. 19, 2020. AP Photo

The opposition leader, who lives in exile, argued that control of information was central to the government’s survival. Millions of Belarusians still follow independent outlets covertly, she said, using virtual private networks and other tools to bypass censorship.

“Independent media are the backbone of our movement,” Tsikhanouskaya said.

She stated that independent reporting had helped ensure that many Belarusians understood the reality of Russia’s war in Ukraine, despite official propaganda, and that most supported Ukraine.

But she warned that the state was adapting as quickly as citizens. “The KGB often uses tech platforms to track, identify, and prosecute opponents,” she said, adding that her team was working with companies including Meta and Alphabet to ensure their platforms were not used to facilitate persecution.

Tsikhanouskaya advised people in Belarus to make digital security a priority, including by using VPNs, keeping separate devices for accessing independent media and avoiding contact with unknown accounts that could be linked to security services.

Related Belarus ban of Euronews sparks debate and support for press freedom across Europe

She said Belarusians were also advised to regularly clear their phones, use pseudonyms online and avoid responding to unknown contacts, which could be attempts by the KGB to recruit or blackmail them. Some independent outlets use accounts that are not branded as “extremist”, she said, allowing audiences to continue accessing information under difficult conditions.

“Difficult conditions force us to be creative,” she said. “That is the only way to survive under a dictatorship.”

She said the “extremist” designation should not deter Euronews from continuing its work.

“Euronews can take this designation as a badge of honour,” Tsikhanouskaya said.

“Many decent people and organisations have been declared ‘extremist’ by the dictator. It means your work matters.”

Despite the crackdown, she urged Belarusians not to see the democratic movement as defeated.

“Our struggle has not ended. It has simply taken a different form,” she said. “It is no longer a sprint, but a marathon.”

Tsikhanouskaya said a strong Ukraine and a weakened Russia could create an opening for democratic change in Belarus, arguing that Lukashenka’s government depended on the Kremlin’s support.

“Without Russian support, Lukashenka’s regime will not survive,” she said. “That is why so many Belarusians hope for Ukraine’s victory.”

Vladimir Putin and Aliaksandr Lukashenka pose for a photo during their meeting in St. Petersburg, Russia,Dec. 21, 2025. AP Photo

Tsikhanouskaya urged western partners to see Belarus “not only as a problem, but also as an opportunity”, arguing that democratic forces must be ready to seize any opening created by a shift in the regional balance of power.

“Dictatorships often collapse when no one expects it,” she said.

Belarusians wanted peaceful change through free elections, without violence, and a future in Europe rather than under Russian control, she said.

“A free, democratic and independent Belarus would make Europe much safer for everyone.”

World.title: Iceland’s EU vote: A nation divided over Europe
World.content:
Security concerns, control over fishing rights and rising living costs are shaping Iceland's debate over whether to restart talks on joining the European Union.

The white church stands alone in the Icelandic countryside. Wind sweeps across the Hvalfjord. Kristjan Ingolfsson, a retired bishop, lives here beside Hallgrimskirkja church in Saubaer, surrounded by silence and vast open landscapes.

But far from this quiet corner of western Iceland, the debate over Europe is heating up. At the end of August, voters will decide whether to reopen accession talks with the European Union. The referendum is not about joining the EU immediately, but about restarting negotiations that were suspended more than a decade ago.

"[Icelandic] people are a bit different to the mainland folks, who always have to think about borders. We have no border, just the sea all around," Kristjan Ingolfsson says.

"That gives a specific feeling of freedom. And I believe that's also part of the whole discussion, that people want to be free."

Whether campaigning for or against closer ties with Brussels, many Icelanders frame the debate around the same ideas: freedom, independence, and sovereignty.

The 'Yes' campaign

At the headquarters of the pro-European group in the capital, Reykjavik, supporters are celebrating the official launch of the campaign. The small office is packed, with volunteers spilling onto the pavement in the afternoon sun. Young people mingle with pensioners. A DJ provides music while beer and soft drinks are kept chilled in ice buckets.

At the center of it all is Snaeros Sindradottir, executive director of the 'Yes' campaign. The 34-year-old mother normally runs an art gallery, but that work is now on hold. Instead, she spends her days campaigning for a closer relationship with Europe.

Snaeros Sindradottir has put her art gallery career on hold to campaign for closer ties between Iceland and the European Union Image: Dmytro Rusanow/DW

The referendum is taking place at a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty. US President Donald Trump's threats toward neighboring Greenland have become part of Iceland's debate over Europe, says Snaeros Sindradottir.

"And it's not a very comforting fact that Trump has mispronounced Greenland as Iceland on several occasions."

Iceland, with its population of about 400,000, has no standing army. Protection is provided through NATO, of which Iceland is a founding member. The country also has a bilateral defense agreement with Washington. During the Cold War, the US maintained an important military base near Reykjavik, although its permanent troop presence ended in 2006.

"I think security would definitely be increased if we enter the EU," says Snaeros Sindradottir.

"Given the situation in the United States, it would be wiser to lean [on] our true allies and friends in Europe."

Iceland is already closely tied to Europe. The country belongs to the European Economic Area (EEA), allowing free movement of goods, services, capital and people between Iceland and most EU countries, even though the island nation is not an EU member. It is also part of the passport-free Schengen zone.

Pawel Bartoszek, chairman of parliament's foreign affairs committee, points to Iceland's small and relatively volatile currency.

"It has cost us much higher inflation and interest rates compared to continental Europe," he says.

Bartoszek argues that joining the euro in the future could lower borrowing costs for households and businesses. Mortgage rates of 8 to 9% are common in Iceland, while borrowers elsewhere in Europe often pay roughly half as much.

The 'No' campaign

In downtown Reykjavik, campaigners from the anti-EU movement are making the opposite case. They have set up a small table where they hand out leaflets and "No" campaign badges. Haraldur Olafsson, a physics professor, currently spends up to 12 hours a day campaigning against membership.

"We are basically here to explain to the people that being members of the European Union is a huge step away from democracy."

"We are giving power to someone else who will make rules that we cannot control," he adds.

For years, Haraldur Olafsson has campaigned against joining the EU. He is the president of the Heimssyn organization, which belongs to the 'No' camp.

Haraldur Olafsson is campaigning against closer ties with the European Union, arguing that Iceland should preserve its independence Image: Dmytro Rusanow/DW

The 'No' campaign's stand is quiet today. Tourists crowd the square opposite parliament, every now and then Olafsson is approached by acquaintances. This is Iceland. People know each other here.

"I do not know anybody in Iceland who fears either the Russians or the Americans," Haraldur Olafsson says.

"Really, I don't think these international matters matter a lot when it comes to local politics. The only threat comes from the European Union. The European Union is the only big power in the world that wants to govern Iceland, that wants to set the laws in Iceland and wants to pass judgment."

Supporters of EU membership reject this argument, saying that as an EU member Iceland would participate in decision-making rather than simply follow rules set elsewhere.

Rich fishing industry

Iceland's thriving fishing industry is one of the foundations of the country's prosperity. That is why the debate over possible EU membership has become highly emotional, with both sides arguing over whether the European Union would gain control over Iceland's valuable marine resources.

"The European Union has nothing to say about the natural resources in Iceland — the sea, the fish," Haraldur Olafsson says.

"The European Union doesn't have the final word on energy, which is a very important natural resource for Iceland."

"The economy of Iceland is very different from the economy of Europe. The main disadvantage is that the EU would take over the administration of [our] natural resources," he argues.

Former fisherman Agust Österby (left) and Haraldur Olafsson reflect on questions of independence, resources and Iceland’s future in Europe Image: Dmytro Rusanow/DW

Haraldur Olafsson heads down to Reykjavik's harbor. Here he meets former fisherman Agust Österby, who is standing on his wooden boat, fixing an old window frame. Österby first went to sea with his father when he was six years old. Today, he restores wooden boats.

Icelanders, he says, are stubborn and independent by nature.

"It is somehow in our genes to deal with [things] ourselves — to deal with life, the sea and the weather."

He adds: "We will never give our freedom to the European Union. We know exactly how to do things in Iceland. We don't need help from abroad."

The former fisherman says he does not think Icelanders feel threatened by anyone — not even Donald Trump.

Referendum to break the deadlock

The belief that Iceland can simply keep a low profile and avoid international pressure is something political scientist Audunn Arnorsson disagrees with. He fears the strategy "might backfire."

If Iceland were ever to face pressure similar to that experienced by Greenland from its "big brother in the West," having the possibility of EU accession could prove valuable, including access to the bloc's common customs protection.

Iceland had already begun accession negotiations once before, in 2010, following the banking and economic crisis. They were later suspended after a change in government and never resumed. Audunn Arnorsson argues that holding a referendum became the only way to break the political deadlock over whether Iceland should reopen negotiations.

Debate dividing Iceland

Members of Iceland's parliament are also divided over whether the country should resume accession talks with the European Union. The debate cuts across traditional party lines.

Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, leader of the opposition Independence Party, believes that a small nation like Iceland may have a bigger voice outside the European Union than inside.

"In the European Parliament, we would have approximately six seats out of 726. We are afraid that we will just disappear in this mass that the European Union is."

Smaller EU member states such as Malta, Luxembourg and Cyprus also hold the minimum allocation of six seats in the European Parliament.

Opinion is divided in Iceland, a country of around 400,000 people, over whether the island nation should resume accession talks with the EU Image: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

For Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, joining the EU is not the solution for strengthening Iceland's security.

"Our strength lies in NATO and our bilateral agreement with the United States of America. And we have not had any discussion from [the] American side that they want to change that agreement that we have had here in Iceland for decades."

But something else concerns the opposition leader deeply: the divisions the debate has created within families and friendships.

"We are building a wound that won't heal [for] years. We can't survive in this harsh country if we don't have solidarity between us, so that we can fight Mother Nature."

Opinion polls predict a tight race, with support for and opposition to closer EU integration running neck and neck. Both camps are now fighting for the same group: the many undecided voters who are likely to determine the result on August 29.

A 'yes' vote would not mean EU membership. It would only open accession talks — with a second referendum required before Iceland could ultimately join the bloc.

But former bishop Kristjan Ingolfsson is confident: "No matter how it turns out — we will remain one people and [it will] not build walls between us."

World.title: Migrant tunnels in Lithuania direct suspicion towards Minsk
World.content:
Lithuania's border guards have discovered tunnels through which migrants are trying to enter the country from Belarus. Analysts see them as a means to destabilize the country.

Migrants are taking a new route to enter the Baltic country Lithuania: underground tunnels. These could be yet another attempt by Belarus to foster political instability, experts say.

The country's border guards say they have found 12 such tunnels since the beginning of the year near the Belarusian border, with a length of up to 25 meters on the Lithuanian side. They are expecting more to emerge.

Lithuania's border with Belarus is about 700 kilometers long, around 550 kilometers of which are fenced.

"We have a ground seismic system, which can detect easily when there's a high level of vibrations over a long period of time," General Rustamas Liubajevas, the commander of Lithuania's State Border Guard Service, explained to DW.

"We then wait [outside a tunnel] for the final stage of the digging and when the migrants come out, we apprehend them," he said, adding that up to 40 migrants exiting such tunnels had been arrested.

Last year Lithuania registered 1652 irregular border crossings Image: Lithuania's State Border Guard Service

Lithuania's prosecutor's office confirmed to DW that a pre-trial investigation was under way concerning approximately 20 people suspected of illegally digging a tunnel. Possible charges also include people smuggling. Due to the investigation, no media visits are currently authorized at the sites.

Liubajevas is surprised migrants would attempt a subterranean crossing.

"It takes a lot of effort to dig a tunnel and the migrants are arrested almost immediately — at most, one small group gets through," he said.

Is Minsk lending a hand?

The elaborate nature of the tunnels has led him to believe the migrants aren't working alone.

"They wouldn't be able to go through with this without logistical support from the Belarusian authorities, as they need a lot of material like wood to strengthen the tunnels' walls," he stressed, adding that Belarus seemingly wanted to "keep the level of tension at the border high."

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenkohas denied facilitating migration flows to neighboring states. Similar migrant tunnels were discovered in the past in neighboring Poland.

Margarita Seselgyte, Director of the Institute of International Relations and Political Science at Vilnius University, seconded Liubajevas' view.

"Belarus is watching its border very closely, and the country doesn't fit in the natural migration route of migrants from Afghanistan, Iran or Sri Lanka," she told DW, adding that Minsk had to at least have turned a blind eye to any digging activity taking place near the border.

Some experts believe the Belarusian state is envouraging the building of tunnels across the border Image: Lithuania's State Border Guard Service

Seselgyte thus sees the tunnels as "a hybrid attack to cause anxiety in our society."

"There is no vacuum in the world of security. As Lithuania has been closing vulnerabilities and reinforcing its border fence, Belarus is now helping migrants pass beneath it," she said.

A long-running issue at the eastern flank of Europe

For her, Minsk is assisting its close ally Moscow. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 partly from Belarus, where it amassed troops under the pretext of military drills.

"Lithuania has been very vocal in terms of defense against Russia, both conventional and hybrid, on an EU and Nato level, and they want to silence that voice by causing chaos in our country," the political scientist said.

"The main goal is probably to weaken support for Ukraine and disrupt European unity," she added.

Linas Kojala, CEO of Vilnius-based think tank Geopolitics and Security Studies Center, noted that the tunnels were keeping the border force busy – even if only a few migrants got through.

He described the tunnels as "just another phase of the attack of weaponized migration we've been facing since 2021."

Most of the Lithuania-Belarus border is lined with fencing Image: Arnaud Dumontier/MAXPPP/IMAGO

That's when tens of thousands of migrants crossed into Lithuania, Poland and Latvia from Belarus. The European Union called the events a "state-sponsored instrumentalization of migrants at the EU external border," organized by Lukashenko.

"Latvia, Poland, Lithuania and other countries have since set up external borders and we've managed to bring down illegal migration to a minimum," Kojala told DW. Lithuania's border guards registered 1652 attempts to enter the country irregularly in 2025.

But this number won't go down to zero unless Minsk deals with the problem on its side, according to Kojala. "And that's unlikely: Belarus is clearly trying to pose as many problems as possible."

'Migration has long been used as a strategic tool'

Belarus would be far from the first country to use migration as a strategic tool, underlined Robert Gonzci, an analyst at the Migration Research Institute in the Hungarian capital of Budapest.

"It's a relatively low-cost, low-risk way of exerting pressure on other countries, and since the 1950s, there've been numerous documented cases of governments creating or manipulating migration flows," he said to DW.

He added that even the Assyrian empire – which collapsed in the seventh century BC – used migration to consolidate imperial control.

Gonzci didn't rule out that autonomous smuggling networks might be behind the recently discovered tunnels, which Belarusian authorities don't fully control.

He added that Belarus and Russia have used weaponized migration to "divert Western attention from Russia's broader strategic agenda and create instability along NATO's eastern flank by fueling political and social tensions within European countries."

Poland's EU border: A threat to nature and people To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The states organizing such operations – often authoritarian regimes – enjoyed an inherent strategic advantage, Gonzci stressed.

"The target is usually a democratic state facing a fundamental dilemma: They must protect their sovereignty by securing their borders while simultaneously upholding their legal obligations and humanitarian commitments," he said.

Eastern countries 'showing resilience'

But experts seem to agree that countries on the EU's eastern flank have been doing rather well in that respect.

"There's increasing cooperation and coordination between the Nordic and Baltic States and Poland, as these countries are facing similar challenges. And the EU Frontex mission has been sending additional equipment," Seselgyte said.

Lithuania is currently receiving technical support from neighboring countries.

"We are testing Polish scanning equipment, through which we can identify empty spaces underground. If these tools work well, we'll buy and deploy them," explained Liubajevas.

World.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy makes first visit to Russia-friendly Serbia
World.content:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy is making his first visit to Serbia. His host, President Aleksandar Vucic, hopes to score points with the EU, while Zelenskyy seeks more arms from a country that remains Russia-friendly.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic have met several times in the past, often on the sidelines of multilateral conferences, and most recently on July 15, 2026, in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv.

On Friday, Zelenskyy arrived in Serbia for his first official state visit to the country.

The talks, however, are likely to require careful political balancing. Despite Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine, Serbia remains widely regarded as Europe's most pro-Russian country.

There have recently been several signs of closer ties between Belgrade and Kyiv. Ukraine's First Lady, Olena Zelenska, visited Belgrade two years ago. But a trip by the Ukrainian president has been postponed several times.

For Vucic, who has ruled Serbia with an iron fist for the past 14 years, the visit is a balancing act ahead of crucial parliamentary elections. A student-led protest movement plans to field its own electoral list, with a realistic chance of seriously challenging Vucic for the first time. The president has been accused of corruption and of exerting control over the media and judiciary.

According to opinion polls, the majority of Vucic's loyal supporters side with Russia and oppose Serbia joining the European Union. Pro-government media outlets, such as the tabloid Informer, have openly backed Moscow in the war.

Nevertheless, Vucic has portrayed Zelenskyy's trip as an ordinary state visit, saying: "We have several important issues to discuss. One is Ukraine's and Serbia's path toward Europe; the second is our bilateral and energy cooperation."

Observers expect the meeting to prove mutually beneficial. "Zelenskyy welcomes anything that comes across as a kind of slap in the face for [Russian President] Putin," political analyst and pollster Djordje Vukadinovic told DW. "That also applies to the European Union, which certainly played a role in making this meeting happen."

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic (left) and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (right) met at the Ukraine–Southeast Europe Summit in Kyiv in July 2026, weeks before Zelenskyy's first official visit to Belgrade Image: Alina Smutko/REUTERS

At the same time, Vucic wants to "present himself as being as open to cooperation as possible with the EU," especially after seeing what happened to Hungary's Viktor Orban. "Brussels still has enough carrots and sticks at its disposal in this part of the Balkans, and Vucic cannot afford to draw criticism from Brussels ahead of the next election," Vukadinovic said.

Serbian-made artillery shells

Zelenskyy may also be looking to secure Serbian munitions. Large quantities of Serbian artillery shells have already been delivered to Ukraine through intermediaries, despite Serbia's pro-Russian stance and opposition to anti-Russian sanctions. The Financial Times newspaper estimated that the value of military goods delivered to Ukraine totaled €1 billion ($1.15 billion) in 2024.

Christopher Hill, a seasoned US diplomat, who recently ended his career as ambassador to Serbia, spoke candidly about how he had brought the Ukrainian military and Serbian defense industry together.

"The US began supporting the purchase of significant quantities of Serbian ammunition, which we knew Ukraine urgently needed," Hill told German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung. Countries such as the Czech Republic and Poland officially bought the weapons before transferring them to Ukraine.

According to the newspaper, discussions are also taking place behind the scenes about building a joint drone factory using Ukrainian expertise, Serbian workers, and investment from the United Arab Emirates. Zelenskyy's team has reportedly already inspected potential locations in secret.

"Ukraine is trying to expand its circle of European partners, including those countries that have not imposed sanctions on Russia," Srdjan Majstorovic of the Belgrade-based think tank European Policy Centre told DW. "At the same time, Serbia has a defense industry whose products matter to Ukraine's war effort."

Flip-flopping between Russia, EU

Although Serbia continues to promote the narrative of an "Orthodox brotherhood" with Russia, the Kremlin has increasingly signaled its dissatisfaction with Vucic. This is particularly evident in the context of Russian gas deliveries, one of Russia's most powerful sources of leverage.

Recently, Serbia has only been offered short-term gas contracts, which has increased economic uncertainty and undermined Vucic's economic model, which aims to attract foreign investors through cheap labor and low energy costs.

Zelenskyy's visit comes as Vucic (pictured) tries to balance Serbia’s traditional ties with Moscow against pressure to align its foreign policy with the European Union Image: Djordje Kojadinovic/REUTERS

That is why some observers say Serbia is forced to flip-flop between Moscow and the EU — by far Serbia's most important trading partner.

Yet political analyst Vukadinovic disagrees. "Superficial observers categorize Vucic's moves as either 'pro-EU' or 'pro-Russia,' but both approaches are equally dishonest — Vucic is looking to spot the greatest threat and how best to benefit, with the goal of holding on to power forever."

Vucic finds himself in a precarious situation. The student protests — which began in late 2024 following the collapse of the Novi Sad train station canopy which killed 16 people — have made the outcome of the upcoming parliamentary election, expected to take place this fall, completely unpredictable. The protesters accuse the government of corruption and incompetence. Some opinion polls even place the movement in the lead.

Vucic's critics therefore fear large-scale efforts to manipulate the election, for instance, through gifts to voters, exerting pressure on public-sector employees, or "importing" voters from Republika Srpska, the Serb entity of neighboring Bosnia and Herzegovina.

EU accession talks

EU criticism of Vucic has so far been both restrained and at times contradictory. While the European Commission has recommended moving ahead with Serbian accession negotiations, some EU member states oppose this due to concerns about democratic deficits in the Balkan country.

"It is quite possible that Zelenskyy's state visit and Serbia's cooperation with Ukraine will be used by some EU member states and the European Commission to push ahead with Serbia's accession talks, especially now that geopolitical considerations risk overshadowing rule-of-law criteria," Majstorovic said.

Yet Vucic also holds a trump card that he regularly plays to his domestic audience whenever he meets Zelenskyy on the sidelines of international summits.

Ukraine, like Russia, has never recognized the independence of the former Serbian province of Kosovo. This fact plays well with Vucic's voters.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Trump to appeal ballroom construction halt to Supreme Court
World.content:
A US Court of Appeals upheld a ruling that saying Trump cannot build a White House ballroom without congressional approval. The president vowed to appeal what he called an "unjust decision."

US President Donald Trump was ordered on Friday to halt construction of a ballroom on the site of the demolished East Wing.

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld a preliminary injunction won by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which had sued Trump over the matter last year.

It was a major setback for Trump, who has touted the project, saying the White House needed a large ballroom to host events.

The court's ruling has been placed on hold for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal the ruling to the US Supreme Court.

Trump confirmed the move, saying his team will be "immediately appealing" to the Supreme Court.

The US president blasted the decision as a "horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful ruling."

"The Circuit Court also refused to acknowledge that the desperately needed, and totally secure Ballroom, which is being built ahead of schedule and under budget, is a Gift from President Trump and Great Patriots of the United States of America," Trump added in a social media post.

What did the court say?

Judges Patricia Millett and Brad Garcia, both appointed by Democratic presidents, said the ‌order does not permanently bar construction of the ballroom, but rather it merely halts above-ground work during the lawsuit and until the White House secures approval from Congress.

"Each President is a temporary tenant, not the ‌owner, of the White House" ⁠and ⁠cannot fundamentally reshape it without congressional approval, the court said.

"Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the panel's majority wrote. "Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People's House — to fit a particular ‌President's desires."

Additionally, the court scolded "the bold assertion that the Executive can act with utter lawlessness, destroying treasured national landmarks and harming the interests of individuals."

The East Wing demolition is the biggest structural change to the White House in over 70 years Image: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

Court rejects 'national security' argument

Work on the 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom began last year with the swift demolition of the White House's entire historic East Wing. It is the biggest structural change to the White House in over 70 years.

White House lawyers argued that the ballroom includes critical security features to guard against a range of threats, such as drones, ballistic missiles and biohazards.

"These upgrades, alterations, and improvements are essential to protecting the President, his family, and his staff, as well as the White House itself, and the entire project flows from them," government attorneys told the court.

But the justices in the majority shot down the argument, saying that national security arguments "are not an automatic get-out-of-law-free card."

World.title: Ceuta: Spain sets up border controls on travelers from Italy
World.content:
Spain had warned Italy it would impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.

Spain's government on Friday moved to impose reciprocal entry checks on people traveling from Italy. The Spanish government had warned that it would do so unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's governemnt lifted the border measures it has implemented against Spain.

Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week.

The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes.

Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy.

Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Spain say about checks on travelers from Italy?

The border controls on Italy will go into effect from midnight ‌on ⁠Saturday ⁠until September 7, the Spanish government said. Border agents will check passport, nationality and visas for Italian passengers and visitors from other ​countries arriving from Italy.

Spain had called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population."

Madrid said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years.

"If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said.

Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15.

Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zoneamid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however.

Italy first made the announcement as images and footage of the border breach were going viral online Image: Atlas/REUTERS

What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain?

Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground.

Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure.

"They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers."

Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities.

"I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough."

EU defends border response after Ceuta crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration

At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration.

Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe.

Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market.

Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare.

"Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years."

World.title: How viable is the potential Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping deal?
World.content:
Iran says a shipping accord with Oman is in its final stages, but analysts warn sanctions, security concerns and rival US-Iran goals could limit its impact.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, said this week that an agreement with Oman, which lies on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz, is in the "final stage" of review and drafting — provided that no external party interfered in the process.

The two Persian Gulf states have agreed on the geographical coordinates of a navigation route through the strait, Baghaei was quoted as saying by state news agency IRNA on Wednesday evening.

Baghaei told journalists that even if an understanding was reached, it would not mean that the strait had become safe for all passing vessels.

"The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests," he said.

What the agreement could look like

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi also said an agreement on new shipping arrangements was nearing completion, IRNA reported.

Gharibabadi stressed that the proposed arrangement would not amount to a full reopening of the strait, but would instead establish a new model for maritime traffic.

According to IRNA, Gharibabadi said the route would be temporary and could remain open for between two and four months.

Shipowners hope Strait of Hormuz will reopen soon To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tehran said that any reopening of the strait must be accompanied by an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports.

Reports cited by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said Iran was planning to block US and Israeli ships from the waterway as part of a deal with Oman.

Iran also argued that vessels passing through the strait should pay fees for safe passage. Oman did not support unilateral Iranian control of the waterway.

Obstacles and skepticism

A proposed deal between Iran and Oman to give Tehran control over ships entering the Persian Gulf ​through the Strait ⁠of Hormuz is not easily workable because of US sanctions and restrictive insurance clauses ⁠on payments, according to industry sources cited by Reuters on Friday.

However, analysts cautioned that any deal on the reopening of the strait should be viewed as a tactical pause rather than a durable settlement.

Security analyst Shukriya Bradost told DW such a pause could benefit Washington more than Tehran.

"The United States could use the period to improve coordination with its regional partners, review its military strategy and prepare stronger options," she said.

"Iran, meanwhile, would continue facing economic pressure, internal divisions and growing political and security costs."

"If this period becomes merely a pause in tensions and Tehran fails to secure a tangible strategic gain, the passage of time may benefit the United States more than any other party," Bradost added.

What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other analysts pointed to fundamental disagreements over the future governance of the waterway.

Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, said Tehran and Washington are pursuing different objectives.

"Iran wants control over vessels entering the strait, while the United States wants completely free passage," Dorbeiki told DW. "These positions cannot easily be reconciled."

Competing views of Iran's role in Hormuz

Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, said both Tehran and Washington could potentially present a deal as a tactical success.

From Iran's perspective, he said any understanding could be presented as an achievement.

"The regime has not collapsed, its missile capabilities remain intact, enriched uranium has not left the country, and for the first time since the war, Iran has reinforced its leverage over the inbound shipping lane of the strait," he told DW.

Salavati added that Tehran could claim domestically that it has preserved the strategic leverage of the Strait of Hormuz.

He said the United States could also portray the situation as a success in the form of "relief from the pressure of soaring energy prices, an opportunity to replenish weapons stockpiles while easing pressure on defence production, and the ability to declare an end to the active phase of the war."

Salavati suggested that Tehran is unlikely to regard any arrangement as the end of the broader confrontation.

Trump has faced pressure from members of his own party in Congress to bring the conflict to a close before November's midterm elections.

Oman has not publicly commented on the reported agreement, which Iran says was negotiated without US involvement.

World.title: Berlin clubs struggle as drink sales dry up and costs rise
World.content:
Berlin's clubs are still drawing crowds, but shorter nights, fewer alcohol sales and rising costs have changed their business model. Door fees, rather than bar takings, are increasingly their real financial lifeline.

Berlin's world-famous club scene has remained in high demand, but venues are increasingly struggling to turn packed dancefloors into sustainable businesses.

A major survey released on Friday found that club revenue has shifted dramatically away from drinks and toward admission fees.

What's happened to Berlin's clubs?

The shift reflects changing nightlife habits since 2017, when around 60% of revenue came from food and drink sales and just 21% from entry fees.

Today, ticket sales account for 59% of revenue, while food and drink generate just 20%.

"People are planning their club nights more consciously, staying for shorter periods, and drinking less,” according to the report, the first comprehensive study of the sector since 2019.

Some 73% of respondents said alcohol consumption was falling, while 60% reported rising demand for non-alcoholic drinks and 57% said guests were staying for shorter periods.

At the same time, costs are rising.

Staff costs were cited as a major burden by 64% of respondents, operating costs by 62%, customers' declining purchasing power by 60%, and rents and leases by 54%.

Some 85% of the clubs polled said financial pressure was already changing their event programs.

Is running a Berlin club lucrative?

Demand remains strong, with 83% of clubs and event organizers reporting occupancy rates of at least 50% and around a third exceeding 75%.

But fewer venues are making enough money to cover their costs.

Club closures in Berlin: The end of an era? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2017, 79% were at least breaking even. By 2025, that figure had dropped to 61%.

Some 39% ended the year in the red, compared with 21% in 2017.

The number of smaller operators has also risen sharply. Some 45% now generate less than €100,000 ($115,595) in annual revenue, compared with 16% in 2017.

Long-term insecurity remains another major problem. Only 8% of operators own their venues, while 31% have rental or lease agreements lasting less than five years.

How are clubs adapting?

Some 23% of respondents said they were considering closing their business within the next 12 months. Since 2020, at least 24 club and cultural venues have closed, but around 25 new ones have opened.

Many venues have already adapted to the pressure.

Some 67% have increased drink prices, 47% have raised admission charges and 39% have expanded private rentals.

The Club Commission is calling for publicly owned buildings to be opened up for nightlife, more reliable long-term funding, formal recognition of clubs as cultural venues and better working conditions.

World.title: Eco wins: Hungary goes solar, marmots go viral and Rome gets an upgrade
World.content:
From Hungary's accidental solar revolution to marmot crowdfunding and a long-overdue upgrade for Rome's big snake, good news comes in strange packages this week.

Hungary's former leader Viktor Orban called European Union climate policy a "utopian fantasy" and effectively banned wind turbines. And yet the country has quietly become Europe's solar leader, with 25% of its electricity now being being generated from the renewable energy source, ahead of sunnier countries like Spain, and Greece.

The boom was driven not by climate concern but by self-sufficiency politics and cheap subsidies. Now a 450-megawatt park, just east of Budapest, is due online by September 2026. It's set to power around 106,000 households.



Marmot researchers find a new way to fund their science

When US federal funding dried up, researchers from UCLA and the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory got creative. They launched OnlyMarms: a free platform posting videos of yellow-bellied marmots eating, digging and scampering in the wild, where fans can donate to support the science.

The team has tracked individually marked marmots in Colorado since 1962, building six decades of data on family lives, social behavior and responses to environmental change — and say studying marmot hibernation could even hold clues about human aging.

Rome's 'big snake' gets a cooler future

Corviale, a kilometer-long brutalist housing complex outside Rome nicknamed "the big snake," was completed in the 1980s and has since fallen into decay. With summers in some parts of Italy's now averaging around 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), life inside has become tough for its more than 4,000 residents.

But upgrades are coming: a new library doubling as a cooling shelter, more trees and energy efficiency improvements, all aimed at helping Corviale stay cool as temperatures keep rising.

Senegalese designer turns discarded textiles into sustainable fashion

Berlin-based designer Mame Khady Badji transforms discarded clothing into bold garments inspired by her Senegalese heritage, combining traditional Ndiakhass techniques with contemporary streetwear. Her creations have drawn musicians, performers and creatives — and recently appeared at Berlin Fashion Week 2026.

After moving to Germany in 2017, Badji built her label with support from Berlin's textile community. Now she's pursuing an ambitious goal: proving that recycled fashion can be both culturally rooted and commercially viable.

World.title: Juan Antonio González Hernández, ‘Toño’, el cronista de los astros de La Palma nos da sus mejores pistas en la isla
World.content:
Guía Starlight y del Observatorio del Roque de Los Muchachos, su pasión por los cielos nocturnos nació hace tres décadas y la ha convertido en su profesión. Una vida dedicada a la divulgación astronómica en la isla canaria, de la que recomienda los mejores miradores

En la isla de La Palma, Juan Antonio González Hernández (La Palma, 1972) es conocido como Toño. Es uno de esos tipos que ha hecho de su afición su profesión. Además de astrónomo aficionado, es divulgador, guía Starlight —parte del primer grupo de profesionales de la isla homologados como tal por el Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias— y del Observatorio del Roque de Los Muchachos (ORM). También es promotor de productos tematizados en astroturismo, astrofotógrafo, consultor, responsable de varios proyectos del Cabildo Insular de La Palma y exgerente de la empresa Cielos-LaPalma.

Una concatenación de hechos a mediados de los ochenta le hizo mirar al cielo y hasta hoy. Primero fue la inauguración, en 1985, del ORM (en el mundo solo hay otros dos observatorios de este tipo: uno en Chile y otro en Hawái) y, un año después, la noche del 12 de abril de 1986, el paso del cometa Halley. Ese fenómeno astronómico lo dibujó a lápiz, con paciencia y con ayuda de unos prismáticos desde el balcón de su casa, en la barriada de El Pilar, en Santa Cruz de La Palma. Su hambre de galaxias, planetas, estrellas y satélites la fue saciando registrando manchas solares durante los recreos del instituto, leyendo libros de astronomía, viendo Cosmos —serie de televisión escrita y presentada por Carl Sagan— y sumándose a la Agrupación Astronómica Palmera (AAP), que llegó a presidir durante 12 años. De la mano de alguno de los miembros de dicha agrupación tuvo la oportunidad de subir al ORM y disfrutar de las vistas del cielo sobre un mar de nubes a casi 2.400 metros de altitud. Son tantas las estrellas que se pueden contemplar a simple vista desde este punto que no es fácil distinguir las constelaciones.

Cielo estrellado sobre el el Observatorio del Roque de Los Muchachos, en la isla de La Palma. Luis Davilla (GETTY IMAGES)

En 1991, con conocimiento y ya equipado con instrumentos de observación, se decantó por la carrera de Astrofísica, “pero no para viajar y hacer investigación. Yo quería enseñar, soñaba con divulgar astronomía, como Sagan”, cuenta a El Viajero de camino a un punto de observación de La Palma. En la Universidad de La Laguna en Tenerife estudió dos años; una etapa personal complicada hizo que abandonase la carrera y regresase a La Palma. De vuelta a su isla natal estudió una FP de Técnico Administrativo y empezó a trabajar como consignatario de barcos en el puerto. Se casó, tiene dos hijos y nunca se cansó ni de contemplar el cielo ni de registrarlo —ha viajado a Novosibirsk (Siberia), donde vio un eclipse total de sol, y a Coquimbo (Chile), adonde fue para conocer cómo trabajaban allí el astroturismo—. Su familia un poco sí, ahora solo le acompañan a ver grandes acontecimientos, como el eclipse solar total del próximo 12 de agosto. Como en La Palma será parcial, lo verán en la provincia de Zaragoza.

Mientras trabajaba, como miembro de la AAP y emprendedor, intensificó su afición por la divulgación de la astronomía. Hasta que llegó un momento en el que su participación en el desarrollo de proyectos, como la Red de Miradores y Senderos Astronómicos, el Taller del Astrónom@ y muchos otros trabajos divulgativos, le demandaba una jornada laboral completa. Así que dio el paso y empezó a vivir profesionalmente de lo que siempre había sido su pasión —hoy trabaja en el departamento de promoción de astroturismo de la Sociedad de Promoción y Desarrollo Económico de La Palma (SODEPAL)—.

El punto de inflexión de ese cambio profesional fue durante la primera Conferencia Internacional Starlight celebrada en La Palma en 2007, donde se habló de la necesidad de desarrollar empresas vinculadas al astroturismo. Por aquel entonces existían algunas iniciativas aisladas en otras islas del archipiélago. Toño, junto a otros miembros de la Agrupación Astronómica de La Palma, presentó un proyecto llamado La Palma y 14 cielos, con la idea de resaltar la calidad excepcional de las noches en cada uno de los 14 municipios de la isla gracias a la aplicación de la Ley de Protección del Cielo. Una ley que él apunta que permite contemplar las estrellas desde cualquier punto oscuro de la isla, incluso a nivel del mar, desde la playa, y no solo desde la alta montaña, donde está instalado el ORM.

El Observatorio Astrofísico del Roque de Los Muchachos (ORM) se encuentra a 2.396 metros de altitud. Jose A. Bernat Bacete (GETTY IMAGES)

En ese contexto, junto con Carmelo González, fundó en 2009 una empresa especializada en astroturismo de la isla. No solo fue pionera en ese campo, “también empezamos a tematizar casas, senderos y experiencias gastronómicas con el cielo”, dice mientras estaciona su vehículo en el mirador de Llano del Jable, un clásico en sus excursiones nocturnas. Detrás de toda esa labor hay una estrategia de sensibilización. No se trata únicamente de pedir a la gente que apague la luz porque interfiere en la observación astronómica, se trata de explicar que cuidar y proteger el cielo beneficia a toda la isla porque la actividad económica que genera.

Atardecer en el mirador de Llano del Jable, en La Palma. Dominic Dähncke (GETTY IMAGES)

Alrededor de La Palma, en puntos estratégicos de su volcánica orografía, hay miradores en los que hasta hace no mucho tiempo la gente se paraba para contemplar las vistas panorámicas, el amanecer y el atardecer. Ahora también lo hacen por la noche para ver las estrellas. Desde que Toño participara en el desarrollo de estos allá por 2009, y gracias al apoyo del Cabildo Insular, los miradores se han convertido en balcones astronómicos equipados con dos módulos: uno compuesto por un panel grande con planisferios (mapas del cielo según las estaciones) con un contenido específico, en algunos casos, del municipio en el que se encuentra: flora, fauna, artesanía, etcétera. Existe un segundo módulo común a todos, el formado por un palo de sendero que señala hacia la Estrella Polar, con una rueda giratoria que ayuda a distinguir las constelaciones circumpolares, junto a un pequeño panel que explica su uso.

Mirador en el inicio del sendero al volcán de San Antonio, con el poste que señala la Estrella Polar y un panel informativo. Autumn Sky (Alamy/CORDON PRESS)

Hay tres tipos de miradores: de montaña, de medianías y urbanos, como el que hay en una plaza de Los Álamos, en Breña Alta. La idea de estos miradores urbanos, desde los que se puede ver la Estrella Polar, es acercar la astronomía al público general y, sobre todo, a los niños. Que los más pequeños vean cómo se monta un telescopio y cómo funciona es sinónimo de despertar su curiosidad y el interés por la astronomía. Si le preguntan a Toño por los miradores de su isla, recomienda el mencionado del Jable (en la parte alta de El Paso), el de Llano de Las Ventas (Breña Baja), El Infinito (San Andrés), el de Buracas (Garafía), el del Molino (Barlovento) y el de las Toscas (Mazo). Enclaves en los que los aficionados y los profesionales de la astronomía instalan sus equipos para ver todos los astros que pueden.

El mirador de Buracas, en el noroeste de la isla. blickwinkel (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Su principal motivación es compartir su pasión por la astronomía. También facilitársela. La accesibilidad para personas ciegas y un planetario son los proyectos en los que anda enfrascado. La Palma dispone de un planetario itinerante e hinchable, pero él quiere uno fijo y con instalaciones y accesos para personas con movilidad reducida. “Desde el Cabildo y SODEPAL estamos trabajando para que la astronomía sea cada vez más inclusiva”, dice orgulloso. Un buen altavoz para contar lo que hacen es Astrofest, donde hay programadas actividades divulgativas para el público general y otras para emprendimientos astronómicos.

El color azul en la red de miradores astronómicos de La Palma identifica los puntos o paneles vinculados a la interpretación del cielo y orientación estelar. Christina Bodendorfer (GETTY IMAGES)

La asignatura pendiente de Toño es ver auroras boreales. En Groenlandia o en el norte de Noruega dice que le gustaría verlas. Él, que ya ha disfrutado de cielos del hemisferio sur, eclipses totales, anulares y parciales, eclipses de Luna y lluvias de estrellas espectaculares, anima a ir a La Palma, isla desde la que quien quiera puede ver una galaxia con sus propios ojos.

World.title: Ajax, ING and Ace & Tate hit by data breach
World.content:
