I believe this provides an additional incentive to give new momentum to our democratic and institutional reforms so that we can achieve EU standards as quickly as possible.

This is our main intermediate goal because we understand that no country can become a full member of the European Union without meeting its standards. Therefore, our primary task is first and foremost to comply with EU standards. […]If we are admitted to the European Union, we will be happy. If we are not, we will still benefit, because Armenia will have become a country that meets European standards, with all the positive consequences that entails,” Pashinyan said at the time.

System administrator Artak Gaboyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Russia pushes back

At the start of the crisis in Armenian-Russian relations, Moscow responded relatively cautiously to Yerevan’s efforts to move closer to Europe. The Kremlin sought to avoid further destabilising the situation, citing Armenia’s difficult historical circumstances. Even Armenia’s effective suspension of its participation in the CSTO did not result in a fundamental reassessment of bilateral relations.

However, Moscow appeared to change its approach in the run-up to the parliamentary elections held in June.

One of the defining moments came during Pashinyan’s meeting with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in April, when the Russian president openly asked him to allow pro-Russian political forces to participate in the elections. He was primarily referring to Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. However, as Karapetyan holds citizenship of several countries, not only Armenia, Armenian law bars him from serving as an MP or becoming prime minister. Pashinyan reportedly made this clear to Putin.

The Kremlin nevertheless continued to support pro-Russian political figures while also taking more concrete steps. Russian regulators began imposing restrictions on imports of Armenian products. Initially, the measures targeted specific companies and categories of goods, but they were later expanded to cover almost all agricultural produce from Armenia.

Businessman Suren Margaryan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

The situation continued to escalate. Armenian officials began openly accusing Moscow of attempting to interfere in the country’s internal affairs and engineer a change of government.

At the same time, international media reported on alleged hybrid attacks against Armenia. Reuters also published a report alleging that the Kremlin had devised a plan to bring 100,000 Armenian citizens into the country to vote for pro-Russian political forces.

Following the elections, Moscow has stepped up its calls for Armenia to decide, once and for all, which direction it intends to take. Russian officials have specifically called for a referendum on whether the country should pursue integration with the European Union or the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), arguing that choosing the EU would require Armenia to leave the EAEU.

“No one is pushing Armenia out of the EAEU. They themselves have said they want to join the European Union. They need to make a choice. And the sooner that choice is made, the better it will be for everyone,” Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksey Overchuk said.

This culminated in a joint statement by the EAEU member states calling for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Central Yerevan. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Armenia says time is not right for referendum

In response to Moscow’s demands, the Armenian authorities say they have no plans to hold a referendum or withdraw from the EAEU—for now. The key word is “for now.” Yerevan intends to remain a member of the EAEU until there is a realistic prospect of joining the European Union. Moreover, under the EAEU’s founding rules, Armenia cannot be expelled from the bloc without its consent.

However, holding a referendum on EU membership appears to be a realistic prospect in the longer term. Opinion polls also suggest such a referendum could succeed. Since the 2020 war, Russia’s popularity in Armenia has declined markedly, while support for European integration has continued to grow.

According to a survey conducted by the International Republican Institute (IRI) in May 2026, 75% of Armenians support the country’s accession to the European Union, while 58% say they would vote in favour of joining the bloc in a referendum. The findings point to a sustained decline in trust in Russia and growing pro-European sentiment among the Armenian public.

Photographer Mane Sergoyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

What do experts say?

Which direction should Armenia take? That is arguably the country’s defining question today. Does Armenia have the capacity to make a definitive choice in favour of the European Union? How might Russia respond if it does? And what security risks could such a shift entail?

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan says Yerevan is pursuing a diversification of its foreign policy, a goal repeatedly articulated by the country’s leadership. In his view, this aligns with the interests of Armenia’s European partners.

“Armenia is already receiving a certain level of support, particularly through its cooperation with France. It is possible that, in the future, security cooperation will expand to include other countries, although there is not yet enough information at this stage to identify them. At the same time, it should be remembered that the EU operates under NATO’s security umbrella. While Armenia is not currently seeking rapid accession to the Alliance, if it succeeds in developing close ties with individual EU member states, it could gain access to additional opportunities as an indirect beneficiary of NATO’s resources,” he said.

Is Armenia ready to become part of the European Union today? Gevondyan argues that the question itself is misplaced, as every country must go through a lengthy accession process before joining the bloc.

“No country is ever fully prepared to begin the integration process overnight. By the time Armenia is ready, it will effectively already be part of Europe. States usually go through a long period of integration, during which they implement reforms across various sectors, align with European standards, improve product quality and reach agreements on mutual trade. This process takes years. Armenia is ready to embark on that journey. At the same time, it is impossible to reconcile EU requirements and the conditions for trading with the West with the standards and requirements that exist within the EAEU. We are only at the beginning of a long road.”

Journalist Marianna Mkrtchyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

“Armenia is still a long way from joining the European Union. But the current trajectory could already result in serious losses—not only economically, but also in terms of the country’s sovereignty,” argues political commentator Hayk Khalatyan, founder of the Analytical Centre for Strategic Studies and Initiatives.

Khalatyan also argues that the Armenian leadership will ultimately be unable to sustain its current course of deepening ties with the European Union while remaining a member of the EAEU:

“Pashinyan’s challenge now, after the elections, is to try to normalise relations with Moscow. He will be expected to take concrete steps demonstrating that he is abandoning his previous foreign policy course. But that would effectively mean turning his back on the powerful external actors who helped him remain in power. The question, then, is which path he will choose: to turn his back on the West and Turkey, or continue down the path of confrontation with Russia and the gradual breakdown of bilateral relations. I very much doubt that Pashinyan will abandon his Western partners and move towards normalising ties with Russia. He would like to preserve the policy he has pursued in recent years—reaping the economic benefits of EAEU membership while, in practice, steadily distancing Armenia politically from Russia. But we are now seeing that Moscow is no longer willing to tolerate that approach.”

Human rights activist and film director Hovhannes Ishkhanyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan.

At the same time, relations between Brussels and Moscow remain deeply confrontational, with some political and security circles even discussing the possibility of a future conflict between Russia and the West.

Whatever the outcome, Armenia is now adapting to a new geopolitical reality while facing Russian trade restrictions. The country is seeking to redirect its exports towards European markets and diversify its trade partners. If it succeeds, Yerevan will remove what many see as its last major economic dependency on Russia.

Yasha Solomonyan, chairman of the Armenian Association of Professional Guides, shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

With the support of the Russian Language News Exchange

World.title: UK embassy in Georgia: Amaglobeli’s sentence ‘disproportionate’ and politically motivated
World.content:
UK embassy condemns Amaglobeli’s sentence

The UK embassy in Georgia has described the sentence handed down to journalist Mzia Amaglobeli as disproportionate and politically motivated, and has called for her immediate release.

“A year ago today Mzia Amaglobeli, a prominent Georgian journalist, was sentenced to two years in prison. We remain concerned that her sentence is disproportionate and politicised and call again for her immediate release,” the embassy’s post on Facebook read.

Mzia Amaglobeli was sentenced on 6 August 2025.

The journalist was arrested on 11 January 2025 on charges of assaulting Batumi police chief Irakli Dgebuadze. On 14 January, Batumi City Court granted the prosecution’s request to remand her in custody pending trial.

The defence’s requests to have the pre-trial detention measure changed were rejected by the courts. Batumi City Court ruled the request inadmissible, while on 19 February 2025 Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the decision to keep Amaglobeli in pre-trial detention.

According to Nona Kurdovanidze, chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association, the court relied on a falsified protocol when justifying her pre-trial detention.

Following her arrest, Mzia Amaghlobeli went on a hunger strike that lasted 38 days. On 18 February 2025, it was announced that she had ended the hunger strike and resumed eating under medical supervision.

World.title: Melbourne teen charged amid 'call Commission' notes, arson probe
World.content:
A teenager has been charged amid an ongoing investigation into notes left on shopfronts across Melbourne telling the owners to "call the Commission" before alleged arson attacks.

Police believe the 17-year-old may be involved in completing criminal tasks on behalf of an offshore crime syndicate.

Police said investigators have linked 19 handwritten or typed notes found in various locations across Melbourne and regional Victoria, instructing shop owners to contact a suspected organised crime group known as "the Commission".

In early July, shopfronts on Victoria Street in Richmond were damaged in a suspected arson attack mere days after a note was found on the front of a local tobacco store instructing the owners to contact "the Commission".

This note asking a business owner to contact a suspected organised crime group was posted on the door of a Richmond business in the days before a fire in early July. (Supplied)

Yesterday, police conducted a search of a 17-year-old boy's home home in the Moonee Valley area as part of an investigation into these incidents.

They seized eight mobile phones and a large number of SIM cards.

The boy has since been charged with trafficking and possessing drugs including cocaine, amphetamine and ketamine, as well as possessing counterfeit money and failing to provide information or assistance to police.

He is due to face the children's court at a later date.

Investigation into arson attacks expands

Police established Operation Eclipse in April to investigate the suspected organised crime syndicate responsible for arson attacks on nightclubs, bars and restaurants across Melbourne, as well as people associated with those businesses.

The operation has expanded to examine other acts of violence directed by this syndicate, which police believe have been undertaken to extort other businesses and control the illicit drug and tobacco markets.

Today's fire is the fourth arson attack in Richmond in just over a month. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Detective Inspector Graham Banks said police were trying to target "every level of the syndicate".

"We are quite often arresting youths who were not previously known to police and who have had no prior police contact," he said in a statement.

"Lured by the prospect of what they are told is some easy cash and anonymity behind encrypted devices, young people are committing serious criminal offences which have grave or life-changing ramifications."

Detective Inspector Banks said the outcomes could be devastating for the wider community and the alleged offenders' families.

"This is not easy cash — these threats are playing with people's livelihoods and their own sense of safety and it will not be tolerated," he said.

World.title: Corruption hunter wants more resources to tackle government contractors
World.content:
WA's corruption watchdog is facing "significant" resourcing challenges and needs new powers to perform its functions effectively, according to its boss.

Corruption and Crime Commission (CCC) chief Michael Corboy's warnings come as a powerful parliamentary committee reviews his organisation's jurisdiction ahead of what would be its first major overhaul in more than two decades.

At the top of Mr Corboy's wish list is the power for the CCC to investigate allegations of corruption against government contractors.

As it stands, the commission only has power over public servants employed by the government.

Michael Corboy has flagged artificial intelligence as a key challenge facing the government. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

Mr Corboy would not provide examples of local investigations that had been hampered by the rules, but pointed to recent scandals in which consulting firms had misused data obtained while working for the Commonwealth government.

"We couldn't investigate allegations that [state] government information had been misused by private contractors," he said.

"There have also recently been allegations made that organised crime has infiltrated the NDIS service providers, who in turn, of course, contract with both Commonwealth and state agencies. Again, we wouldn't be able to investigate those allegations."

Michael Corboy became commissioner after the retirement of long-time chief John McKechnie. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

Mr Corboy also said the CCC would not be able to investigate the types of allegations levelled against the CFMEU on the east coast, including that its infiltration of government projects had cost Victorian taxpayers about $15 billion.

Subcontract concerns

Mr Corboy said no allegations of corruption on major infrastructure projects had been made to the CCC and that major contracts were generally well scrutinised, but risks remained.

He said there were concerns when dealing with a "plethora of subcontracts".

"The more fragmented the contractual structure, the more there is the potential for misconduct and corrupt conduct," Mr Corboy said.

He said there was also "significant concern" regarding the use of contract workers within government departments, some of whom could sit in senior positions for a "long time".

Michael Corboy has called for the CCC to be given more resources to investigate corruption in government contractors. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

"And there have been occasions where we have not been able to pursue allegations against private contractors," Mr Corboy said.

A state government spokesperson said major projects were subject to "robust procurement, contracting, audit and compliance frameworks" that contractors were expected to apply to subcontractors.

A spokesperson for the Public Sector Commission said public sector managers monitored the conduct of contracted workers and addressed issues through "contract management".

Corruption hunters

Mr Corboy said if funding allowed he would like to do more proactive hunting for corruption within the state government.

"[With] more money I would do more investigations, I would produce more reports, but I would very much like, in particular, to do more engagement across the public sector," he said.

Mr Corboy also flagged the possibility of digging into more "thematic issues".

The CCC would be in line for its first overhaul in more than two decades. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

Another potential area of focus, if more money was available, was reviewing how police are handling family and domestic violence cases, which has been overhauled in the wake of high-profile failures in recent years.

Mr Corboy said the CCC could also review more complaints itself, instead of sending them back to government agencies and supervising their investigations.

"If we had more resources, we would do more independent investigations," he said.

'Exceptional job'

Mr Corboy laughed when asked if the commission was properly resourced and said: "I think if you ask any agency head, then the answer to that will be no."

But that resourcing challenge was so great that he was unable to say if WA's public service, on the whole, was seeing higher or lower levels of corruption over time, because there was no budget for that kind of work.

Michael Corboy says his organisation could do more independent investigations with more resources. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

Efforts to provide outreach into communities had also been hampered, he revealed, saying a request for money to engage with Aboriginal people was knocked back.

"The Corruption and Crime Commission does an exceptional job investigating serious corruption and misconduct in the Western Australian public sector, as evidenced by its many published reports," Attorney-General Tony Buti said in a statement.

"The commissioner … has briefed me on opportunities to expand the commission's work and the funding required to do so.

"I welcome any submissions from the CCC on these opportunities."

AI challenge

Mr Corboy, who previously served as deputy commissioner, has now held the top job for nine months.

The rollout of artificial intelligence across the public sector will be one of the greatest issues for the CCC to grapple with over the remainder of his term, he said.

Michael Corboy has been in the top job for nine months, following a decades-long career as a lawyer and 13 years as a Supreme Court judge. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

"On the positive, there are ways in which we can be using AI in our work which will significantly, I think, enhance our efficiency and the speed at which we're able to complete out work," Mr Corboy said.

"So one of the legacies I'd like to leave is that in the five years' time we have a deep understanding of both the benefits and the risks of AI for the public sector as a whole and also for this commission."

More scrutiny on guards

Mr Corboy is also asking for the CCC to be able to level more scrutiny against officers exercising "police-like powers", including prison officers and transit guards.

In 2024 the CCC raised concerns about the Public Transport Authority's handling of internal investigations, after one found "no issues with the force used" when a man was thrown to the floor of a train station.

"There is very little external oversight of the way in which transit officers and corrections officers use their coercive powers, whether or not they are using their powers lawfully," Mr Corboy said.

Michael Corboy would like to see more scrutiny on people who wield police-like powers, such as transit guards and prison officers. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

The Public Transport Authority, for example, recorded about 1,500 incidents of the use of force every three months, he said.

But Mr Corboy said there may be an under-reporting of incidents to the commission.

The Public Transport Authority and Corrective Services argued against the CCC being given those oversight powers when appearing before the parliamentary committee, saying their existing internal oversight was sufficient.

World.title: Trump's White House ballroom project stalled
World.content:
A federal appeals court has ordered Donald Trump's administration to stop construction on a $400 million ballroom on the site of the White House's demolished East Wing, dealing the Republican leader a major setback in a case testing his presidential authority.

"Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House," and could not fundamentally reshape it without congressional approval, the Washington-based US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit said in a 2-1 opinion on Friday, local time.

Donald Trump is consuming Washington Project by project, Donald Trump is altering the United States capital.

The order upheld a preliminary injunction won by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued last year after the administration tore down the East Wing and began building an 8,360-square-metre ballroom without seeking authorisation from Congress.

"Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for executive self-help," the panel's majority wrote.

The appeals court placed its ruling on hold for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal to the US Supreme Court.

The White House said private donations, including from Donald Trump himself, would pay for the planned ballroom. (AP: Martinez Monsivais)

Mr Trump has increasingly claimed that the ballroom project was a security necessity. He referred to the structure as a "military centre" in a post on Truth Social on Friday and said the administration would appeal to the Supreme Court.

He called the decision "horrendous" and politically motivated and said it left him, other White House officials and visitors exposed to attack.

"This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety," Mr Trump said.

He said the ballroom plan included bomb shelters, medical facilities, shielding from drones and missiles, and other security features that were "all tied together as one big, expensive, and very complex unit".

National Trust President Brent Leggs said in a statement that the ruling marked "a great day for our country and for the American people's right to voice their opinions about the historic places they cherish, including the White House".

Loading...

Mr Trump appealed after US District Judge Richard Leon, an appointee of Republican former President George W Bush, twice blocked above-ground construction on the site while allowing underground work to continue.

The ballroom plan, which the administration has described as necessary for large formal functions and to preserve the safety of the White House, is the grandest of several Trump efforts to reshape central Washington's landscape of government buildings and national monuments.

A judge in a separate lawsuit recently said Mr Trump's name was illegally added to the exterior of the Kennedy Center performing arts venue and ordered its removal.

Appeal to national security

In the ballroom case, Justice Department attorney Yaakov Roth said during DC Circuit arguments on June 5 that the courts had no role in weighing the privately funded project.

He said the National Trust's "architectural preference" should not take precedence over national security concerns, claiming evidence that the former East Wing left the president and others in the White House vulnerable to attack.

Artist renderings and diagrams of the new White House East Wing and Ballroom. (AP: Jon Elswick)

The Democratic-appointed judges in the appeals court's majority — Circuit Judges Patricia Millett and Brad Garcia — said their order did not permanently bar construction of a ballroom, but halted above-ground work during the lawsuit and until the White House secured approval from Congress.

National security arguments "are not an automatic get-out-of-law-free card," they said.

"The bold assertion that the executive can act with utter lawlessness, destroying treasured national landmarks and harming the interests of individuals, and that no court can stop it, flouts our constitutional order," the judges wrote.

Circuit Judge Neomi Rao, whom Mr Trump appointed during his first term, said in her dissent that the trial judge's injunction blocking the project "is beyond the proper province of the federal courts" and that construction should be allowed to continue.

"The district court seized supervision of construction at the White House, and my colleagues affirm this judicial overreach," Ms Rao wrote.

Mr Trump has defended his ballroom's price tag, which has doubled from initial projections.

In a post on Truth Social in May he said that the cost rose because "it is approximately twice the size, and a far higher quality, than the original ⁠proposal" and promised, "it will be magnificent, safe, and secure!"

Reuters

World.title: Crippling costs force family to close mushroom farm after 45 years
World.content:
Joanne and Steve Willemse did everything they could to keep the gates open at their commercial mushroom farm at Chevallum, on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.

They downsized their business, sold an apartment, and the investment property they had bought to fund their retirement.

"It's got to the stage now where we're not making any money at all, we're actually losing money," Ms Willemse said.

" On average, we're losing about $10,000 a week. "

Joanne Willemse holds one of the last boxes of Swiss brown mushrooms produced at the farm. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Family-owned SjW Mushrooms supplies IGA supermarkets, as well as dozens of fruit shops and markets.

Ms Willemse said while the price of a box of mushrooms had barely changed over the past 20 years, the cost of growing them had increased dramatically.

Price hikes caused by the Iran war have also fuelled their financial pain.

Steve and Joanne Willemse have made the difficult decision to leave the industry. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Mushrooms are nutritious, low in kilojoules and high in vitamin B, minerals and antioxidants.

But Australian production has continued to drop since 2021.

The most recent figures from the Australian Horticulture Statistics Handbook for 2024/25 show mushroom production decreased by 12 per cent to 52,784 tonnes, valued at $338.3 million.

Consumers purchased 7 per cent fewer mushrooms that financial year.

Ingredients for vegan dan dan noodles including fresh noodles, Swiss brown mushrooms and Chinese broccoli. (ABC Life: Hetty McKinnon)

"[People are] not buying mushrooms because they're expensive. The fruit shops, they're struggling as well," Ms Willemse said.

"It's a vicious cycle.

"They want us to keep our prices down so that they can keep their prices down, so they can attract more customers."

The Willemse family has farmed mushrooms in Queensland since the 1950s.

The couple branched off on their own 15 years ago, taking over a farm at Woodford and expanding to Chevallum a year later.

Workers at the Chevallum farm were devastated to learn of the impeding closure. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

They once employed 65 staff, but that has dropped to 15.

"They've all been with us since day one so there's been quite a few tears and a lot of beautiful notes they've handed over," Ms Willemse said.

" Even our customers have sent us beautiful texts and emails. "

Their tough decision to close has meant their adult children, who help run the farm, have had to look for work.

"I have grandkids as well, and we were hoping that they would eventually take over, but that's not to be," Ms Willemse said.

The last of the mushrooms will be picked over the next week. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

'Less choice' for consumers

Adam Forbes, from wholesale fruit and vegetable supplier The Produce Partner, said he was "devastated" to learn of the farm's closure.

"We get up to a tonne of mushrooms through those guys weekly," Mr Forbes said.

"They were such a great local farm … it's really going to put a dent in the local market.

"It's going to push pricing up across the board.

Adam Forbes says growers are under increasing pressure and struggling to stay afloat. (Supplied: The Produce Partner)

"Chefs, restaurants, they can't push their prices up any further and so the farmers are getting the rough end of the stick."

Tough environment

AUSVEG spokesperson Andrew MacDonald said business conditions were "extremely challenging".

Vegetable costs rise Farmers kept planting through the uncertainty of the US Iran war. Now they're paying for it.

He said production costs had surged, compliance burdens were more unsustainable, and skills and workforce shortages made it challenging to secure viable returns.

"It's continued to get harder … the Middle East war has compounded pressures," he said.

Describing Australian vegetable consumption as "critically low and declining," Mr MacDonald said practical support from government and consumers was "crucial for our food security".

New industry entrants

There is still optimism for the future of fungi farming.

Martin Anfosso and his partner Elona Kovach rented an industrial shed in Coolum after their business outgrew their garage.

Every week, they grow 50 kilograms of spray-free gourmet mushrooms for chefs, cafes and retail stores.

The Coolum-based business grows nine different varieties of gourmet mushrooms. (Supplied: Fleur de Fungi)

"We're about to bump up from next week to roughly 70 kilograms … everything is sourced from Australia," Mr Anfosso said.

Mountaintop Mushrooms closes its doors The business a young couple crowdfunded to grow a head-turning array of tasty, colourful fungi in a century-old pineapple packing shed closes.

But Ms Kovach said they were keenly aware of several Sunshine Coast mushroom businesses closing in recent years.

"Being a small business, I think in any niche, is very difficult," she said.

Back at SjW Mushrooms, Ms Willemse said farmers needed support.

"We pay a lot of taxes, farmers, just like any other business. However, we're a primary producer," she said.

"We feed the country."

World.title: Teenage girls film attack on former police officer in WA's far north
World.content:
A former police officer attacked and filmed by a group of teenage girls in Western Australia's Kimberley says she feels unsafe remaining in town.

Sina, who did not want her surname published, is a German expat who has been staying in Australia on a working holiday visa.

She and a friend were riding through Broome, 2,000 kilometres north of Perth, on Monday when they passed the group of five teenage girls.

"They were shouting to us and we asked, 'What's the matter?' and … we stopped because we couldn't hear them," Sina said.

"Then they start running in our direction with sticks and that was the moment we realised we should go."

Police say they are investigating an assault incident in the Birra Court area in Broome. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

The women tried to ride away but reached a dead end.

Sina said the group was "waiting for us at the end of the street" when they turned their bikes around.

"They tried to attack us, chased us through the park, I said, 'Stop it, otherwise I'll call the police' and this made them angrier," she said.

"They just threw balls on my head, a basket on my head, luckily I wore a helmet … then they had sticks, they had stones, they were throwing it at my friend and me.

" I felt like I'm not a human any longer for them; I'm not worth it. "

Sina said one of the girls was filming the incident on her phone, with the teenagers attempting to break their bicycles.

The attack left them both bruised and bleeding, with scratches on their knees, stomach and back.

Sina says she was riding her bicycle with and friend when the girls started shouting and throwing sticks. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Police's 'lazy' response

When the women eventually escaped, they immediately contacted Broome police.

But Sina said she received a disinterested response that struck her as "a bit lazy".

She said police told her it "wouldn't make sense" to proceed because Sina's impending departure from the country would mean the case could not go to court.

The former officer was also told the girls would be unlikely to receive any serious consequences due to being under 16.

Broome police said they were unable to respond to criticisms levelled against them as inquiries into the incident were still ongoing. (ABC Kimberley: Mya Kordic)

"I called the police for a reason, not to just tell them my story and just have a chat," Sina said.

"It doesn't matter if I'm in Germany or in Australia, because at the end, it's a crime.

"I'm on a video, I don't want to be on this video so there are two crimes to punish; the hurting me and they took a video of me."

After enjoying her time in Broome, she said she was now wary and scared of being attacked again.

A WA Police spokesperson confirmed the incident was being investigated, but was unable to make further comment.

Sina said Broome police only reached out to her after the ABC's initial inquiries about the attack.

World.title: 'Bad luck' for Australia's bird flu epicentre, but worse is to come
World.content:
South Australia has been a victim of bad luck, having borne the brunt of H5 bird flu's arrival to Australia, the state's chief veterinary officer says.

To date, SA accounts for more than three quarters of Australia's confirmed bird flu cases.

That figure did not include a "mass mortality" event of an estimated 80 birds near Cape Jaffa in late July.

"Unfortunately, we were just unlucky to be the first place where this did spread into our resident birds," SA's chief veterinary officer Dr Skye Fruean told ABC News Stateline.

Authorities across the country are tightening biosecurity and monitoring captive bird populations, with the Royal Adelaide Show confirming birds competitions will not be held in September and Victoria locking down poultry flocks.

But experts warn the spread is unlikely to remain confined to coastlines and could penetrate inland Australia.

Australia has been waiting for this arrival for years

The H5N1 variant has spread on every other continent of the planet, including Antarctica, since it was discovered in Chinese geese in 1996.

Authorities outside Australia have attempted to protect their poultry from wild birds landing near them or sharing water sources to prevent spillovers, which occur when the disease is transmitted from one population to another — such as from wild to domestic birds, or from birds to mammals.

When spillovers occur, the only available action is "depopulation" — or culling — entire infected flocks, sometimes numbering thousands of birds, and imposing quarantine and containment areas around farms.

Skye Fruean says South Australia has been a victim of bad luck as the location for a majority of H5 cases. (ABC News: Simon Goodes)

"Bird flu is a disease that they [farmers] have been concerned about for decades," Dr Fruean said.

"While it's awful to watch, it's allowed us time to prepare to come here.

"Certainly, the poultry industry has very much been at the forefront of that preparedness."

Though no deadly spillovers from wild birds have occurred in South Australia, H5N1's path is following similar beats to the international experience.

From the coast and beyond?

In South America, the disease spread from birds, infecting and killing thousands of sea lions and elephant seals since 2022.

Australia's first H5N1 detection was among elephant seals on its remote Heard Island territory about 3,000 kilometres south-west of Perth in November.

Thousands have since died.

Efforts are now being made to secure and protect endangered sea mammal herds in places like Kangaroo Island, which has recorded positive cases in birds.

South Australia's cases have mostly been in coastal areas, including in the south-east region and Kangaroo Island.

That was until a confirmed case was recorded at Monarto — 20 kilometres inland from Lake Alexandrina.

Cases have also been largely in greater crested tern species, though migratory giant petrels and silver gulls (seagulls) have also been infected.

Chris Purnell, who is Birdlife Australia's manager of wetland and migratory shorebirds, said ducks would most likely be the culprit of any future spread inland.

"Ducks are going to be one of the major vectors because of their ability to stay alive and carry the disease further [inland]," Dr Purnell said.

"The disease survives longer in fresh water is the other factor.

"They're defecating in the water, they're feeding in the water and lots of other birds are feeding in the same water column where the disease is surviving. That's the issue."

Chris Purnell says ducks could carry the H5 variant further inland. (Supplied: Birdlife Australia)

Dr Fruean, who oversees SA's bird flu response, said the rapid increase in confirmed cases in the state was "not unexpected".

"As soon as we had that evidence of local transmission in resident birds here in South Australia we knew it was going to continue to spread and that is what we're now seeing," she said.

" We would expect the spread to continue, [but] unfortunately I can't tell you how quickly that will happen. "

Low human concern, but fears for other animals

H5 bird flu is an influenza virus that can infect humans, but this has been relatively rare.

Fewer than 1,000 people globally have contracted the disease since it was first identified three decades ago, and usually biosecurity or farm workers exposed to sick or dead animals were at greatest risk.

"Only if you're in really close contact with animals that have really high amounts of virus are you able to get infected with this H5 virus," La Trobe University viral immunologist Emma Grant said.

"This has happened in people who work in poultry, this has been seen in live poultry markets in various parts of the world, and in the US in the dairy industry."

A similar form of H5N1 has been circulating in US cattle herds since 2024. (Reuters: Jim Vondruska)

Those US cattle have been infected by the same H5N1 "clade" as the one now in Australia, though a different genotype.

"Could that occur in Australia? It could if you've got collections of birds near free-ranging cattle," said Wayne Boardman, a wildlife veterinarian and expert in wildlife health at Adelaide University.

"You can't dismiss it, that's for sure — it's probably less of a serious consequence, but it seems like many mammal species can get affected by it."

But it's less about the cattle for experts like Dr Boardman, who are most concerned about native animals.

"We've got scavenging birds like white-bellied sea eagles … wedge-tailed eagles, or other species that might pick up carrion," Dr Boardman said.

" But also the mammalian carnivores as well, like quolls, Tasmanian devils, we've got no idea how susceptible they might be to the virus. "

What can we do?

While the concern for inland spread and the spread into other animals like cows exists, experts say these are yet to be realised.

They said there were still some actions from humans that could help.

For Birdlife Australia's Chris Purnell, it is as simple as leaving birds alone.

"It's just critically important to reduce any unnecessary disturbance to these birds that might pique their cortisol, get them moving," he said.

"It not only disturbs them from the site but also reduces their immune response and increases the likelihood that they're going to shed more disease."

For all the anticipation of H5N1's arrival, its early impact in South Australia has not been an easy one for communities. Sadly, as the international example has often shown, the worst is yet to come.

"I think the Australian population will be utterly devastated," Dr Boardman said.

"Particularly if we go into iconic endangered species like glossy black cockatoo, for example, or the plains wanderer or the orange-bellied parrot … if it got into Australian sealions, which is an iconic South Australian species.

"If you see the virus getting into these populations, then people are going to be thinking 'is there any more we can do?'"

World.title: Vulnerable patients fear implications of stoma nurse shortage
World.content:
David Platt was unsure what his future held when he awoke from surgery with a urostomy bag.

Living in Mount Gambier, in regional South Australia, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2004, but the disease spread throughout his body, including to his bladder.

It required the removal of his bladder and the creation of a stoma, a surgical opening which helped Mr Platt pass waste into the urostomy bag.

"I looked down, I thought, 'Well, I've got this thing stuck on me, what do I do?'" Mr Platt said.

The first couple of months were difficult for Mr Platt and his wife Paula, but a stoma nurse at Mount Gambier hospital helped him understand his new life.

David Platt says having support nearby allows those with a stoma to be more independent. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"I think I went up there for about four changes and in the end she said, 'Look, you've mastered it, you can actually do it yourself now,'" he said.

Mr Platt eventually came to view the urostomy bag as "just part of my body".

But reaching that understanding can take time and support.

It is why he tries to help others who are still coming to terms with their own stoma bags.

Mr Platt says the medical guidance and support which helped him is under threat by a stoma nurse shortage in Mount Gambier.

The largest SA city outside Adelaide has gone from having two full-time staff to one nurse on one day a week.

Recruitment troubles

More than 200 people in the South East region have some form of stoma and Mr Platt runs the region's stoma support group.

Urostomy bags, like Mr Platt uses, collect urine, while colostomy bags collect stool and gas when organs like the colon have been removed.

"Stoma bag" is typically used to encompass both types.

Mr Platt said while everyday maintenance, such as changing bags, was typically conducted at home, more serious emergencies required a specialist nurse.

David and Paula Platt run Mount Gambier's support group. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"I know there's a couple of women have had to go to Adelaide because they can't get the help here," he said.

"I mean it's rough really for them to have to travel all the way, especially as they're not young, they're older people in their 80s."

Limestone Coast Local Health Network (LCLHN) chief executive Emma Poland said recruitment was underway for a specialist stoma nurse in Mount Gambier.

The two previous nurses had left the position for other opportunities.

"We acknowledge we face growing competition from intrastate, interstate and overseas for qualified professionals," Ms Poland said.

Mount Gambier hospital is the largest public health facility in regional South Australia. (ABC South East SA: Bec Whetham)

"While we continue recruitment efforts, our Nursing Education Team is providing education on wound, stoma, and continence management to staff across the Limestone Coast region."

Ms Poland said staff across the region had received training in wound, stoma and continence management and some staff had undertaken workshops in Adelaide.

"LCLHN is also engaging with nursing locum agencies to identify suitably qualified candidates to temporarily support our service," she said.

"We are committed to providing a safe and high-quality stoma and continence service to support consumers across our region."

Nurse training call

Independent Member for Mount Gambier Travis Fatchen has raised the issue in state parliament and called for a rethink of how stoma nursing is incorporated into the health system.

He said nursing degrees should look at adding stoma training to the curriculum.

"Have they reached out to any of the local nurses to see what is involved to do some further training?" he said.

Travis Fatchen says a better system of stoma care should be explored. (ABC News: Josh Brine)

"That may [create] a bit of a buffer where you've got three or four nurses that are day-to-day doing their normal role, but they can be called on if and when needed to help fill these gaps."

In South Australia, the qualification course to become a stoma nurse takes a year to complete and costs $14,000.

Mr Platt said outside of specialist nurses, stomas were a knowledge gap for some health staff.

Mount Gambier has gone from having two full-time stoma nurses to just one nurse who is only available one day a week. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

He said he helped educate a new nurse on basic stoma care during a recent hospital stay.

"She said, 'I've never seen one of them before,'" he said.

"She's a fully qualified nurse and she didn't know about stoma."

Importance of community

Helen Colliver helped lead the charge for a permanent stoma nurse in the Yorke Peninsula.

She had to travel to Adelaide for support when she first received a stoma after surgery for a perforated bowel.

Helen Colliver received a stoma after bowel surgery. (ABC North and West SA: Jenae Madden)

"Fortunately for me, I didn't have a huge amount of trouble, but you're always worried that it might smell or bulge or break all of a sudden," she said.

"It really makes you antisocial.

" You don't want to go out for fear of embarrassing yourself and everybody else. "

SA Health appointed a permanent stoma nurse for the Yorke Peninsula in 2021, when the area had about 140 residents in need.

Newspaper clippings detail a community push for a stoma support nurse in the Yorke Peninsula. (ABC North and West SA: Jenae Madden)

Ms Colliver said it made a world of difference to herself and everyone else with a stoma in the community.

"At our ostomy meetings, we talk about [how] the things we ask our stoma nurse, people would really be absolutely aghast if they could hear what we talk about, because it would be very embarrassing for them," she said.

"But it's quite common for us to talk about."

World.title: Gun owner candidate says signage rules make him a target
World.content:
As a staunch firearms advocate, Phillip Bigg says he is regularly "going after criminals" by pushing for stronger punishments for those who steal guns and use them to commit crimes.

He is concerned a Tasmanian law that requires him to include an address on any election material he puts up for his upcoming council tilt may turn his home into a target for potential gun thieves.

"Putting my address out there while I'm attacking criminals, it's a disaster waiting to happen," the Tasmanian president of Shooters Union Australia said.

"It's just an absolutely idiotic idea that we need to do this.

"We have technology these days where you are so easily contactable, unlike when this [law] was first introduced."

Phillip Bigg says the current advertising authorisation requirement is "a disaster waiting to happen". (Supplied)

According to the Local Government Act 1993, all election material such as s, signs or pamphlets must include the "true name and address" of whoever produced them.

The address must be either where the person resides, or somewhere they can be readily contacted. It cannot be a post office box or an email.

Candidates running with major parties have typically used their party headquarters for the address, but this was not necessarily an option for independent candidates.

Loading...

Mr Bigg, who is running for a spot on the Derwent Valley Council in southern Tasmania, said it was an outdated law that put candidates at risk.

"There are so many candidates out there that have experienced threats of violence or death threats," he said.

The firearms advocate said he had personally received two death threats within the past year and his home had been targeted in a "ram raid".

Concern for domestic violence survivors

Emma Goyne is an elected member for Clarence City Council on Hobart's eastern shore where she plans to run for re-election.

She said as a domestic violence survivor the requirement to publicise an address was a significant concern.

Emma Goyne says having to publicise where she lives is "concerning". (Supplied)

"I understand there's obviously a lot of people in similar situations that don't want to nominate because they don't want to disclose their address," Cr Goyne said.

" Particularly as women and mothers, highlighting the family home where your child resides and that being published is quite concerning. "

Cr Goyne said she "cannot see any logic" behind the law, especially in the digital age when most people are quite easily contactable.

She said candidates should be permitted to list an email address, a phone number or a PO box.

"If they're not going to allow it as a blanket rule, allow [candidates] to apply for an exemption under special circumstances," Cr Goyne said.

'Tricky' to update law ahead of elections, MLC warns

Mick Tucker, president of the Local Government Association of Tasmania (LGAT) and Break O-Day council mayor, said the concerns raised by Mr Bigg and Cr Goyne were "extremely valid".

He said LGAT recommended the law be changed, but it was unclear if this would be supported by the state government.

Mick Tucker says it's important for candidates to remember that it does not have to be their home address. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The submission was to the draft local government amendment bill, but Cr Tucker said the bill was unlikely to be updated before Tasmania's upcoming council elections in October.

"This year's election will operate under the current rules so it's really important for the candidates to note the address does not have to be their home address," he said.

" It can be a work address or another address where the person can be contacted if they need to be. "

Cr Tucker said it was "necessary" for the Tasmanian Electoral Commission (TEC) to hold the real addresses and contact details of potential councillors to ensure they were genuine candidates.

He said LGAT believes it was not necessary for it to be put on public signage.

Independent MLC Meg Webb also warned it could be "tricky" to update the legislation in time for this year's elections.

Meg Webb says from a safety perspective the request to change the requirement is worth considering. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Ms Webb is chair of the joint standing committee on electoral matters within Tasmanian parliament, which formally reviews electoral law issues and makes recommendations to the government.

"I think this is a really valid concern … and it's certainly a matter to consider from a safety perspective," she said.

Mr Bigg said he had a meeting scheduled with local government minister Kerry Vincent in which he would push to have the laws updated this year.

"I think this can be fixed this year quite easily with a couple of single line amendments in legislation," Mr Bigg said.

"If [Mr] Vincent returns to parliament next week and perhaps tables an amendment bill, I don't see any reasons why members of parliament wouldn't support and pass it."

Some states have updated law

A government spokesperson said the requirements for advertising authorisation reflected state and federal electoral acts and were "ensuring consistency across all levels of government".

Robert Hortle, deputy director of the Tasmanian Policy Exchange, said the rule reflected the principles of transparency, accountability and traceability that existed in many electoral laws.

Mr Hortle said the same requirement was in place for state and federal elections.

However, some states have updated their legislation at a local government level.

"New South Wales and Western Australia have the same rule as Tasmania, but Victoria and Queensland, for example, are a little bit different," Dr Hortle said.

"[In those states] they allow people running for local government to use PO boxes as their contactable address."

Dr Hortle also said in New Zealand, candidates were able to use a phone number or a website with a contact form, instead of a physical address.

"The key thing is, as long as we're upholding that principle of accountability and transparency, then I'm sure there are plenty of more modern solutions that we could look at," he said.

Mr Bigg said if the rule could not be amended ahead of the local government elections, he would consider pursuing the matter in court, as he felt it contradicted privacy and protection laws.

World.title: ‘Massive loss’: Roosters enforcer weighs in on Panthers’ injury blow
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Massive loss’: Roosters enforcer weighs in on Panthers’ injury blow Christian Nicolussi August 8, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Isaah Yeo has been described as the “heartbeat” of the Penrith Panthers by Spencer Leniu, who won premierships alongside the lock forward – but will now try to heap more misery on his old mates on Thursday night. What was shaping as one of the NRL games of the year – and a potential grand final preview – between the Panthers and Sydney Roosters at CommBank Stadium has lost a superstar in Yeo because of a suspected pectoral injury. Isaah Yeo could be out for the remainder of the season for the Panthers. NRL Imagery Yeo flew back to Sydney with his teammates on Saturday morning following the 28-12 loss to the Warriors at Go Media Stadium in Auckland where he lasted 33 minutes. The co-captain immediately winced in pain and grabbed at his right pec before he made his way from the field.



Penrith coach Ivan Cleary confirmed after the game: “It doesn’t look great.” The 31-year-old is expected to undergo scans on Sunday, with the worst-case scenario to end Yeo’s season – and more than likely his dreams of captaining Australia to a World Cup win on home soil. Loading Leniu was saddened to hear the Yeo news when informed in the sheds after the Roosters’ gritty 20-18 win over Canterbury on Friday night. “No way. That’s a massive loss – he’s the heartbeat of their team,” Leniu said.



“Knowing Penrith, they’re a world-class team, and they’ll have that next-man-up mentality. “They’ve done it the last couple of years, they fill those voids when it comes around, and it will be no different next week if he’s out. Loading “He’s the captain, and when a lot of experience like that goes off the field, you definitely notice it. “But Penrith are a well-oiled machine. With that next-man-up mentality, if you get the tap on the shoulder, you’ve got a duty to perform and wear the jersey with pride.



“That’s been the Penrith Panthers the last few years. That’s why they’ve been such a great team. Another perspective Opinion

NRL 2026 These are the forbidden phrases the NRL won’t let you hear Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “They’ll still be pushing for that premiership at the end of the season. Next week will be another day in the office.” The Panthers won 40-4 against the Roosters in round three when Tom Jenkins raced in four tries. But the Roosters have won their past seven games, and are building momentum at the right time. They are also set to welcome back skipper James Tedesco from an ankle injury. “I’ve got a lot of confidence in this team, the boys inside the four walls have confidence in each other, it was a scrappy win [against the Dogs], but we got the win,” Leniu said.



Naufahu Whyte has been a standout for the Roosters, and in Leniu’s opinion is on track to be crowned one of the Dally M props of the year. “He’s a no-nonsense player, he comes into training, if you ask him how he’s going, he’ll tell you, ‘same old, same old’,” Leniu said. “That’s who he is. He goes about his business, he doesn’t try to be anyone else but himself, and flourishes when he goes out there.”

World.title: The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass Paul Cully August 8, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Les Kiss’ first Test as Wallabies coach could easily turn into the shocker in Osaka. The heat and humidity they are likely to encounter is one factor, but aside from that, Japan are a competitive Test side underpinned by an improving domestic competition filled with high-quality coaches from around the world. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Les Kiss chat at training ahead of Saturday’s match against Japan. Getty Images The Brave Blossoms were messed around by Ireland’s recent refusal to travel to Japan in the Nations Championship, but they have won the scheduling battle for this two-Test series against the Wallabies. Kiss would have copped the odd hospital pass as a player. Now, as a coach, he’s got a high ball well above his shoulders with Eddie Jones steaming in from 20 metres away.



The Wallabies could lose this Test. The bar for success in Kiss’ debut as coach is a win of any nature: get the job done and get out of there. It is a Test with a high-risk profile, and Kiss was never going to be able to fully mitigate that risk, no matter how he selected his team. Loading However, his 23-man squad and the make-up of the bench have increased the likelihood of Japan getting away to the fast start they desperately want. Josh Canham and Miles Amatosero are a young pairing, and they will face Warner Dearns, the best second-rower in Super Rugby Pacific this season, while prop Aidan Ross is more solid than spectacular and certainly won’t offer the same mobility around the field as Angus Bell.



Jones has prioritised speed from the outset, preferring Jack Cornelsen in the second row ahead of Harry Hockings, and Amatosero is going to be tested by the speed of the game if Japan get the quick ball they want. Clearly, the Wallabies’ strategy is to finish the Test strongly with their stacked bench, but they won’t want to be chasing the game with the combative Hockings and that old warrior Michael Leitch providing serious nuisance value off the bench for Jones. Eddie Jones and Japan will be ready for the challenge posed by the Wallabies. Getty Images The Wallabies must have considered the opposite approach – trying to overwhelm the Japanese early. That is something the French did well in June. Japan probably don’t even know themselves what a good side they are, but their self-belief will soar if they start well and exert scoreboard pressure on the Wallabies.



A Japan XV side put themselves in a great position against the Maori All Blacks in late June, racing into a 24-7 lead at halftime during their game in Nagoya, before that lack of self-belief kicked in. They were chased down and lost 38-31. But they will have learnt something from that defeat and young No.10 Ryunosuke Ito probably banked some valuable lessons as he continues his crash-course introduction to Test rugby. Loading The other player to look for is Japan No.6 Ben Gunter, who is on a big collision course with Wallaby Rob Valetini. Gunter, who grew up in Australia, has arguably the biggest shoulders in Test rugby and is not afraid to use them. He has snuck under the radar this week with all the focus on Hockings, but Gunter is the better player. He is an old-fashioned hitman who will also be lining up Harry Wilson if the Wallabies captain comes off the back fence.



The Jones factor is also inescapable, and the former Wallabies coach will have some clear views on how and where Kiss’s side can be vulnerable. Related Article Australian rugby Hoop dreams: How growing up on a court turned Josh into a Wallabies ‘baller’ But it’s a factor that is easy to overplay in a rugby world in which the degrees of separation between Australian rugby and Japan are decreasing anyway. For example, new Wallabies defence coach Scott McLeod almost won the Japan Rugby League One title in June (against Dave Rennie’s Kobe) as an assistant at Kubota Spears. In a classic clash of styles, Kubota employed a kicking and defence-based game plan, using the tactical nous of new/old Waratahs No.10 Bernard Foley.



Against Rennie’s ball-in-hand style – and Kobe superstar Ardie Savea – it almost worked too: Kubota might have won the game but for a knock-on by former Crusaders halfback Bryn Hall with the tryline in sight. That decider was a good showcase for the tactical variety and physicality of the Japanese game, and their players are increasingly well-prepared for the demands of Test rugby. Kiss, therefore, has been handed a tricky first assignment – and if he marks it with a victory, it is a bigger positive than he will get credit for. World.title: My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss
World.content:
NationalGen Z Opinion My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author August 8, 2026 — 9:30am

August 8, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I can’t believe,” says my daughter as I navigate our rented manual car around the narrow, cobbled streets of Nazaré, Portugal, “that you used to have to read maps to travel.” As the gears grind yet again under my rusty touch, I glance at her and laugh: “But we were using a whole part of our brain that you guys don’t touch now.” She shrugs, tapping on her phone. Illustration by Dionne Gain Remember maps? Calling from a phone box? Aerogram letters? Post-school travel for those born in the ’70s meant disappearing into Europe like a gumboot into quicksand, swallowed whole by different cultures. We were not being monitored, surveilled, tracked: we were finding our own paths, new ones. We didn’t have mobile phones with location data, downloadable maps, apps to make bookings. This, too, confounds my daughter: “But your parents wouldn’t know if you were dead.” I guess they just waved us off and hoped for the best. There was something delightful about the invisibility, being out of range and absolved of all responsibility. We were just gone, and we’d be back in a few months. Sure, I’d call home every week or two – collect, to the eye-rolls of my parents – and send the odd postcard, but that was it. We took photos on little cameras and mailed the film back home to be developed: they were unfailingly blurry, unflattering, often tilted or poorly framed. But it wasn’t about how we looked, it was about what we were looking at. There are few things as genuinely thrilling about entering and inhaling a new country for the first time. We took terrible risks, sleeping on beaches, train stations, boat shacks, all to save money, and relied on overnight train trips to get some rest, zigzagging around the continent with a heavily stamped Eurail Pass.



My daughter and her friends are too smart to do stupid things like sleep in public places. But I watch the reels and feeds of this Euro-generation, who save up and go year after year to the prettiest places in Europe, navigating swelling crowds, and I am gobsmacked. Julia Baird in Venice during her own backpacker adventure. First, they look so good. Polished and picture-perfect. I think I packed a hairbrush, but I can’t be sure. Maybe an eyeliner? Nothing more. I was gripped by an Oscar Wilde biography (the superb work by Richard Ellmann) and was somehow inspired by that to invest in several vintage Spanish brocade jackets which were hopeless in the cold and probably looked half mad, paired with scuffed Doc Martens and cut-off jeans. Today I scroll through Instagram and see a string of girls in bikinis and impeccable, tasteful clothes. Carousels of cute poses. Second, there is an ease to travel we did not know, facilitated by the phone and by the now-widespread fluency in English across Europe. If we didn’t make an effort to learn the local language, we were cooked: Google Translate didn’t exist. According to travel research group MMGY’s 2025 Portrait of European Travellers (surveying France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK), Gen Z (aged 14-29) is responsible for the travel boom in Europe, and is planning to spend more on global travel and take more vacations than any other age bracket. Unsurprisingly, Italy, Spain and Greece are considered the most desirable, while the US flags in popularity. They are using planning tools and AI to map out itineraries.



But tech isn’t just aiding travel, it’s shaping and changing it. The most picturesque, Insta-worthy places are swamped by young people looking for the perfect shot to post, much to the annoyance of locals. Sweating crowds in sweltering Europe jostle around landmarks and crowd the most photogenic vistas. Today in the centre of Lisbon, where I have come to research a book, on the way to the train station I wove past dozens of people in Instagram poses, hands on hips, laughing, tilting heads, pouting, flexing. What they are missing is the joy of not being seen. Of waking up on beaches with panda eyes, not worrying someone will take a shot and post it. I remember speaking a year ago to one teen who was preparing for a Mediterranean trip by having her eyelashes, nails and brows done: “No way am I going to be chopped [look unattractive] in Greece,” she said. The prevalence of social media has also led to milder behaviour, according to a 2024 survey by youth travel agency StudentUniverse. It found only one in five young Australians planned to party when travelling overseas: 84 per cent of Gen Z full-time students scheduled trips where there would be no drinking. Many parents would cheer, given the genuine concerns about drink-spiking and safety, but 27 per cent of Gen Z also said they just didn’t want to be snapped doing something embarrassing.



Related Article Opinion

Tourism Idiots are ruining travel for the rest of us Ben Groundwater Travel writer StudentUniverse’s Will Jones told Student Traveller this trend – of “dry-trippers” – had been rapid and widespread: “This is the first generation to be setting this trend. I’m a Millennial and I remember when I was their age having holidays focused on drinking and partying. So it is amazing how much, and how quickly, this has changed. “Australians used to be seen as big party people, but this Gen Z is the first global generation. Because of social media, they all seem to be following the same trends and doing the same things.” This is a generation that is having less sex, drinking less and reading fewer books (although they are reading in digital formats). But they are travelling more often. War or global instability haven’t deterred them, with only 1.5 per cent of Australians under 30 cancelling trips to Europe in 2026. Home ownership is hard, almost impossible; holidays are within reach.



In 2023, The Guardian declared “gritty gap years” were out and “grand tours of Europe’s charisma” were in. Is it weird to be nostalgic about the grit? A time when we could run wild, unobserved, learning how to fend for ourselves? When we could just have fun – or not – instead of feeling like we also had to look like we were having fun? I realise this makes me seem ancient. I also feel like I’m describing the daily life of ancient explorers. But in trading concealment for convenience, evaporation for ease, surely we are in danger of losing the pleasure of forgetting ourselves and truly paying attention, marvelling. Julia Baird is a journalist, author and regular columnist. Her latest book is Bright Shining: How grace changes everything. Washington: The Pentagon will invest more than half a billion dollars in a “world-first” mining project in central western NSW that produces scandium, a rare critical mineral used in fighter jets, spacecraft and other tools of war. The $US400 million ($560 million) loan is intended to expand production at Sunrise Energy Metals’ Syerston Scandium Project near Fifield, south-west of Dubbo, as the US seeks to urgently diversify its supply chain for rare earths. Sunrise Energy Metals’ Syerston scandium project in NSW. Last year, Sunrise announced a deal for US weapons contractor Lockheed Martin to buy up to 15 tonnes of scandium oxide over five years. The move came just days after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and US President Donald Trump signed a critical minerals deal in Washington. Scandium – used to strengthen aluminium – is already used widely for defence, aerospace and energy applications, but nearly all supply comes from China, Russia and Ukraine.



The US has not mined scandium since 1969. The Pentagon said foreign competitors accounted for about 80 per cent of global scandium production and nearly 100 per cent of processing. Trump announced the Pentagon’s investment on Friday (Washington time) during a televised roundtable with mining executives at the US State Department. The White House described the Sunrise venture as “the world’s first primary scandium mine”. The US Department of Defence said the conditional loan from its Office of Strategic Capital would build a “complete, US-aligned value chain from mine to finished metal”, securing a vital supply of scandium for the US defence and commercial industrial base. World.title: The Nordic country’s pitch to Queensland for multibillion-dollar industry
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCritical minerals The Nordic country’s pitch to Queensland for multibillion-dollar industry James Hall August 8, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The ambassador of Finland was busily working the corridors of power in Queensland this week, eager to offer the Nordic nation’s services to help kick-start a multibillion-dollar minerals production industry. Queensland is flush with mineral deposits in the state’s north and northwest but industry experts have long warned of the lack of economic benefits to a “dig and ship” approach, with the real value coming from onshore processing and refining. Queensland has rich deposits of critical minerals, including copper. This is where Finland comes in, Ambassador Arto Haapea told this masthead in an interview, a nation highly regarded for developing mining and production technology. The Crisafulli government last week unveiled its 2026-30 critical minerals strategy which flags investment in processing through local refining and manufacturing. This is broadly in-line with the federal government’s Future Made in Australia industrial policy.



“I would argue a lot of the Finnish technology is something that enables you to do that,” Haapea said. “You need the technology partners that will help you get to that next level of processing, and there is a number of areas in the wide spectrum of minerals where Finnish counterparts would be more than happy to work with Australia.” The Ambassador spruiked Finland’s technological prowess in the mining industry. AAPIMAGE Finland, which joined NATO in 2023 in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, has become increasingly vocal on geopolitical tensions. Haapea stressed this global threat, stemming from Russia in Europe and China in the Asia Pacific, placed greater significance on collaboration on sensitive industries such as critical minerals and artificial intelligence.



This fear has triggered the creation of US-led global coalitions such as the Pax Silica Initiative, which both Finland and Australia are signatories. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Finland joins NATO in historic shift, Russia threatens ‘counter measures’ “We really need to work together when it comes to critical minerals because there’s a reason why they are being called critical raw materials,” Haapea said. “That’s just something that we are working towards, and we are always on the same side of the fence with Australians.” Chris Vernon, CSIRO chief research scientist and critical minerals lead, said Queensland’s plan to accelerate approvals and project developments will be well-received by the industry.



But he said the promise to support downstream processing to refine and manufacture provided significant economic value. “That’s what we’ve been missing in the critical mineral space,” Vernon told this masthead. Arto Haapea with Natural Resources and Mines Minister Dale Last. “These are not dig and ship opportunities – you really have to do some processing and refining to capture the economic value. “It’s totally unlike iron ore, where you can get maybe a quarter of a value just from digging it up with a shovel. Critical minerals are worth pennies in the dollar as ores and concentrates, and to break into the market – particularly the ex-China market – you need to come to the party with something that’s a purified oxide or a metal or something that a manufacturing nation can use.”



The Finnish diplomat’s visit to Parliament and One William Street came just a week after meetings with US Consul-General Jeremy Cornforth, who will inspect critical mineral projects later this month. Natural Resources and Mines Dale Last told said the critical minerals plan to 2030 focused on cashing in on global demand and attracting international investment. “Queensland is entering a defining decade with a once-in-a-generation opportunity to become a global supplier of critical minerals and the Crisafulli government is working with trusted trading partners to unlock the possibilities that lay beneath our feet,” he told this masthead.
