World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Massive loss’: Roosters enforcer weighs in on Panthers’ injury blow Christian Nicolussi August 8, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Isaah Yeo has been described as the “heartbeat” of the Penrith Panthers by Spencer Leniu, who won premierships alongside the lock forward – but will now try to heap more misery on his old mates on Thursday night. What was shaping as one of the NRL games of the year – and a potential grand final preview – between the Panthers and Sydney Roosters at CommBank Stadium has lost a superstar in Yeo because of a suspected pectoral injury. Isaah Yeo could be out for the remainder of the season for the Panthers. NRL Imagery Yeo flew back to Sydney with his teammates on Saturday morning following the 28-12 loss to the Warriors at Go Media Stadium in Auckland where he lasted 33 minutes. The co-captain immediately winced in pain and grabbed at his right pec before he made his way from the field.



Penrith coach Ivan Cleary confirmed after the game: “It doesn’t look great.” The 31-year-old is expected to undergo scans on Sunday, with the worst-case scenario to end Yeo’s season – and more than likely his dreams of captaining Australia to a World Cup win on home soil. Loading Leniu was saddened to hear the Yeo news when informed in the sheds after the Roosters’ gritty 20-18 win over Canterbury on Friday night. “No way. That’s a massive loss – he’s the heartbeat of their team,” Leniu said.



“Knowing Penrith, they’re a world-class team, and they’ll have that next-man-up mentality. “They’ve done it the last couple of years, they fill those voids when it comes around, and it will be no different next week if he’s out. Loading “He’s the captain, and when a lot of experience like that goes off the field, you definitely notice it. “But Penrith are a well-oiled machine. With that next-man-up mentality, if you get the tap on the shoulder, you’ve got a duty to perform and wear the jersey with pride.



“That’s been the Penrith Panthers the last few years. That’s why they’ve been such a great team. Another perspective Opinion

NRL 2026 These are the forbidden phrases the NRL won’t let you hear Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “They’ll still be pushing for that premiership at the end of the season. Next week will be another day in the office.” The Panthers won 40-4 against the Roosters in round three when Tom Jenkins raced in four tries. But the Roosters have won their past seven games, and are building momentum at the right time. They are also set to welcome back skipper James Tedesco from an ankle injury. “I’ve got a lot of confidence in this team, the boys inside the four walls have confidence in each other, it was a scrappy win [against the Dogs], but we got the win,” Leniu said.



Naufahu Whyte has been a standout for the Roosters, and in Leniu’s opinion is on track to be crowned one of the Dally M props of the year. “He’s a no-nonsense player, he comes into training, if you ask him how he’s going, he’ll tell you, ‘same old, same old’,” Leniu said. “That’s who he is. He goes about his business, he doesn’t try to be anyone else but himself, and flourishes when he goes out there.”

World.title: The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass Paul Cully August 8, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Les Kiss’ first Test as Wallabies coach could easily turn into the shocker in Osaka. The heat and humidity they are likely to encounter is one factor, but aside from that, Japan are a competitive Test side underpinned by an improving domestic competition filled with high-quality coaches from around the world. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Les Kiss chat at training ahead of Saturday’s match against Japan. Getty Images The Brave Blossoms were messed around by Ireland’s recent refusal to travel to Japan in the Nations Championship, but they have won the scheduling battle for this two-Test series against the Wallabies. Kiss would have copped the odd hospital pass as a player. Now, as a coach, he’s got a high ball well above his shoulders with Eddie Jones steaming in from 20 metres away.



The Wallabies could lose this Test. The bar for success in Kiss’ debut as coach is a win of any nature: get the job done and get out of there. It is a Test with a high-risk profile, and Kiss was never going to be able to fully mitigate that risk, no matter how he selected his team. Loading However, his 23-man squad and the make-up of the bench have increased the likelihood of Japan getting away to the fast start they desperately want. Josh Canham and Miles Amatosero are a young pairing, and they will face Warner Dearns, the best second-rower in Super Rugby Pacific this season, while prop Aidan Ross is more solid than spectacular and certainly won’t offer the same mobility around the field as Angus Bell.



Jones has prioritised speed from the outset, preferring Jack Cornelsen in the second row ahead of Harry Hockings, and Amatosero is going to be tested by the speed of the game if Japan get the quick ball they want. Clearly, the Wallabies’ strategy is to finish the Test strongly with their stacked bench, but they won’t want to be chasing the game with the combative Hockings and that old warrior Michael Leitch providing serious nuisance value off the bench for Jones. Eddie Jones and Japan will be ready for the challenge posed by the Wallabies. Getty Images The Wallabies must have considered the opposite approach – trying to overwhelm the Japanese early. That is something the French did well in June. Japan probably don’t even know themselves what a good side they are, but their self-belief will soar if they start well and exert scoreboard pressure on the Wallabies.



A Japan XV side put themselves in a great position against the Maori All Blacks in late June, racing into a 24-7 lead at halftime during their game in Nagoya, before that lack of self-belief kicked in. They were chased down and lost 38-31. But they will have learnt something from that defeat and young No.10 Ryunosuke Ito probably banked some valuable lessons as he continues his crash-course introduction to Test rugby. Loading The other player to look for is Japan No.6 Ben Gunter, who is on a big collision course with Wallaby Rob Valetini. Gunter, who grew up in Australia, has arguably the biggest shoulders in Test rugby and is not afraid to use them. He has snuck under the radar this week with all the focus on Hockings, but Gunter is the better player. He is an old-fashioned hitman who will also be lining up Harry Wilson if the Wallabies captain comes off the back fence.



The Jones factor is also inescapable, and the former Wallabies coach will have some clear views on how and where Kiss’s side can be vulnerable. Related Article Australian rugby Hoop dreams: How growing up on a court turned Josh into a Wallabies ‘baller’ But it’s a factor that is easy to overplay in a rugby world in which the degrees of separation between Australian rugby and Japan are decreasing anyway. For example, new Wallabies defence coach Scott McLeod almost won the Japan Rugby League One title in June (against Dave Rennie’s Kobe) as an assistant at Kubota Spears. In a classic clash of styles, Kubota employed a kicking and defence-based game plan, using the tactical nous of new/old Waratahs No.10 Bernard Foley.



Against Rennie’s ball-in-hand style – and Kobe superstar Ardie Savea – it almost worked too: Kubota might have won the game but for a knock-on by former Crusaders halfback Bryn Hall with the tryline in sight. That decider was a good showcase for the tactical variety and physicality of the Japanese game, and their players are increasingly well-prepared for the demands of Test rugby. Kiss, therefore, has been handed a tricky first assignment – and if he marks it with a victory, it is a bigger positive than he will get credit for. World.title: My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss
World.content:
NationalGen Z Opinion My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author August 8, 2026 — 9:30am

August 8, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I can’t believe,” says my daughter as I navigate our rented manual car around the narrow, cobbled streets of Nazaré, Portugal, “that you used to have to read maps to travel.” As the gears grind yet again under my rusty touch, I glance at her and laugh: “But we were using a whole part of our brain that you guys don’t touch now.” She shrugs, tapping on her phone. Illustration by Dionne Gain Remember maps? Calling from a phone box? Aerogram letters? Post-school travel for those born in the ’70s meant disappearing into Europe like a gumboot into quicksand, swallowed whole by different cultures. We were not being monitored, surveilled, tracked: we were finding our own paths, new ones. We didn’t have mobile phones with location data, downloadable maps, apps to make bookings. This, too, confounds my daughter: “But your parents wouldn’t know if you were dead.” I guess they just waved us off and hoped for the best. There was something delightful about the invisibility, being out of range and absolved of all responsibility. We were just gone, and we’d be back in a few months. Sure, I’d call home every week or two – collect, to the eye-rolls of my parents – and send the odd postcard, but that was it. We took photos on little cameras and mailed the film back home to be developed: they were unfailingly blurry, unflattering, often tilted or poorly framed. But it wasn’t about how we looked, it was about what we were looking at. There are few things as genuinely thrilling about entering and inhaling a new country for the first time. We took terrible risks, sleeping on beaches, train stations, boat shacks, all to save money, and relied on overnight train trips to get some rest, zigzagging around the continent with a heavily stamped Eurail Pass.



My daughter and her friends are too smart to do stupid things like sleep in public places. But I watch the reels and feeds of this Euro-generation, who save up and go year after year to the prettiest places in Europe, navigating swelling crowds, and I am gobsmacked. Julia Baird in Venice during her own backpacker adventure. First, they look so good. Polished and picture-perfect. I think I packed a hairbrush, but I can’t be sure. Maybe an eyeliner? Nothing more. I was gripped by an Oscar Wilde biography (the superb work by Richard Ellmann) and was somehow inspired by that to invest in several vintage Spanish brocade jackets which were hopeless in the cold and probably looked half mad, paired with scuffed Doc Martens and cut-off jeans. Today I scroll through Instagram and see a string of girls in bikinis and impeccable, tasteful clothes. Carousels of cute poses. Second, there is an ease to travel we did not know, facilitated by the phone and by the now-widespread fluency in English across Europe. If we didn’t make an effort to learn the local language, we were cooked: Google Translate didn’t exist. According to travel research group MMGY’s 2025 Portrait of European Travellers (surveying France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK), Gen Z (aged 14-29) is responsible for the travel boom in Europe, and is planning to spend more on global travel and take more vacations than any other age bracket. Unsurprisingly, Italy, Spain and Greece are considered the most desirable, while the US flags in popularity. They are using planning tools and AI to map out itineraries.



But tech isn’t just aiding travel, it’s shaping and changing it. The most picturesque, Insta-worthy places are swamped by young people looking for the perfect shot to post, much to the annoyance of locals. Sweating crowds in sweltering Europe jostle around landmarks and crowd the most photogenic vistas. Today in the centre of Lisbon, where I have come to research a book, on the way to the train station I wove past dozens of people in Instagram poses, hands on hips, laughing, tilting heads, pouting, flexing. What they are missing is the joy of not being seen. Of waking up on beaches with panda eyes, not worrying someone will take a shot and post it. I remember speaking a year ago to one teen who was preparing for a Mediterranean trip by having her eyelashes, nails and brows done: “No way am I going to be chopped [look unattractive] in Greece,” she said. The prevalence of social media has also led to milder behaviour, according to a 2024 survey by youth travel agency StudentUniverse. It found only one in five young Australians planned to party when travelling overseas: 84 per cent of Gen Z full-time students scheduled trips where there would be no drinking. Many parents would cheer, given the genuine concerns about drink-spiking and safety, but 27 per cent of Gen Z also said they just didn’t want to be snapped doing something embarrassing.



Related Article Opinion

Tourism Idiots are ruining travel for the rest of us Ben Groundwater Travel writer StudentUniverse’s Will Jones told Student Traveller this trend – of “dry-trippers” – had been rapid and widespread: “This is the first generation to be setting this trend. I’m a Millennial and I remember when I was their age having holidays focused on drinking and partying. So it is amazing how much, and how quickly, this has changed. “Australians used to be seen as big party people, but this Gen Z is the first global generation. Because of social media, they all seem to be following the same trends and doing the same things.” This is a generation that is having less sex, drinking less and reading fewer books (although they are reading in digital formats). But they are travelling more often. War or global instability haven’t deterred them, with only 1.5 per cent of Australians under 30 cancelling trips to Europe in 2026. Home ownership is hard, almost impossible; holidays are within reach.



In 2023, The Guardian declared “gritty gap years” were out and “grand tours of Europe’s charisma” were in. Is it weird to be nostalgic about the grit? A time when we could run wild, unobserved, learning how to fend for ourselves? When we could just have fun – or not – instead of feeling like we also had to look like we were having fun? I realise this makes me seem ancient. I also feel like I’m describing the daily life of ancient explorers. But in trading concealment for convenience, evaporation for ease, surely we are in danger of losing the pleasure of forgetting ourselves and truly paying attention, marvelling. Julia Baird is a journalist, author and regular columnist. Her latest book is Bright Shining: How grace changes everything. World.title: Beloved Nelson cafe forced to close after landlord dispute and roadworks woes
World.content:
A popular Nelson cafe and gallery has announced its closure, after a dispute with the landlord and ongoing roadworks made it untenable to continue.

Red Art Gallery & Café owners Ant and Suzi Stevens say after nine years in business, its closure was forced after the landlord chose not to renew the lease, a devastating blow after months of roadworks on the two adjacent streets had seriously impacted revenue.

The work, part of the $78 million Bridge to Better project, has seen water pipes and other infrastructure along the the length of Bridge Street replaced, causing disruption to a number of businesses since it first began last year.

The couple said the decision to close in September was not the outcome they wanted, especially on the back of a tough few years,

"It's just heartbreaking, I just feel like I'm losing a child to be honest, it's just been my baby for so long," Suzi said.

The business had survived a global pandemic, a recession and roadworks which effectively left them an island, with the cafe and gallery entrance hidden behind fences, trucks and diggers.

Bridge Street and Haven Road either side of the business have been closed for months while the roads are ripped up and pipes replaced, with customers having to walk down narrow, uneven gravel paths between temporary fences to reach the business.

The gallery represented about 60 artists, most of them from Nelson and Tasman, and they had taken on more after [https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/ninetonoon/audio/2019034008/nelson-gallery-shop-stops-stocking-the-work-of-40-local-artists the Suter Art Gallery made the decision to stop stocking the work of around 40 local artists], after getting advice from external retail specialists.

Roadworks in Nelson are taking a toll on local businesses. Samantha Gee/RNZ

Since announcing the closure on social media, the couple had received hundreds of comments in support.

The cafe was full on Friday morning when RNZ visited. Within an hour, it had made as much money as it had over the previous two days combined.

"We knew there would be strong support, but not the way it's been with the messages, with the people coming in," Ant said.

"Love and compassion and heart will beat greed any day."

He said the council told the couple they would be the "most impacted business" given their proximity to the roadworks, but there had been "zero talk of compensation or help in any way", except to be asked whether they had two hard years in them until the upgrade was complete.

"It'll be wonderful for someone else, but it won't be us," Ant said.

Council agrees to defer rates if landlords come to the party

Nelson mayor Nick Smith previously said he had met with a number of "very distressed" business owners who were feeling the pressure of the ongoing roadworks.

Staff had gone to "tremendous effort" to try and minimise disruption in the city by promoting businesses, he said.

Smith acknowledged the work was "incredibly disruptive" but said it was essential to renew and upgrade infrastructure that, in some places, was over 100 years old.

Once complete, Bridge Street was tipped to be a "people-focused corridor" with utility services capable of supporting inner city development.

At a council meeting on Thursday, elected members agreed to allow affected businesses to defer rates from the current year, with repayments split over the next three years, if landlords agreed to provide the equivalent financial relief to the tenant.

Nelson's mayor says council staff are trying to minimise disruption in the city by promoting businesses. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Nelson Tasman Chamber of Commerce chair Venus Guy said it was disappointing to see the closure of long-standing local businesses.

"Red Gallery has been part of our city centre, and our thoughts are with the owners and everyone affected by this decision."

She said while the Bridge to Better project was an important investment in Nelson's future, the major infrastructure work placed very real pressures on businesses during construction.

"It is essential that we continue working together to minimise disruption, support affected businesses and remind our community that our city centre remains open for business.

Central city businesses feeling the hurt

Longstanding cafe and food store Prego Mediterranean Foods & Comida Cafe shut its doors in June, and the owners said at the time that the [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/625679/road-closures-and-rising-costs-force-closure-of-nelson-businessongoing ongoing roadworks were one of the factors in its closure].

Further down Bridge Street, Pizzeria Bella owner Yusef Corten said he thought more could be done to support businesses affected by the infrastructure works.

At lunchtime on Friday, his restaurant was empty and the noise of roadworks outside made it hard to be heard when speaking.

He had organised a meeting with about 30 Bridge Street business owners that were also struggling around two months ago.

He said the rates deferral scheme made little difference. It gave relief of about $80 per month, but would have to be paid back in the years to come.

Pizzeria Bella owner Yusef Corten sits in front of his restaurant and behind a fence while work is done on Bridge Street. Samantha Gee/RNZ

Corten, who had owned and operated hospitality businesses in Nelson for more than a decade, said he bought Pizzeria Bella a year ago. He started out with nine employees, but was now down to three. Only he and his son were working full-time, with debt that kept rising.

Pizzeria Bella's revenue was down 80 percent since the roadworks began. On Tuesday, Corten made $300 between the lunch and dinner services. His accountant had told him he needed turnover of $2000 a day to survive.

"Every day I am more negative, more negative."

Corten said two businesses had closed and it was possible that more would follow.

World.title: City Rail Link 'First Look' events begin
World.content:
On Saturday morning, Aucklanders will have a chance to see inside the City Rail Link (CRL) for the first time.

New Zealand's largest transport infrastructure project will open on 13 September.

A series of 'First Look' events will be held over the next three Saturdays.

It will begin with Maungawhau Station (formerly Mt Eden), with a free, one-hour tour from 8am.

There will be food and activities in the surrounding streets, as well as busking and community performances inside the train station.

Maungawhau Station in Auckland's Mt Eden, August 2026. Liu Chen / RNZ

"This striking new station combines world-class transport infrastructure with thoughtful design inspired by the surrounding volcanic landscape and deep cultural connections to nearby maunga," Auckland Transport's website said.

"Its dramatic architecture, natural materials and spacious platforms create a station experience unlike anything else in Auckland."

World.title: Underground counters lose track of who's visiting nature
World.content:
The Department of Conservation's (DOC) systems for counting visitors and activities at 700 sites on public conservation land are old and plagued by delays, and data loss and backlogs.

Its counters are also mostly installed underground and have to be checked manually by staff to download the data.

Now the department is asking companies what type of automated system it could replace it with, paid for out of the international visitor levy.

A document for a tender that closed on Friday showed officials were particularly interested in AI and cameras among other things.

"The current Activity Counter System ... faces end-to-end challenges across hardware, firmware, data flow, and verification, resulting in inconsistent data and operational inefficiencies," said the document.

"Manual processes dominate downloading and validation, causing delays, data loss, and backlog."

Added to this were hardware inconsistencies, while a lack of telemetry prevented real-time monitoring.

"Fragmented reporting limits stakeholder access to timely insights."

'It makes sense'

Conservation Minister Tama Potaka. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

DOC wants a new system to help it analyse visitors' activities, and be easy to install and reliable in some tough environments and not stick out too much visually.

Minister Tama Potaka said better information on visitor numbers and patterns would help with deciding where facilities, funding and staff were most needed.

"Nature is our most important economic asset and underpins our tourism industry, so it makes sense to use International Visitor Levy ... funding to invest in technology that supports visitation while protecting the environment," said Potaka in a statement to RNZ.

On AI's role, the department said a tender participant had asked about if DOC was open to higher AI capability.

"The department expects that some high-value sites will have multiple monitoring technologies in place to serve multiple use cases," it told RNZ.

Visitor counting was the basic use case; if more high tech could be added to get more uses then it wanted to hear from firms how this would function.

"We'll evaluate the proposals and consider where AI could add value."

The international visitor levy collected through the border control system is $100 a person.

Other charges

DOC could charge international visitors $20-$40 to visit Milford Sound and other top nature spots. 123RF

As for a new charge to visit top nature spots for international visitors, DOC said the earliest this could come in was next summer 2027-28.

It depended on the progress of legislation, the Conservation Amendment Bill, that had passed its first reading.

"No decisions have been made on how much the charges will be, and this will be set via regulations," DOC told RNZ on Friday.

The talk has been of a charge of $20-$40 at Milford Sound, Aoraki Mount Cook, Mautohe Cathedral Cove and Tongariro Alpine Crossing, which DOC papers said could raise over $60 million a year.

In the process of amending conservation law to take a more commercial-development bent, DOC looked at three different potential approaches including charging all visitors the same whether New Zealanders or from overseas, charging everyone but charging locals less, and charging only international visitors.

Though the government finally landed on this third option, papers showed DOC's initial recommendation was to have maximum flexibility to charge both NZers and international visitors, such as by introducing a "parks pass".

That would have raised the most money and been simplest, papers said.

World.title: Weather: One of NZ's warmest Julys followed by record-breaking lows
World.content:
MetService is forecasting a warmer and wetter weekend, following a record-breaking week of icy temperatures.

Heavy rain watches for parts of Northland and eastern Bay of Plenty are in force.

The north and east of Northland can expect periods of heavy rain from now until Sunday evening.

MetService has also issued a heavy rain watch for the eastern ranges of Bay of Plenty from Sunday afternoon until Monday morning.

It said rain was no longer expected to approach warning criteria in Grey, Buller and western Tasman, and the watch there was now lifted.

Winter chills

Meteorologist Braydon White said parts of the country plunged to record-breaking minimum temperatures on Thursday and Friday.

"Taumarunui and Rotorua both broke their coldest temperatures ever recorded. Rotorua's records go back to 1972, so that's quite a notable record to be broken."

White said Taupō, Palmerston North and Whangerei all broke their August minimum temperature records this week.

He added that rain was on the way for much of the country, with a heavy rain watch in place for the northwest corner of the South Island until Sunday morning.

"We are not expecting extremely high rainfall intensities, but due to the duration there could be a fair amount of rain that drops in the area. So, we do have a moderate risk of it being upgraded to a warning."

Snow fell in Wellington earlier this week. RNZ / Pokere Paewai

White said the rain was forecasted to move north and most of the North Island could expect a wet Sunday.

World.title: Russia dismisses German drone incident as 'fabricated provocation'
World.content:
The Russian embassy in Berlin has dismissed a suspected drone attack at a major German air freight hub this week as "fabricated provocation", saying it was another example of accusations against Russia without evidence.

"The embassy is expressing its concern about a new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany," said a statement published on Friday on its website in German and Russian.

German federal prosecutors launched a probe this week into what they described as a serious attack that could have impacted foreign and domestic security.

Airport workers discovered the drone late on Tuesday at Leipzig-Halle airport, an important civilian freight and NATO logistics hub in eastern Germany that is also a base for several giant An-124 cargo planes operated by Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.

The drone was equipped with explosives and a detonator, according to prosecutors.

Additionally, a cargo plane that performed a go-around due to a runway closure near the airport collided with an object that prosecutors believe was another drone. The jet, operated by logistics group DHL, sustained slight damage and was eventually diverted to Hanover in northern Germany.

A Ukrainian "Antonov" cargo plane at the German airport Leipzig-Halle in Schkeuditz on Wednesday. AFP/ John MacDuogall

German government members and other officials have not blamed any foreign countries publicly for the incident, but some lawmakers have pointed the finger at Russia, which launched a full-scale invasion in Ukraine in 2022.

"It is obvious that this hastily fabricated provocation only serves the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political class," the Russian embassy said in its statement.

In the past, German officials have often blamed Moscow for what they call hybrid attacks - incidents of aggression that fall short of acts of war.

World.title: Man critical after serious assault at Rotorua lakefront
World.content:
A man is in critical condition after a serious assault at the Rotorua lakefront early on Saturday morning.

Police were called to the lakefront at about 3.15am after receiving a report a man had been assaulted.

The victim was found in a critical condition when police arrived and was taken to the hospital.

Police were working to establish the full circumstances of what happened and charges were being considered.

World.title: Privacy experts warn of gaps in NZ law, as camera glasses hit Kmart shelves
World.content:
Privacy experts are warning that wearable camera technology, dubbed by some as "pervert glasses", expose significant gaps in New Zealand's laws.

University of Canterbury professor Annette Mills said the devices, which were often marketed as smart glasses, were "essentially a computer on your face", combining cameras, microphones, speakers and AI-powered functions in everyday wearable technology.

The Anko Camera Glasses. Supplied / Kmart

Her warning comes as Kmart begins selling its Anko Camera Glasses for just $99, a price point expected to make the technology far more accessible than premium smart glasses such as Meta's Ray-Ban range.

She said that while the glasses offered some benefits, especially as assistive technology for people with disabilities, the technology's growing popularity raised serious privacy concerns.

"We expect to be recorded in some places, such as by CCTV cameras in supermarkets," Mills said.

"But we certainly don't expect to have that everywhere we go."

Mills said that unlike smartphones, which required users to visibly raise a device before taking a photo or recording video, smart glasses could capture footage far more discreetly, making it difficult for bystanders to know whether they were being filmed.

She said overseas cases had already shown how wearable cameras could be misused, including secret recordings in bathrooms and people approaching women in public before uploading the footage to social media without their consent.

Mills said future developments, including facial recognition technology, could make the privacy implications even more significant.

"You could literally look at someone and say, 'Tell me everything there is about this person'. That can make someone feel very vulnerable."

Laws designed for organisations, not individuals

Mills believed New Zealand's privacy framework had a fundamental weakness when it came to wearable technology.

"Our privacy regulations are primarily aimed at protecting individuals, but they are targeted at organisations and what organisations do," she said.

"They are not set up to deal with personal information collected by individuals."

While existing laws could apply to intimate recordings, harmful digital communications and some forms of stalking, Mills said many everyday uses of camera glasses may fall outside current legal protections.

Her concern extended beyond what people record.

Once footage was uploaded to cloud services, it could be processed, analysed and potentially shared in ways many users - and the people they record may not fully understand.

"I think we need to come up with not just regulations that deal with the use, but also controls that deal with the deployment of these devices," she said.

University of Canterbury professor Annette Mills. Supplied / University of Canterbury

'Serious privacy harms'

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner said the Privacy Act was largely focused on regulating the actions of businesses and organisations, not individuals and it applied regardless of what technology was used.

"Tools like CCTV, drones, and smart glasses make it easier for individuals to record each other. If individuals do not use them in a responsible manner, that can lead to serious privacy harms," a spokesperson said.

It said that individuals using glasses to film covertly should be aware that their actions might breach the Privacy Act if the collection, use or disclosure of the personal information was highly offensive to a reasonable person.

"Other laws are also likely to be relevant, such as the Harmful Digital Communications Act, stalking offences or other crimes under the Crimes Act."

Surveillance concerns extend beyond the wearer

Meanwhile, University of Auckland commercial law professor Gehan Gunasekara raised questions about the companies behind the devices.

University of Auckland commercial law professor Gehan Gunasekara. RNZ / Phil Pennington

His concern was not simply that individuals may misuse camera glasses, but that platforms operating the technology could collect vast amounts of information about where people went, what they looked at and how communities behaved.

"The platform also knows all of that information," he said.

"They can map trends, see where people travel and the kinds of stores they shop at."

Even where companies anonymised data before using it to improve artificial intelligence systems, Gunasekara said the aggregated information remained commercially valuable and raised broader questions about privacy and data sovereignty.

A 'game-changing' technology for blind New Zealanders

However, not everyone saw the technology as a threat.

Blind Low Vision New Zealand chief executive Andrea Midgen described AI-enabled smart glasses as the most significant technological advancement her community had seen.

Blind Low Vision chief executive Andrea Midgen. Supplied / Blind Low Vision NZ

The glasses could read street signs, restaurant menus and other visual information aloud while allowing users to keep both hands free for a white cane or guide dog.

"This is the most exciting game changer thing that we've had in technology for our community ever," Midgen said.

She acknowledged privacy concerns but said they stemmed from how people chose to use technology, rather than the technology itself.

"This is just a different form of what already happens with smartphones," she said.

'Use responsibly' - Kmart

A Kmart Group spokesperson confirmed that its Anko Camera Glasses were available to buy in New Zealand.

"The Anko Camera Glasses are part of an established and increasingly mainstream category of wearable technology, with similar products available globally from major technology and eyewear brands. Like other products in this category, they allow users to capture photos and video while also providing audio and connectivity features," the spokesperson said.

"As with any device capable of recording images, we expect customers to use the product responsibly, respectfully and in accordance with applicable laws and community expectations around privacy."

World.title: All Blacks run in four late tries to beat Stormers 21-38 in South Africa
World.content:
The All Blacks have survived a fierce examination in the opening match of their South African tour, pulling clear with four late tries to win 38-21 in Cape Town.

The tourists overcame three yellow cards and a stubborn, forward-based game from the hosts to win, finally removing the errors from the game in the final 15 minutes in finishing with six tries to three.

They crossed four times in that late period, with the scores having been locked 14-14 when Stormers wing Seabelo Senatla scooted over under the crossbar

New Zealand led 14-7 at the interval through tries to forwards Samisoni Taukei'aho and Simon Parker, but there were worrying signs in the first 40 minutes.

Second-five Anton Lienert-Brown and Parker were both shown yellow cards - reducing them to 13 men for a spell - as the All Blacks struggled against the rugged Stormers, who were missing nine Springboks but whose blunt kick-based mauling game created problems.

Patrick Tuipulotu in action against the Stormers. Ron Gaunt/www.photosport.nz

New Zealand captain Patrick Tuipulotu told Sky Sport his side didn't respond well initially to the Stormers' approach.

"We came into this game knowing full well that the Stormers would be very physical and throw everything at us and be set piece-dominant," he said.

"That's what they did. They put a lot of pressure on us and we made a lot of mistakes tonight.

"A lot of the messaging was around trying to keep our discipline as well as trying to play, keep the ball in hand.

"They tested our discipline, played in our half and made us defend quite a bit."

Tuipulotu was relieved his side found their rhythm late in the match.

"In the end we managed to hold the ball, not give away as many penalties and try to tire them out.

"There's a lot to learn there in terms of resilience and trying to stay in the game. I think we've got to be happy with how the Stormers tested us and we'll take that as the start of our tour."

As the home side flagged, the tourists came alive with tries to outside backs Rieko Ioane, Leroy Carter and Josh Moorby, before replacement hooker Asafa Aumua crossed on the final whistle.

Ioane's try came after the veteran had been shifted from wing to centre, following an apparent shoulder injury suffered by midfielder Billy Proctor.

Leroy Carter in action against the Stormers. Ron Gaunt/www.photosport.nz

Carter's try came off a slick break from No.8 Peter Lakai, who was among the best All Blacks while Moorby scored from a charge down.

The Stormers' late score was a penalty try after Moorby was deemed to have committed a professional four to prevent fullback opposite Warrick Gelant from scoring.

There were international debuts off the bench for prop Siale Lauaki and first-five Josh Jacomb.

Lock Fabian Holland impressed in his first All Blacks appearance of the year, following a long-term shoulder injury.

The second match of the All Blacks' tour is against the Sharks in Durban on Wednesday morning.

The Sharks team will feature veteran former All Blacks midfield great Ma'a Nonu, with the 43-year-old having been included on the bench.

World.title: Surprise parents' visit inspires new leader in Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney launched a decisive attack up Mont Ventoux to win the seventh stage of the Tour de France Femmes and take the overall lead from Marlen Reusser.

The 2024 champion was in tears as she put on the yellow jersey and now leads 2023 champion Demi Vollering by 15 seconds and Reusser by 39 with two stages left.

"I'm just so tired and so blown away with what just happened," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"When I started climbing I looked to the right and I saw my parents standing on the roadside. They came today by surprise. I saw my father yelling for me and I thought I had to make him proud."

Reusser and Vollering could not follow Niewiadoma-Phinney when she broke away about 9km from the top of Ventoux, one of the most iconic climbs in cycling with its barren, lunar aspect.

It was a first Tour stage win for Niewiadoma-Phinney, who won the 2024 edition without claiming a stage. Gritting her teeth in the final few hundred metres, the Polish rider dug deep and with the sun gleaming behind her, raised her arms after crossing the line.

She then almost lost balance through fatigue and had to be helped off her bike. Moments later, she was all smiles as she sat on the road and poured cooling water over her head.

"I never chase victories for the sake of winning, I target them because I like this beautiful feeling I have right now," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"I came here (before) to Mont Ventoux with my friends and my husband, and we rode up the climb three times.

"The feeling of reaching the top of this mountain was amazing. From that moment, I just wanted to experience that feeling again. The pure joy of riding, as if I was a kid."

Vollering dropped Reusser in the closing stages of the 15.7km ascent of Ventoux, which has featured several time on the men's Tour. In one of the darkest days in Tour history, British rider Tom Simpson died after collapsing during a tortuous ascent in 1967.

World time trial champion Reusser battled gamely but lost valuable time in the title fight. The Swiss rider finished the stage fourth as Vollering and two-time Giro d'Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy both placed ahead of her.

There were three smaller climbs heading to Ventoux, which was ranked as a Hors Catégorie ascent — the hardest category — and had a gradient of nearly 9 per cent.

Vollering moved ahead first, and Reusser and Niewiadoma-Phinney joined her as others lagged behind. Niewiadoma-Phinney then attacked and, although Vollering stood up in her saddle to chase her the new race leader was riding a brilliant tempo and proved too strong.

"My idea was that I had to make it to Chalet Reynard on my own," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"Because from then on the headwind would be quite strong and the chasers would try to stay on each other's wheel for as long as possible."

The eighth stage is a flat 172km route for sprinters finishing in Nice, where the race ends after another mountain stage on Sunday night.

Stage nine features four sharp climbs of Col d'Èze, nestled in the hills overlooking the Principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on the final stage to win the race by just four seconds.

World.title: AFL issues Cats a 'please explain' over defender's concussion contract
World.content:
Geelong has been handed a belated 'please explain' notice from the AFL after initially avoiding sanction over its controversial secret deal with defender Jake Kolodjashnij, a player with a history of concussions.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who on Friday evening identified himself as the player in question, whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

The bombshell concussion case emerged on Thursday and pressure mounted on the league and Geelong after the AFL didn't hand down any punishment that night.

On Friday afternoon, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking said he had signed off on the deal and confirmed the 'please explain' notice.

Geelong's Steve Hocking said the club would provide information to the AFL about Kolodjashnij's contract. (AAP Image: Erik Anderson)

"I take responsibility for the fact that we didn't lodge it with the AFL and the (AFL)PA," Hocking told reporters in Geelong.

"… I have received a letter of 'please explain' from the AFL in relation to this matter, so we'll deal with that over the coming days."

Hocking said not registering the deal was a "misstep" and was uncertain what consequences Geelong would face.

"We've got a 'please explain' letter, and at the appropriate time we'll work through that with the AFL," he said.

"We'll have to respond to that, and then it'll be up to the AFL, and whatever that is, we'll accept."

Later on Friday, Kolodjashnij issued a statement through Geelong, confirming he was the previously unnamed player.

"While I appreciate the efforts made not to identify me, the speculation has left me feeling I needed to address this personally," Kolodjashnij said.

"I participated fully in the AFL's independent concussion panel process, respected its independence, and was comfortable with the outcome. I have continued playing AFL football since.

"What disappoints me most is that my private medical information has been made public. Everyone deserves the right to keep their confidential medical information private.

"… I am healthy, feeling good, and focused on playing my role for the team for the remainder of the season."

The 2022 premiership defender, 30, has played 209 games.

Kolodjashnij's twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, retired prematurely in 2020 due to concussion.

On Thursday night, calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL had insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

Geelong also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

Grief-stricken mother of star footballer reveals AFL executive phone call West Coast Eagles star Adam Hunter's mother Joanne Brown says AFL executive Laura Kane reached out to her, but the grieving mother says the phone call was "too little, too late".

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board when the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the AFL statement.

Drummond did not front the media and issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Many AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and former number one draft pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham 'Polly' Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multimillion-dollar concussion class action against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

World.title: Grief-stricken mother of star footballer reveals AFL executive phone call
World.content:
The late West Coast Eagles star Adam Hunter's mother Joanne Brown has revealed AFL executive Laura Kane reached out to her, but the grieving mother described the phone call as "too little, too late".

Mrs Brown also accused the league of a brain injury "cover up", dubbing it "disgusting".

The call to Mrs Brown came four weeks after Four Corners reported Adam Hunter was one of 33 Australian Rules players to have been diagnosed with the degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), exposing the scale of the AFL's brain trauma crisis.

Adam Hunter was diagnosed with a degenerative brain disease after his death in February 2025. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

The Four Corners investigation has since triggered a WorkSafe Victoria investigation into the AFL over player safety and concussion management during contact training.

Mrs Brown told Four Corners she had not heard from the AFL since her son's death in February 2025 and subsequent CTE diagnosis.

Hunter was a West Coast Eagles premiership player and played 151 games.

But last week Mrs Brown said Ms Kane called and said the AFL had initially failed to reach out because the clubs "handled" grieving families "very well".

Joanne Brown described a phone call from Laura Kane, pictured, as "too little, too late". (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

"I said to [Ms Kane], 'It's been 17 months since Adam passed', and said this should have been done in the first month," Mrs Brown said.

"I said, 'Why didn't someone call then?'"

"Laura said, 'Oh, we thought the clubs handled this thing very well.'

"I said, 'But they play for you. You're the AFL. They play for you.'

"[Laura replied], 'Oh yes, I’ll take that on board and forward it on.'

"But it's too late. Too little too late."

Mrs Brown said Ms Kane told her the AFL was continuing to improve player health and safety and said it intended to reduce contact in training from this pre-season on in an attempt to decrease a footballer's exposure to repetitive hits.

CTE is linked to repetitive hits to the head and body.

A coroner looking into the death of former Richmond player Shane Tuck, who died by suicide at 38 and had CTE, recommended the AFL reduce contact in training back in 2023.

If you or someone you know needs help, call: Police: 000 (Triple Zero) in an emergency

Lifeline: 13 11 14

MensLine Australia: 1300 789 978

Suicide Call Back Service: 1300 659 467

Beyond Blue: 1300 224 636

SANE: 1800 187 263

Shane Tuck took his own life after receiving repeated head knocks as a footballer and boxer The coroner investigating footballer Shane Tuck's death says the AFL should limit contact training sessions to reduce the risk of concussion.

Mrs Brown told the AFL that the league had failed to act fast enough on the coroner's key recommendation.

"She was going on about what they're trying to do to combat head injuries and I said, 'But wasn't that in 2023 that you were supposed to stop physical contact at training?'

"And she goes, 'Yes, but we're working on it.'

"I said, 'That's three years ago. How many players have been affected in those three years?

"And she just waffled on like she did in the interview … that Four Corners did and I just went, 'They're just trying to cover up or make up' … and it's just disgusting."

The Herald Sun on Thursday revealed Geelong player Jake Kolodjashnij, with a history of concussion, had been presented with and signed a waiver.

The document Kolodjashnij signed waived his legal responsibility for future on-field head trauma.

Geelong dumped the waiver after the Herald Sun report. The AFL said it had not approved the arrangement.

Cats avoid sanction Geelong will not be penalised by the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

However, the agreement was signed off by Geelong's board, which was headed by the current AFL Commission chair, Craig Drummond.

Mrs Brown said she found the story upsetting and believed her son would have done the same, and signed a waiver, despite his history of head injuries.

"I felt disgusted, absolutely disgusted that that [waiver] was allowed to go ahead," she said.

"How can that go ahead?

"And gutted in my heart. I know Adam would have done the same thing [signed it]. Because you know how much they want to play, right?"

In a statement on Thursday night, the AFL and the AFL Players Association said it had not approved the agreement.

It also said Geelong was removing it and all other clubs would be advised not to strike similar deals with "at-risk" players to exonerate themselves from future legal action.

Mrs Brown's statement comes just a month after Adam Hunter's "grieving best mate" Dave Andrews penned an open letter to the AFL Commission saying it had "failed" in its duty of care to players.

"You have failed him," Mr Andrews wrote in the five-page letter that touched on Hunter's sacrifice for the game and pleaded for the AFL leadership to better inform its players of the CTE risk.

Mr Andrews is yet to receive a response from the AFL Commission.

The AFL has been contacted for comment.

World.title: The unexpected day jobs of Australia's female footballers
World.content:
When Caitlin Reid is not re-arranging her patient's vital organs you will find her on the training field.

Such is life for many professional female athletes, whose sporting income falls short of providing a sustainable living.

"A lot of us [AFLW players] don't earn enough to survive on the footy alone," she said.

The 29-year-old's typical day starts from first light at the SCG working on her ruck craft with the football.

After midday is usually when she heads off to St Vincent's Hospital to start her shift as a surgical registrar working on the frontline of patient care.

"I'm usually working if not seven days a week, six days a week," Reid said.

Caitlin Reid trains with the Sydney Swans several days a week while balancing her job as a surgical registrar. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Growing up, girls' football didn't exist for Reid. It was not until halfway through her medical degree that she discovered the league.

Initially the tall ruck said her passion was in basketball, but COVID cancelled the NBL1 star's season with the Albury Wodonga bandits.

So Reid took a chance playing in an AFL Nines competition to maintain her fitness through the season.

"By the time basketball was ready to go back I loved footy more than I loved basketball," she said.

'Double life'

Emily Pease followed her two passions in football and love for animals to get the best of both worlds. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Emily Pease is performing the same juggling act as a winger for GWS while wrangling wildlife at Sydney's Taronga zoo.

"It's my double life. I'll start with meetings, a gym session and a field session with the Giants, then flip it to the zoo greeting guests and interacting with the animals," Pease said.

"It's actually really cool having footy life and also having something outside of it which I'm really passionate about."

The 24-year-old started playing Aussie rules in Canberra and had the opportunity to train with the Giants academy before making her way to the team.

GWS Giants winger Emily Pease trains several days a week while balancing her job at Taronga Zoo. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Most of her co-workers at the zoo do not know about her double life.

"A lot of my colleagues kind of just go 'wow'. No-one really expects that I'm playing footy. It's like I'm revealing a superpower," Pease said.

She hopes to be a full-time zookeeper one day, preferably working with primates.

'It's a team sport'

According to data, the average wage of an AFLW player in the 2026 season is $79,414. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

The latest data from the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) tracked that 3 per cent of AFLW players work full-time outside of playing on the field, down from 6 per cent last year.

Across 540 listed players in the women's league an additional 62 per cent work part-time or casual jobs.

And according to AFLPA data, the average wage of an AFLW player in the 2026 season is $79,414.

From 2027 AFLW players will move from the current four-tier system pay to a salary cap model similar to the men. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"Some people ask why I do both jobs. I think for me it's a bit of an outlet," Pease said.

"I'm able to take my mind off footy when I'm at the zoo and vice versa.

"I think just being given the opportunity to follow my passions. I had a passion for footy and for animals".

Reid has not had a holiday in two and half years, not because she does not want to, but because she has used most of her annual leave to accommodate her other career.

AFL strikes historic joint collective bargaining agreement The five-year collective bargaining agreement covering male and female players features significant wage rises and a longer AFLW season.

"There's certainly an element of guilt I feel playing football because I'm not at the hospital and we are short-staffed as is everywhere in New South Wales," Reid said.

"My co-workers have to work extra hours because I'm not there. I love my job at the hospital but I also love my job at the club.

"I've said it before, medicine is a team sport and the closeness you feel towards your footy teammates is the closeness I feel towards my co-workers."

The 11th AFLW season begins this Sunday with a clash between St Kilda and Carlton at Docklands Stadium.

World.title: Travis Head pips star duo to win second-straight Allan Border Medal
World.content:
Travis Head has pipped fellow Ashes hero Alex Carey to claim a second consecutive Allan Border Medal.

During a function in Brisbane on Friday night, held six months later than normal due to scheduling conflicts, the star batter was again crowned Australia's leading male cricketer.

Head had 153 votes, just ahead of his South Australian teammate Alex Carey on 152.

Player of the Ashes, Mitchell Starc, finished third on 150 votes despite having ditched one of the three international formats.

Head pipped Carey and Starc to the gong. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Still a force in Tests and ODIs, Starc ended his T20 international career last September in a bid to extend his red-ball career.

Starc won the Shane Warne Test player of the year award, while Mitchell Marsh took out the ODI award.

Big-hitting Tim David was named Australia's best T20 player.

Head joins Ricky Ponting, Michael Clarke, Shane Watson, Steve Smith and David Warner as multiple winners of the Allan Border Medal, which was first handed out in 2000.

The 32-year-old made 30 appearances for Australia across all three formats during the 2025/26 season, scoring 1,437 runs.

Head belted a famous 123 from 83 balls to guide Australia to a stunning victory in the opening Ashes Test in Perth.

He took that form into his home Test in Adelaide, flailing 170 in a memorable partnership with Carey.

During a career-best season, Carey scored 1,079 runs in 24 games across all formats.

Carey hit a stunning century at the Adelaide Oval, while his glovework during the Ashes was exceptional with 28 dismissals.

Normally held during a gala event in Melbourne at the end of summer, the Allan Border Medal was delayed due to organisers wanting the cricketers to be in the room for it.

Last year, the all-conquering women's team attended the event, but the men's players were in Sri Lanka for a Test tour, so Head had to accept the medal via video.

Earlier this year, Annabel Sutherland won a second-consecutive Belinda Clark Award and was also named the women's ODI player of the year.

AAP

World.title: Ruthless Lions send ominous warning to AFL rivals by dismantling Hawks
World.content:
Jarrod Berry (left) and Ryan Lester (right) celebrated their milestone matches in style as the Lions recorded a 67-point win. (Getty Images)

Brisbane has bounced back from last week's thumping by Carlton to thrash Hawthorn by 67 points at the Gabba.

Led by Kai Lohmann's five-goal haul, the premiers stayed firmly in the top four hunt with a convincing 18.17 (125) to 8.10 (58) win over the third-placed Hawks.

The victory was a perfect response to the 76-point loss to the Blues as the Lions celebrated a double milestone night with Jarrod Berry making his 200th AFL appearance and veteran defender Ryan Lester marking his 250th AFL game with a late goal that delighted the sell-out crowd.

Defeat for Sam Mitchell's team ends a four-game winning run ahead of next weekend's clash with Collingwood at the MCG and will raise questions heading into the finals about their genuine premiership credentials.

In a week where his own visit to Magpies HQ was a focus, Lachie Neale was a standout for the Lions with 35 disposals, seven marks, eight tackles and six clearances.

As well as Lohmann, the Lions had four multiple goalkickers with Logan Morris kicking four majors in the first half, Charlie Cameron booting three and Eric Hipwood scored two including a booming third-quarter shot from well outside 50.

Will Ashcroft had a game-high 39 disposals including 13 score involvements while Harris Andrews delivered another defensive masterclass, snaffling 10 marks as the Hawks forward line struggled to get clean ball all night.

Hawthorn was no match for the rampant reigning premiers at the Gabba. (Getty Images)

The Hawks though were also guilty of missing crucial chances in the opening two quarters with Harry Morrison and Sam Butler both offending as the Lions surged into a winning position.

The hosts were only six clear at the end of the first term but scored three quickfire goals at the start of the second to break the game open and never looked back, the Hawks unable to mount any meaningful resistance.

In the end Jack Gunston finished with three majors while Josh Ward had 28 disposals but it was a disappointing night for the Hawks who were simply second-best across the park.

AAP

World.title: New jumper revealed as NRL grants Perth Bears salary concessions
World.content:
The NRL's newest side, the Perth Bears, have unveiled their inaugural playing jersey on the same day they were granted salary cap concessions ahead of their entry to the competition in 2027.

In an event coordinated between Perth and North Sydney, where the unveiling was live-streamed, the Bears revealed the jersey by dropping the design from the famous WACA Ground light towers.

The design, which features red hoops on a black background, pays homage the North Sydney Bears, which left the NRL at the end of the 1999 season and currently play in the NSW Cup competition.

Peter V'landys (second from left) announced the concessions alongside WA Premier Roger Cook (speaking), Bears CEO Anthony De Ceglie, and Perth coach Mal Meninga (left). (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

The unveiling of the jersey marks a major step towards the Bears' entry into the NRL, which club chief executive Anthony De Ceglie said was on track to have 35,000 members by the beginning of the 2027 season.

Salary boost

In a big boost to the club, Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys announced the Bears would be granted a concession for signing a marquee player.

"They will be given a 20 per cent dispensation for any player above a million dollars [salary]," V'landys said.

"If the player is worth $1.5 million, they can pay another 20 per cent from a sponsor and that won't be counted in the salary cap.

" So that gives them the opportunity to get somebody because they've got a 20 per cent bonus for that player from the sponsor. "

The Perth Bears will play in the 2027 NRL season. (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

Additionally, the Bears will have first rights to any player who wants to leave their club but is under contract for 2027.

"You may have a marquee player that's not happy in a particular club and the club and the player want to separate. That player can only go to Perth in the first instance," V'landys said.

"There will be some good players that will come up and be given the opportunity to play in Perth."

The concessions will help the Bears land a high-profile player, which has so far being lacking in their signings.

Meninga happy with progress

Bears inaugural coach Mal Meninga says he is "really happy" with the club's progress to date and talked down the need for a marquee player.

"We've worked within the conditions of obviously our entry into the NRL and you know … let me be frank with this … I'm really excited about the roster we've built," he said.

"You look through the team, we've got some high-profile players already.

"We've certainly got players of the future, there's no doubt.

"I really appreciate Peter and the club's great concessions, but I'm really happy with where we are at the moment."

Bellamy excited

Veteran Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy said the arrival of the Bears was exciting for the league.

And he said the club was in good hands with coach Mal Meninga steering the ship.

"I worked with Mal, I played with Mal and I know the amount of work that he puts in and the amount of work he will put into the coaching," he said.

"I'm sure it will be a very successful venture."

The Storm has already seen two of their players, Nick Meaney and Tyran Wishart, sign on with the Bears, but the coach was magnanimous about their departure.

Tyran Wishart of the Storm will line up for the Bears next season. (AAP: Morgan Hancock)

"They're very excited to be coming over here," he said.

"They're obviously doing what they think's best for them and best for their families.

"They're still doing a great job for us.

"That's just the way the game is."

World.title: 'Doesn't look great': Fears Penrith captain could miss rest of NRL season
World.content:
Penrith captain Isaah Yeo may miss the rest of the NRL season after injuring his pectoral muscle, while the Sydney Roosters joined the Panthers on top of the table after defeating the Canterbury Bulldogs.

Yeo came off in the first half of Penrith's 28-12 loss to the New Zealand Warriors in Auckland on Friday night, with the Auckland-based side solidifying their status as a genuine premiership threat in 2026.

Yeo was clutching his pectoral muscle after reeling out of a tackle, with scans needed to confirm if he has sustained a tear.

Should scans confirm a pectoral tear, he could be out for the rest of the season.

"It doesn't look great," Panthers coach Ivan Cleary said during his press conference.

"Obviously Yeoy's a big loss and hard to replace, but that's how it goes.

"If that's the case, we'll have to (replace him)."

The Roosters have joined the Panthers on 36 points at the top of the NRL ladder, surviving a scare to pip the Bulldogs 20-18.

The Roosters held an 8-2 lead at half-time, but the Bulldogs scored three tries in 11 minutes to take an 18-8 lead with 25 minutes to play.

But two quick tries in the final 15 minutes for the Roosters earned them a hard-fought win.

Meanwhile, Craig Bellamy says he will be coach of the Melbourne Storm in 2027, despite recent health issues.
